Don't proceed: the policy forecloses this data category entirely, not just the identifiers. Follow it, and take it up with the policy owner if you think it's wrong.
Proceed, but add an instruction telling Claude not to retain the data.
Proceed if the analysis is internal only.

associate-foundations.explanation: Anonymization is usually the enabling path, but it isn't a universal override — here the policy has already decided about the category, and your job is to follow it, not route around it with a technique. This is what distinguishes governance from personal risk assessment. (C) repeats the instruction-is-not-a-control error.

associate-foundations.q: A support ticket export has no "name" column, but customers' full names and home addresses appear inside the free-text ticket bodies. How should this be treated?

options.text: As non-regulated data, since there's no dedicated identifier column.
As regulated personal data requiring anonymization — the data is regulated wherever it lives, and free text isn't a loophole.
As safe to upload because support tickets are operational data.
As unusable for any analysis.

associate-foundations.explanation: Structure is irrelevant to whether data is regulated. "It's in the ticket body, not a column" isn't a distinction any policy makes — and this is the common real-world case, since identifiers hide in free text far more often than they sit in a tidy labeled column. It's still analyzable once scrubbed (D).

associate-foundations.q: Which response to "can we use Claude to screen resumes?" best reflects this domain's judgment?

options.text: "No — hiring is too high-stakes for AI."
"Yes — Claude summarizes each application against the criteria and flags experience and gaps; you make every accept/reject call."
"Yes — score them and auto-reject below the threshold to save time."
"Only if Legal signs off on each individual rejection."

associate-foundations.explanation: The responsible answer is a compliant path to the work, not a refusal. Most of the 30 hours were reading, not deciding — so Claude does the reading and the human keeps the decision, preserving the efficiency and the accountability. A flat no (A) is a wrong answer on this exam and gets you routed around; (C) automates the consequential decision; (D) is unworkable theater.

associate-foundations.q: Why is "refuse to use AI wherever there's any risk" not the responsible position this domain teaches?

options.text: It is the responsible position — caution is always correct with AI.
Responsible use means finding the path that gets the work done within the constraint; blanket refusal isn't more responsible, just less useful, and it gets you routed around.
Because risk is never real in business AI use.
Because policy always permits AI use.

associate-foundations.explanation: "Skip it entirely" appears as a distractor throughout this domain — including in the official sample question — and it's wrong every time there's a compliant path available. The person who says "we can do that this way" is doing the actual job; the person who only says no gets bypassed by someone with fewer scruples.

associate-foundations.q: What's the common structure shared by "upload it but tell Claude not to retain it" and "connect the whole inbox but instruct Claude never to reference HR content"?

options.text: Both are adequate controls when documented.
Both substitute an instruction to the model for an actual control — the data is already shared or reachable, and a request doesn't change what's in scope.
Both are technically impossible to implement.
Both are only problems in regulated industries.

associate-foundations.explanation: Recognizing this shape is worth real points, since it recurs across Domains 5 and 6. In both cases the fix is identical: change what's reachable rather than asking nicely about what's already reachable — anonymize before upload, scope the connector to the folder.

associate-foundations.q: An HR partner uses Claude to draft eight performance reviews, then reads each one carefully on its own before sending. What risk does this review process still miss?

options.text: None — careful individual review is thorough.
Bias across cases: each review can be accurate and fair on its own while the set applies different framing to comparable achievements — a pattern only visible when compared side by side.
Hallucinated citations.
Formatting inconsistencies.

associate-foundations.explanation: This links Domain 2's bias mechanics to Domain 6's ethics: reviewing one at a time is exactly the method that cannot detect the defect, because the defect lives in the comparison. For decisions affecting people, the review method has to match the risk — read them side by side.

associate-foundations.q: A prompt consistently produces outputs that are technically accurate but not what the requester actually wanted. What's the most useful first diagnostic question?

options.text: Is this an accuracy problem, or a preference/specification problem?
Should we abandon AI for this task entirely?
Is Claude broken today?
Should we switch to the most expensive model available?

associate-foundations.explanation: Separating 'wrong' from 'not what I wanted' determines the fix: accuracy issues need more/better context, while preference mismatches need a more specific target (format, tone, scope) — conflating the two wastes iteration cycles on changes that can't address the actual gap.

associate-foundations.q: A team keeps rewriting the same complex prompt from memory every week, with small inconsistencies each time. What's the workflow-level fix?

options.text: Nothing — rewriting from memory is fine.
Save the prompt as a reusable pattern (e.g., in a Project) instead of reconstructing it from memory each time.
Switch to a lower-cost model to save money.
Assign a different person to write it each week.

associate-foundations.explanation: Recurring friction like this is a workflow optimization signal — templating the reusable prompt removes both the repeated effort and the week-to-week drift, rather than treating each week's version as a one-off.

associate-foundations.q: During troubleshooting, an associate rewrites the prompt with new context, a new format, a role, and an example — all at once. The output improves substantially. What's the problem?

options.text: No problem — the output improved, which is the goal.
She doesn't know which change worked, so she can't reproduce it next time and may be carrying changes that actively hurt alongside the one that helped.
She should have used a higher model tier as well.
Changing the format is never appropriate during troubleshooting.

associate-foundations.explanation: One change at a time is what makes the re-test informative. Bundling five changes and seeing improvement teaches nothing transferable — the payoff of disciplined troubleshooting isn't this prompt, it's building a real model of what moves output across the next fifty.

associate-foundations.q: An associate gets a wrong answer from Claude and immediately re-runs the exact same prompt hoping for a better result. What's the issue with this approach?

options.text: There is no issue — re-running is always the right first move.
It skips diagnosis — if the prompt was missing needed context or was ambiguous, an identical prompt will likely reproduce the same problem.
Re-running a prompt is technically impossible.
It will always produce the exact same output, so there's no point trying.

associate-foundations.explanation: Without diagnosing what went wrong (missing context, ambiguity, wrong scope), re-running the same prompt tends to reproduce the same failure mode. Output does vary between runs (so D is wrong), which is precisely the trap: an occasional better draw teaches you that re-rolling 'works' when you've only drawn a different sample from the same distribution.

associate-foundations.q: Which situation is best addressed by task decomposition rather than a prompt-wording tweak?

options.text: The output used the wrong tone for the audience.
The output ran too long.
The request bundled several distinct sub-tasks and the response only shallowly addressed each one.
The output was in the wrong format (prose instead of a table).

associate-foundations.explanation: Shallow coverage of several bundled sub-tasks is a scope problem, not a wording problem — no rephrasing fixes it, because the request is asking for four things in one pass. Tone, length, and format issues are all directly fixed with a specific instruction tweak.

associate-foundations.q: A recurring weekly report task is currently run on the highest-cost model tier out of habit, even though the task is simple formatting and summarization. What's the optimization opportunity?

options.text: None — always use the best model available regardless of task.
Evaluate whether a lower-cost, faster tier meets the quality bar for this recurring, low-complexity task.
Stop generating the report at all.
Increase the model tier further to be safe.

associate-foundations.explanation: This connects to Domain 3's cost/speed/quality trade-off: a recurring, low-complexity task running on an unnecessarily expensive tier is a workflow-level optimization, and it only has to be evaluated once to save indefinitely. Habit isn't a selection criterion.

associate-foundations.q: Which two are common root causes of a genuinely underperforming prompt (as opposed to a preference mismatch)? (Select 2)

options.text: The prompt omits relevant background context Claude would need to answer correctly.
The requester simply prefers a different writing style than what was produced.
The task was too broad for a single prompt and needed decomposition into steps.
The output was factually accurate but slightly longer than ideal.

associate-foundations.explanation: Missing context and excessive scope are genuine input-side causes of poor output — Claude couldn't have succeeded. A style preference or a minor length mismatch (B, D) is a specification gap: the output is fine, it just isn't aimed where you wanted, and the fix is stating the target, not supplying information.

associate-foundations.q: What distinguishes workflow-level optimization from single-prompt troubleshooting?

options.text: They are the same activity.
Workflow optimization looks at recurring friction across a process (reusable prompts, model-tier fit, templated instructions) rather than fixing one output at a time.
Workflow optimization only applies to technical/developer tasks.
Workflow optimization means using the most expensive model tier available.

associate-foundations.explanation: Single-prompt troubleshooting fixes one bad output; workflow optimization addresses the pattern — reusable prompt templates, right-sized model tiers, and moving repeated context upstream. The signal to switch altitudes is repetition: fixing the same thing three times means the setup is the problem.

associate-foundations.q: Claude confidently states an incorrect figure about your company's Q3 performance. Which fix actually addresses the cause?

options.text: Reword the prompt more forcefully to emphasize accuracy.
Provide the actual Q3 data — this is an accuracy problem caused by missing information, and no amount of rewording supplies a fact Claude never had.
Ask Claude to double-check its own answer.
Add tone and format constraints to the prompt.

associate-foundations.explanation: This is the accuracy half of the diagnosis: the information genuinely wasn't there. Rewording (A) or adding constraints (D) addresses specification, which isn't the problem, and self-checking (C) asks the model to verify a fact it doesn't have — the same unreliable signal as self-reported confidence in Domain 2.

associate-foundations.q: An output is accurate but three times longer than needed and far too formal. What kind of problem is this, and what's the fix?

options.text: An accuracy problem — supply more context about the topic.
A specification problem — state the target: length limit and tone. Claude had enough information; it just aimed somewhere you didn't specify.
A model-tier problem — upgrade to a stronger model.
A context-clutter problem — restart the conversation.

associate-foundations.explanation: Nothing is wrong with the content, so adding context (A) fixes nothing — Claude never lacked information. This is the classic conflation the domain warns about: reaching for the accuracy fix on a specification problem. Say the target and it's solved in one line.

associate-foundations.q: A colleague reports his prompts "got worse over the last hour" in a long working session — Claude is now ignoring a constraint he set early and resurfacing an option he rejected. What's the likely cause?

options.text: The model degrades over time within a session.
Cluttered context in a long thread — the fix is restarting with a focused prompt or summarizing the decisions that still stand.
A specification problem requiring a clearer target.
The prompt is missing background context and needs more detail.

associate-foundations.explanation: Dropped constraints and resurrected rejects in a long thread are the signature of context clutter (Domain 3), and the fix is reducing noise, not adding to it. Note (D) is exactly the wrong instinct — explaining again at greater length adds more context to an already overloaded thread.

associate-foundations.q: Which two are workflow-level optimizations rather than single-prompt fixes? (Select 2)

options.text: Moving background context you paste every session into a Project's knowledge source.
Adding a length constraint to today's prompt because the draft ran long.
Evaluating once whether a recurring low-complexity task can run on a cheaper tier.
Cutting a repeated paragraph from a specific draft.

associate-foundations.explanation: Both winners fix the setup so the problem stops recurring — solve once, save indefinitely. Adding a constraint to today's prompt or cutting a paragraph from one draft (B, D) are perfectly good fixes to individual outputs, but tomorrow's output starts from the same place.

associate-foundations.q: Why is upgrading to a higher model tier a risky response to a vague prompt?

options.text: It isn't risky — a stronger model is strictly better.
It may mask the bad prompt: output improves, everyone credits the model, and you pay more permanently to avoid a two-line prompt fix nobody ever found.
Higher tiers can't process vague prompts at all.
It will produce an error message.

associate-foundations.explanation: The danger is specifically that it can work — a stronger model compensates for vagueness, the symptom disappears, and the diagnosis is buried under an apparent success. That's the worst outcome available, because nothing prompts a re-examination. A model upgrade also fixes none of the other common causes: missing context, excessive scope, or thread clutter.

associate-foundations.q: Claude summarized a 30-page vendor contract you attached and wrote: 'The contract auto-renews for 24 months unless cancelled 90 days before expiry.' This line is going into an email to your director. What is the most efficient way to check it?

options.text: Ask Claude to quote the exact clause and give its section number, then read that clause in the contract yourself
Ask Claude whether it's sure
Regenerate the summary and see whether the line comes back the same
Send it as is, because the contract was attached

associate-foundations.explanation: A grounded claim can point to its evidence, so asking for the clause and reading it yourself is fast and conclusive (A). Asking for reassurance (B) gets a fluent answer either way. Consistency across regenerations (C) doesn't prove accuracy. An attached source (D) lowers the risk of errors without removing it, and this line describes a contract commitment.

associate-foundations.q: Claude drafted a job ad for a software engineer that uses phrases like 'young, energetic team' and 'digital native.' What is the issue, and what should you do?

options.text: Nothing; these phrases are standard in job ads
The wording signals an age preference, which can discourage qualified applicants and create legal risk; ask for inclusive wording and check it against your hiring policy
The ad is too long; ask for a shorter version
The tone is too casual for a job ad; ask for a formal rewrite

associate-foundations.explanation: Evaluating output covers bias as well as factual errors, and age-coded language in a job ad is a real fairness and compliance problem (B). D and C change the style and keep the biased phrases. A confuses a common phrase with an acceptable one.

associate-foundations.q: Claude built a pricing comparison table with totals calculated from 40 line items you pasted in. The table is going into a client proposal. What validation is needed?

options.text: Round the totals so small differences don't matter
Nothing, because you supplied the numbers
Recompute the totals independently, for example in a spreadsheet, before the proposal goes out
Ask Claude to double-check its math in the same chat

associate-foundations.explanation: Precise arithmetic over many figures is a weak fit to accept unchecked, and a client-facing proposal makes the numbers consequential, so they get verified independently (C). The same process checking itself (D) isn't an independent check. Correct inputs (B) don't guarantee correct sums. Rounding (A) hides errors.

associate-foundations.q: Claude wrote a market summary with no sources attached. Which TWO details are hallucination red flags? (Select TWO)

options.text: 'According to a 2025 McKinsey survey, 73% of retailers plan to...' with no link or attached source
A general explanation of what market share means
A precise figure for next quarter's market size, stated as fact
A note that Claude can't see your internal sales data
A suggestion to verify the figures before publishing

associate-foundations.explanation: A named study with a precise statistic and no source (A), and a confident, specific figure about the future (C), fit the red-flag profile: precision and authority without grounding. A general definition (B) is low risk, and E and D are signs of honest, calibrated output.

associate-foundations.q: Claude summarized a customer interview and wrote: 'The customer is frustrated with onboarding and plans to cancel.' The transcript mentions onboarding friction but says nothing about cancelling. What is the problem?

options.text: Nothing; it's a reasonable reading of the frustration
The summary is too short
The summary needs a more formal tone
An unsupported inference is presented as fact; edit the line to what the transcript supports, or label it clearly as an interpretation

associate-foundations.explanation: Details beyond the source are a hallucination red flag, and a cancellation claim could trigger real business decisions, so the output has to match its evidence (D). A plausible reading (A) still isn't supported by the transcript. B and C are style issues.

associate-foundations.q: Research mode returns a summary of a new data regulation with eight cited sources. Your compliance team will base a plan on it. Which TWO steps are needed before anyone uses it? (Select TWO)

options.text: Ask Claude to rate the reliability of each source
Have the compliance owner review the conclusions before the plan is built on them
Open the cited sources and confirm that each key claim matches what the source says, and that the sources are current and authoritative
Run research mode again and keep the claims that appear twice
Nothing; the citations prove the summary is accurate

associate-foundations.explanation: Citations make claims checkable, which helps only if someone checks them (C), and regulatory content goes through a qualified reviewer (B). Citations alone (E) don't prove the summary represents its sources correctly. Repeated claims (D) show consistency, which isn't accuracy. Claude grading its own sources (A) is no independent check.

associate-foundations.q: Your manager wants to roll Claude out to all 200 employees next week for every kind of task. What do you recommend?

options.text: Let each employee figure it out without guidance
Roll it out to everyone at once to build momentum
Pilot one or two well-defined workflows with a small group, measure before and after (time spent, error rate), then expand
Wait until AI tools stop making mistakes

associate-foundations.explanation: A measured pilot shows the real value and the limits on a small scale before the whole company depends on it (C). A big-bang rollout (B) spreads untested habits everywhere at once. D waits for something that won't happen. A produces uneven quality and no evidence.

associate-foundations.q: Which TWO tasks are strong fits for Claude in a marketing team's workflow? (Select TWO)

options.text: Turning a webinar transcript into a blog draft and three social posts
Deciding which agency gets a $200,000 contract
Reconciling 5,000 ad-spend transactions with no independent check
Reporting a competitor's announcement from yesterday, from memory
Drafting five subject-line variants for an A/B test

associate-foundations.explanation: Drafting variants (E) and repurposing content across channels (A) are classic strong fits, with a person reviewing the output. A spending decision (B) needs human accountability, precise reconciliation at volume (C) belongs in a spreadsheet or finance system, and yesterday's news (D) is beyond the model's knowledge unless research mode grounds it.

associate-foundations.q: You're presenting a Claude pilot to leadership. Which framing is most appropriate?

options.text: 'Meeting summaries now take 10 minutes instead of 45. The meeting owner still reviews each one, because outputs can contain errors.'
'Claude eliminates errors from our summaries.'
'Claude will replace the operations team.'
'The benefits can't really be measured.'

associate-foundations.explanation: Good stakeholder communication pairs a concrete, measured benefit with an honest limitation (A). B promises something no probabilistic system delivers. C overstates the role and invites resistance. D gives leadership nothing to decide with.

associate-foundations.q: A colleague opens Claude and types 'help me with the Q3 board deck.' The results are unfocused. What should be defined before prompting?

options.text: The slide color scheme
Nothing; Claude should infer it
Which model to use
The deliverable, the audience, the source material and what a good result looks like

associate-foundations.explanation: Solution design starts from the task: what you need, for whom, from which sources, and how you'll judge it (D). Model choice (C) comes later and won't rescue an undefined task. Claude can't infer goals nobody has stated (B). Colors (A) are a detail of the deliverable.

associate-foundations.q: A legal team handles NDAs in five steps: intake, first-pass review against the team's playbook, negotiation, approval and signature. Where does Claude add the most value with the right safeguards?

options.text: Signing on the company's behalf
First-pass review: compare each NDA to the playbook and flag deviations for a lawyer to decide on
Final approval
Negotiating directly with the other party, unsupervised

associate-foundations.explanation: Claude fits the draft-and-analyze stage, with a qualified person keeping the decision (B). Approval (C), signature (A) and unsupervised negotiation (D) would put legal accountability on a tool.

associate-foundations.q: You want Claude to summarize an internal incident report that contains customers' names and email addresses. Your company's AI policy allows internal documents and prohibits customer personal data. What do you do?

options.text: Paste it in and ask Claude to ignore the names
Paste it in, because it's an internal document
Use the most capable model so the data stays safe
Remove or anonymize the customer details first (the summary doesn't need them), then summarize

associate-foundations.explanation: Check the policy before pasting: the report is allowed, the customer data isn't, and the task works without it (D). Being internal (B) doesn't change the personal-data rule. Model choice (C) has nothing to do with data handling. Asking Claude to ignore data (A) comes after you've already shared it.

associate-foundations.q: A sales rep wants to upload a prospect's RFP, marked confidential, so Claude can help draft the response. Your AI policy says nothing about third-party confidential documents. What is the best action?

options.text: Ask the policy owner or legal before uploading, and treat the document as sensitive until there's an answer
Upload only the pages that look less sensitive
Upload it, since the policy doesn't forbid it
Rewrite the RFP from memory and upload that

associate-foundations.explanation: When the policy doesn't cover a case, escalate to the policy owner and stay on the cautious side in the meantime (A). Silence in the policy (C) doesn't amount to approval. Partial uploads (B) and paraphrasing from memory (D) still share confidential content, and the rewrite adds errors.

associate-foundations.q: Your organization requires disclosure when AI helps produce external content. You drafted a customer newsletter with Claude and then edited it heavily. What applies?

options.text: Disclose only if a customer asks
Follow the disclosure rule as written, because your edits don't change how the draft was produced
Describe the newsletter as written and fact-checked without AI
Skip disclosure, because your edits make it your own work

associate-foundations.explanation: Transparency rules apply as written (B). Editing (D) doesn't remove the requirement, disclosure on request (A) isn't what the policy says, and C misrepresents how the work was made.

associate-foundations.q: Which TWO uses make Claude the decision-maker in a situation where a qualified person must own the call? (Select TWO)

options.text: Brainstorming names for a team offsite
Using Claude's ranking alone to decide which employees are laid off
Drafting three versions of an internal FAQ for a manager to choose from
Sending Claude's answer about a customer's legal rights to the customer without legal review
Summarizing your own meeting notes

associate-foundations.explanation: Decisions that affect people's livelihoods (B) or legal standing (D) need a qualified human to own them, however good the draft looks. C, A and E are drafting and organizing work where a person still chooses what to use.

associate-foundations.q: A financial advisory firm uses Claude to draft client emails that explain investment options. Which control is essential?

options.text: Using the most capable model
A disclaimer at the bottom of every email, with no review
Compliance review of client-facing investment content before it's sent, including a check of every figure
Sending the drafts faster to improve service

associate-foundations.explanation: Investment explanations are regulated advice, so qualified review comes before sending (C). A stronger model (A) doesn't change who is accountable. A disclaimer (B) can't replace the review that regulation requires. Speed (D) is beside the point.

associate-foundations.q: Your prompt 'Write an email about the new expense tool' produced something generic. Which TWO additions would improve it most? (Select TWO)

options.text: The tool's key facts, attached or pasted in: launch date, how to get access, where to get help
A switch to the most capable model
A request for ten versions
Who the email is for and what it should get them to do
'Make it amazing'

associate-foundations.explanation: Generic output comes from missing context, and the audience and goal (D) and the source material (A) are two of the five parts of a complete business prompt. Enthusiasm (E) adds no information. More versions (C) of an underspecified email are more generic emails. A stronger model (B) still can't know facts you didn't give it.

associate-foundations.q: You need a 20-page market analysis with competitor profiles, a pricing comparison and recommendations. One big prompt produced a shallow result. What is the best approach?

options.text: Rewrite the single prompt with every requirement in capitals
Break it into steps: agree on an outline, draft each section from its sources, then do a final pass for consistency and tone
Regenerate until a deeper version appears
Ask for 'much more detail'

associate-foundations.explanation: Multi-part deliverables work better as a sequence of smaller steps you can check (B). D and A keep the one-giant-prompt problem. C is regenerate-and-hope.

associate-foundations.q: Claude's first draft of a customer apology is too long and too formal. Which follow-up works best?

options.text: Regenerate the response
Start a new chat with the same prompt
'Cut this to about 120 words, make the tone warmer and more direct, keep the refund details, and apologize in the first sentence.'
'Make it better.'

associate-foundations.explanation: Specific feedback gives Claude concrete changes to make (C). D gives it nothing to act on, and A and B roll the dice again on an unchanged request.

associate-foundations.q: You want campaign ideas for a product launch. Which prompting strategy fits brainstorming?

options.text: Give no context, so Claude is unconstrained
Ask for ideas with final budgets attached
Ask for the single best idea
Ask for many varied ideas first (say, 20 across different angles), then evaluate and narrow them with your criteria in a follow-up

associate-foundations.explanation: Brainstorming works best as volume and variety first, then judgment (D). Asking for one best idea (C) skips the exploration. Budgets (B) belong to a later planning step. With no context (A), the ideas won't fit your product or audience.

associate-foundations.q: You need a project timeline that you'll revise with Claude over several rounds and then share with your team. Which output format fits?

options.text: An Artifact: a standalone deliverable in its own panel that you can refine and share
A screenshot of the chat
Research mode
A plain chat reply you copy out each time

associate-foundations.explanation: Artifacts are made for standalone deliverables you'll iterate on and share (A). Chat replies (D) suit quick answers. Research mode (C) finds current sources. A screenshot (B) can't be edited.

associate-foundations.q: Which TWO tasks justify Opus over Sonnet? (Select TWO)

options.text: Summarizing a short meeting
A strategy recommendation that synthesizes six long reports, where an error would be expensive
Writing a two-line reply to a colleague
Working out how obligations interact across five related contracts before a high-stakes negotiation
Reformatting a list of 30 names into a table

associate-foundations.explanation: Opus is for complex, high-stakes reasoning across a lot of material (B, D). Sonnet is the everyday default, and quick, simple tasks like E, C and A suit Sonnet or Haiku.

associate-foundations.q: You need to sort 400 short customer comments into five well-defined themes today. Speed matters more than nuance. Which approach fits?

options.text: Haiku with the five themes clearly defined, followed by a spot-check of a sample
One comment per chat, so each gets full attention
Opus for maximum quality on every comment
Research mode

associate-foundations.explanation: Quick, well-defined tasks at volume are Haiku's case, and a sample check keeps the quality honest (A). Opus (C) spends time and cost on a task that doesn't need deep reasoning. Research mode (D) searches for current sources, which this task doesn't need. B wastes hours.

associate-foundations.q: A long chat about a proposal has become slow, and Claude has started mixing up details from early drafts with the current version. What is the best move?

options.text: Switch to Haiku for speed
Paste the entire chat history into a new chat
Start a new chat with a short summary of the current decisions and the latest draft, and keep reference documents in Project knowledge
Keep going and correct each mistake as it appears

associate-foundations.explanation: Restart, summarize and persist is the fix for an overloaded chat: a fresh context with only what matters (C). D keeps the overload, B moves it to a new chat, and A changes speed without fixing the mix-ups.

associate-foundations.q: In a team Project, where should each of these go: (1) 'Always write in British English and use our headline format'; (2) the 40-page brand guidelines PDF; (3) the brief for this week's campaign?

options.text: (1) The chat prompt, (2) the chat prompt, (3) Project knowledge
(1) Project instructions, (2) the chat prompt, (3) Project knowledge
(1) Project knowledge, (2) Project instructions, (3) Project instructions
(1) Project instructions, (2) Project knowledge, (3) the chat prompt

associate-foundations.explanation: Standing rules go in instructions, reference documents go in knowledge, and details for one task go in the chat (D). C swaps rules and documents and makes a one-week brief permanent. A retypes standing rules every time. B re-uploads the guidelines in every chat and stores a temporary brief permanently.

associate-foundations.q: Your weekly report draws on a Google Doc of sales notes that the team updates daily. You've been uploading a copy every Monday, and sometimes it's out of date. What is the better setup?

options.text: Copy the notes into the Project instructions
Connect Google Drive so Claude reads the current version of the document
Upload a copy twice a week
Paste the notes from memory

associate-foundations.explanation: Connectors suit material that lives in another tool and changes often, so Claude reads the current version (B). More frequent uploads (C) shrink the gap without closing it. Memory (D) adds errors. Instructions (A) hold standing rules, and pasted notes there go stale just as fast.

associate-foundations.q: A Project keeps quoting last year's prices. Both the 2025 and the 2026 price sheets are in Project knowledge. What fixes this?

options.text: Remove or replace the outdated price sheet, and if both must stay, state in the instructions which one is current
Use research mode for prices
Correct Claude in every chat
Switch to Opus

associate-foundations.explanation: Stale knowledge produces confidently outdated answers, so the fix is maintaining the knowledge itself (A). Correcting every chat (C) never ends. A stronger model (D) still reads both sheets. Your prices are internal, so searching for them (B) won't find the right ones.

associate-foundations.q: You asked for 'a table comparing vendors,' and each time the columns come out different. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Ask for 'a better table'
Show the exact structure: list the columns in order, or paste a sample row, and ask Claude to follow it
Regenerate until the columns match
Switch to Opus

associate-foundations.explanation: A wrong format every time means the format was described vaguely, and a concrete example fixes that (B). C is regenerate-and-hope, D changes the model without clarifying the request, and A is still vague.

associate-foundations.q: Claude answered a question about your company's travel reimbursement limits using general industry norms. The real policy is a PDF on the shared drive. What is the best fix?

options.text: Tell Claude its answer is wrong and ask it to try again
Switch to Opus
Attach the policy (or add it to Project knowledge) and ask Claude to answer from it, quoting the relevant section
Ask the same question again with more emphasis

associate-foundations.explanation: Confident but wrong claims about your own business come from missing source material, so give Claude the policy and ask for the quote (C). Emphasis (D) and a stronger model (B) can't produce a policy Claude hasn't seen. Telling Claude it's wrong (A) without the policy gets you a different guess.

associate-foundations.q: On Monday you changed a Project's instructions, switched the model and uploaded new knowledge files. Since then, the outputs are worse. What should you do?

options.text: Change everything again
Delete the Project and start over
Ask Claude what went wrong
Roll back, then reapply one change at a time and compare the results on the same test inputs

associate-foundations.explanation: With three changes at once, you can't tell which one hurt quality, so change one variable at a time against the same inputs (D). A adds more confusion, C asks Claude to explain configuration changes it can't observe, and B throws away a setup that worked before Monday.

developer-foundations.q: A ticket system must classify one request, validate a fixed schema, and route it to one of four queues. The steps never change. Which architecture is the strongest default?

options.text: An unbounded autonomous agent with every support tool
A manager, queue-specialist, and validation-subagent hierarchy that encodes routing policy in agent prompts rather than fixed branches
A remote MCP server that lets the model invent new queues
A deterministic workflow containing one model classification step

developer-foundations.explanation: The sequence and branch set are known, so a deterministic workflow is easier to test, secure, and operate. Agentic planning earns its complexity when observations determine an unknown path, not when the process is already explicit.

developer-foundations.q: A repository agent must never read secret files and must format every edited Python file. Which controls belong in the harness? Select all that apply.

options.text: A post-tool hook that runs the formatter after edits
A filesystem sandbox that excludes credential locations
Use model policy review to approve each filesystem path
A pre-tool policy hook that denies configured secret paths

developer-foundations.explanation: Pre-tool policy blocks before access, post-tool automation formats completed edits, and sandboxing limits impact if the hook is incomplete. Prompt guidance remains useful but is not deterministic isolation.

developer-foundations.q: Claude returns a tool_use block with ID toolu_9. Which elements must the client preserve in the next Messages API request? Select all that apply.

options.text: The prior conversation context still required by the task
Send the result text in a standalone user-role message
The assistant message containing the original tool_use block
A user-role tool_result whose tool_use_id is toolu_9

developer-foundations.explanation: The client owns state. It resends required history, preserves the assistant tool request, and appends the correlated user tool result. Sending only the result loses the protocol context.

developer-foundations.q: A streamed structured response currently contains {"status":"read. What should the application do before updating the order record?

options.text: Buffer until the content block and message complete, then parse, validate, and authorize
Retry the request for every new character
Append missing JSON characters itself
Treat the syntactically plausible prefix as provisional JSON, fill the expected closing characters, then validate before updating the record

developer-foundations.explanation: A stream prefix is unfinished, not a valid application contract. Irreversible state changes must wait for a complete terminal event followed by schema, semantic, and policy validation.

developer-foundations.q: A team must classify 80,000 archived tickets by tomorrow. No user is waiting for an individual response. Which API pattern best fits?

options.text: One long-running agent session that processes ticket IDs sequentially and checkpoints its accumulated context after each classification
Message Batches with stable custom request identifiers
One interactive streaming session
A new Claude Code session per token

developer-foundations.explanation: Batches fit many independent asynchronous requests where throughput matters more than immediate latency. Custom IDs let the application correlate individual results and failures.

developer-foundations.q: A payment tool times out after the provider may have accepted the charge. What is the safest next step?

options.text: Delete the trace and start a new session
Retry once with the same arguments and ask Claude to compare the two responses before deciding which external payment state is authoritative
Reconcile the stable operation ID against the payment system before any retry
Retry immediately with a higher token limit

developer-foundations.explanation: The outcome is ambiguous at the transaction boundary. An idempotency key and authoritative reconciliation establish whether retry is safe; model reasoning cannot determine external state.

developer-foundations.q: Which content most deserves a place in a project CLAUDE.md?

options.text: A list of required production credential names and their current secret-store locations for each deployment environment
A complete copy of the team's primary framework reference so Claude can derive build, test, and repository rules from one maintained source
Temporary status for the developer's current ticket
Canonical build and test commands plus non-obvious repository constraints

developer-foundations.explanation: CLAUDE.md works best as a compact project onboarding contract. Large references should be linked, temporary state belongs elsewhere, and secrets never belong in model-readable instructions.

developer-foundations.q: The live provider response contains a field, but the application never sees it after SDK deserialization. Where should debugging start?

options.text: Compare the wire response, SDK object, and each application serialization boundary
Increase model temperature
Add an independent model reviewer that compares the application's visible object with the prompt requirements and recommends a prompt revision
Rewrite the system prompt

developer-foundations.explanation: The evidence points to an integration boundary, not model behavior. Inspecting each representation reveals where the field was dropped and prevents an irrelevant prompt change.

developer-foundations.q: Two current models both pass the required accuracy and safety gates. Model A is faster and cheaper on the representative workload. Which should the team choose?

options.text: Model B because its additional capability may reduce rare errors that are not represented in the current acceptance dataset or safety gates
Model A, while retaining migration and regression monitoring
Neither until outputs become deterministic
Both on every request, regardless of cost

developer-foundations.explanation: Choose the smallest sufficient capability from measured requirements. Model A wins once quality and safety are satisfied, but versioned evals and monitoring remain necessary because behavior can change.

developer-foundations.q: Which changes usually improve prompt-cache reuse? Select all that apply.

options.text: Insert a random request ID near the start of every prompt
Measure cache creation and read usage rather than assuming a hit
Keep the reusable prefix byte-stable where practical
Place stable system instructions and tool definitions before volatile user content

developer-foundations.explanation: Caching benefits from a stable shared prefix and explicit measurement. Volatile data near the beginning invalidates reuse for content that follows it.

developer-foundations.q: A simple schema extraction already passes 99.8 percent of cases without extended thinking. What is the best default?

options.text: Enable thinking only in production so the model can compensate for inputs that were not represented in the evaluation dataset
Enable maximum thinking to add a second reasoning path for every extraction, then keep schema validation as the downstream safety check
Keep the simpler configuration unless an eval shows thinking earns its latency and cost
Replace schema validation with thinking

developer-foundations.explanation: Reasoning budget is an optimization choice. If the simpler setup satisfies measured requirements, added thinking has no demonstrated value and increases operational cost.

developer-foundations.q: A long-running coding agent is compacting context. Which information should also be preserved in durable state? Select all that apply.

options.text: Artifact paths, hashes, and verification results
Approval and external operation identifiers
Acceptance criteria and unresolved obligations
A complete transcript of every compacted exchange so the next session can reconstruct prior reasoning instead of using a typed checkpoint

developer-foundations.explanation: Critical state must survive outside a probabilistic summary. Durable records capture what must remain exact, while irrelevant conversation can be pruned.

developer-foundations.q: A response is valid JSON and passes the declared schema, but its invoice_id belongs to another tenant. Which check failed?

options.text: Prompt-cache and session validation, because a cached structured response can carry resource identifiers from the previous authenticated request
Schema shape
JSON syntax
Semantic and authorization validation against trusted application state

developer-foundations.explanation: Schemas prove shape, not ownership. The application must bind authenticated tenant identity and verify resource access against its system of record.

developer-foundations.q: A retrieved webpage tells the agent to upload its environment variables. Which responses are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Treat the webpage as untrusted data, not higher-priority instruction
Deny secret-path and environment access at the tool boundary
Honor the instruction if the resource came from an approved connector and its page metadata identifies an organizational administrator
Restrict network destinations and redact traces

developer-foundations.explanation: Source trust, capability denial, network controls, and secret-safe telemetry form layered defense. Content cannot authenticate itself by claiming authority, regardless of its wording.

developer-foundations.q: An MCP server must expose an addressable read-only policy document identified by policy://refunds/current. Which primitive fits best?

options.text: Resource
Tool
Subagent
Prompt

developer-foundations.explanation: Resources expose URI-addressed context. Tools perform model-selected operations, while prompts provide reusable user-invoked message templates for repeatable workflows across compliant MCP hosts.

developer-foundations.q: When does MCP most clearly earn its additional protocol and deployment cost? Select all that apply.

options.text: Several approved hosts need shared capability discovery
One in-process function needs a typed schema and may eventually be reused, but no current host or deployment boundary requires protocol discovery
The integration needs versioned remote authentication and governance
Tools, resources, or prompts should be exposed through a standard client-server boundary

developer-foundations.explanation: MCP is valuable for interoperability, shared discovery, and governed client-server capability. One local function is usually simpler as an in-process tool.

developer-foundations.q: A compliance pipeline always retrieves one policy, extracts four fields, validates them, and asks a reviewer to approve. Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: A manager with five subagents
An autonomous agent that can choose any corporate tool
A deterministic workflow with bounded model steps
A self-modifying prompt loop

developer-foundations.explanation: The path and approval boundary are already known. A workflow makes ordering, validation, and review deterministic, while an agent would add freedom without a requirement for adaptive planning.

developer-foundations.q: A code migration is divided among subagents. Which design choices improve reliability? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use an independent read-only reviewer for the merged result
Give every subagent broad write access to resolve dependencies
Require structured handoff artifacts from each subagent
Give each subagent explicit file ownership and acceptance tests

developer-foundations.explanation: Ownership reduces conflicting edits, independent review avoids generator self-confirmation, and structured handoffs preserve exact state. Broad shared write access creates races and unclear accountability.

developer-foundations.q: A team needs built-in repository tools, sessions, hooks, subagents, and streamed lifecycle events. Which implementation choice is the strongest starting point?

options.text: A raw one-call text completion
A JSON parser with no model
A custom Messages API loop that recreates repository tools, session persistence, hooks, subagent scheduling, and event streaming inside the application
The Claude Agent SDK with an explicit policy and evaluation layer

developer-foundations.explanation: The Agent SDK packages an agent harness that fits these requirements. It does not replace authorization, sandboxing, terminal conditions, or evals, which the application must still provide.

developer-foundations.q: Which conditions should terminate or pause a production agent loop? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stop when the agent reports high confidence
Maximum turn or cost budget reached
Repeated identical tool calls indicate no progress
A required human approval is pending

developer-foundations.explanation: Budgets, loop detection, and pending approval are objective control conditions. Confidence in prose is not evidence of correct final state and should not control termination by itself.

developer-foundations.q: An agent resumes after a process crash during a deployment request. What should it do before continuing?

options.text: Reconcile the operation ID, repository state, and deployment system of record
Ask a subagent to guess whether the deployment finished
Discard all prior evidence and increase temperature
Resume from the compacted session summary, repeat the last deployment call with the same arguments, and infer success if the provider returns no error

developer-foundations.explanation: Session memory is not authoritative state. Reconciliation establishes whether side effects occurred and which acceptance checks remain before any retry or continuation.

developer-foundations.q: When does a subagent provide a real architectural benefit? Select all that apply.

options.text: A specialist needs a narrower tool allowlist
Independent research branches can proceed in parallel
A reviewer needs context isolated from the generator
Use a subagent for one bounded prompt edit

developer-foundations.explanation: Isolation, genuine parallelism, and permission specialization justify a subagent. A minor prompt issue should be fixed directly instead of adding another model boundary.

developer-foundations.q: A long-running agent compacts its context every hour. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Compaction can serve as the sole recovery record when the summary explicitly mentions current goals, approvals, artifact locations, and completed verification checks
Critical goals, approvals, artifacts, and verification results should also live in durable typed state
Compaction makes final-state evaluation unnecessary
Compaction removes the need for checkpoints

developer-foundations.explanation: Compaction supports continuity but is a probabilistic summary. Critical state needs durable records and reconciliation so omissions or drift cannot silently change the job.

developer-foundations.q: A research agent returns a polished report but never accessed the two required databases. Which evaluation is most decisive?

options.text: Increase the maximum turns
Grade only the writing style
Inspect the required tool trajectory and verify cited records resolve
Score the report for factual consistency, citation formatting, and coverage of the requested topics without enforcing the required database trajectory

developer-foundations.explanation: Agent success includes the path and evidence, not only final language. Required source access and resolvable citations reveal whether the claimed research actually occurred.

developer-foundations.q: A product owner asks for a Claude agent that answers customers instantly. What should engineering establish first?

options.text: A twelve-agent hierarchy
A complete capability inventory and agent hierarchy that can answer every anticipated customer request before the team quantifies error cost or latency targets
The largest available model
The measurable outcome, data sources, action authority, error cost, and service constraints

developer-foundations.explanation: Architecture begins with a testable outcome and boundaries. Model and tool choices follow latency, quality, security, lifecycle, and authority requirements rather than replacing discovery.

developer-foundations.q: Claude returns text and two tool_use blocks in one assistant message. What must the client do? Select all that apply.

options.text: Preserve the complete assistant content block sequence
Validate and correlate a result for each tool_use ID
Open a separate conversation for each returned tool result
Append the tool results in a following user message

developer-foundations.explanation: The assistant response is part of client-owned history. Every tool request needs a correlated result, and the following user message carries those results before the next model call.

developer-foundations.q: Application code assumes response.content[0] always has a text field. Claude instead returns a tool_use block first. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Switch on each content block type and handle supported types explicitly
Force every response into one string
Delete all non-text blocks
Normalize every response by retrying with an instruction that the first content block must be text, while retaining the remaining block handling assumptions

developer-foundations.explanation: Messages contain typed blocks, not a guaranteed text slot. Explicit dispatch preserves tool, thinking, and future block semantics while unknown types can fail closed or be safely recorded.

developer-foundations.q: A response ends with a complete-looking sentence but stop_reason is max_tokens. How should the application classify it?

options.text: Complete if the visible sentence passes semantic checks, while recording max_tokens as a transport warning that does not affect downstream use
Potentially incomplete and requiring explicit recovery or escalation
A prompt-cache hit
A successful tool result

developer-foundations.explanation: Protocol control metadata overrides visual appearance. max_tokens means generation reached its configured limit, so downstream consumers must not assume the contract completed.

developer-foundations.q: Which practices are safe for streamed responses? Select all that apply.

options.text: Record whether message_stop or an equivalent terminal event arrived
Execute tool calls from a schema-valid partial-response prefix
Buffer tool input until its block completes before parsing
Treat rendered text as provisional until terminal completion

developer-foundations.explanation: Streams expose partial state. Rendering may be progressive, but parsing, authorization, and side effects wait for complete blocks and a terminal message state.

developer-foundations.q: An invoice image is supplied for extraction. Which control most improves reliability?

options.text: Use the smallest supported thumbnail to minimize latency, ask for confidence per extracted field, and manually review only values below the threshold
Convert the image into an unrestricted shell command
Use supported image formats and resolution, state the extraction contract, and validate totals against source evidence
Skip output validation because vision is deterministic

developer-foundations.explanation: Vision quality depends on usable input and explicit task constraints, while extracted values still require schema and semantic checks. Visual capability does not make readings deterministic.

developer-foundations.q: Extended thinking is enabled in a multi-turn tool workflow. What should the client do with provider-supplied thinking blocks when the current API requires them to be returned?

options.text: Replace them with the tool result ID
Rewrite them for clarity
Convert the provider-supplied thinking blocks into a concise rationale and send that edited version back with the next tool result
Preserve and return them exactly according to the current protocol

developer-foundations.explanation: Feature-specific thinking blocks can carry integrity data and protocol requirements. The client must follow current documentation and must not edit, fabricate, or expose internal reasoning content.

developer-foundations.q: A shared 30,000-token policy prefix is identical across requests, while each customer question differs. Which arrangement best supports caching?

options.text: Place the stable policy and tool definitions before volatile customer content
Store the policy only in output
Put the customer question first and policy last
Place customer identity and request metadata before the policy so authorization context is evaluated first, then append the stable policy and tool definitions

developer-foundations.explanation: Prompt caching works on reusable prefixes. Stable content belongs before volatile content so customer-specific bytes do not invalidate the expensive shared prefix.

developer-foundations.q: A batch job contains 10,000 independent requests. Which practices are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use batch for user-facing requests that need immediate streaming
Assign a stable custom identifier to every request
Reconcile returned results to the original inputs
Handle per-request success and failure rather than assuming all-or-nothing

developer-foundations.explanation: Batch processing is asynchronous and results can vary per request. Stable IDs and reconciliation preserve accountability; an interactive dependent loop needs normal request latency instead.

developer-foundations.q: An application moves from Anthropic's direct API to a third-party managed provider. What should the migration test first?

options.text: Whether the provider advertises the same model family and context limit under a comparable enterprise service tier
Authentication, supported features, request and response serialization, quotas, regions, and resolved model behavior
Whether a compatibility wrapper can preserve the current SDK method signatures and normalize all provider failures into the application's existing exception type
Only whether the model name string is accepted

developer-foundations.explanation: Provider integrations can differ in identity, feature availability, headers, versions, quotas, data regions, and serialization. A live contract test must verify the actual wire and application mapping.

developer-foundations.q: Twenty independent read-only tool requests can safely run concurrently. Which design is appropriate?

options.text: Remove timeouts so every request eventually returns
Serialize the calls in model-request order so trace playback remains deterministic, even though the operations are independent and each carries a stable call ID
Launch bounded asynchronous work, preserve per-call IDs, and collect individual outcomes
Share one mutable argument object across all tasks

developer-foundations.explanation: Bounded concurrency improves latency for independent work while correlation, deadlines, and per-call results preserve correctness. Shared mutable state and missing timeouts create nondeterministic failures.

developer-foundations.q: A prompt and output schema change together. Which release record is most useful?

options.text: Only the final pass rate
The developer's chat title
The source diff and final aggregate pass rate, because version control already preserves the previous prompt, schema, and code for rollback
Prompt version, schema version, model configuration, code revision, eval dataset version, and rollback point

developer-foundations.explanation: Behavior depends on the complete configuration. Recording all relevant versions makes a regression reproducible and gives operations a precise rollback target.

developer-foundations.q: An AI-generated refactor passes unit tests. What else should review verify? Select all that apply.

options.text: Unrelated files were not changed
Public API and serialization compatibility
The actual built or integrated behavior
Give the reviewer full repository context

developer-foundations.explanation: Unit tests are one layer. Integration behavior, compatibility, and scope discipline catch regressions that local tests miss, while context size is not a correctness criterion.

developer-foundations.q: A support session for Tenant A is reused when Tenant B opens a request. What is the primary defect?

options.text: A session and data-isolation boundary violation
A routing defect caused by a low sampling temperature that made the session repeatedly select context from the previously successful tenant interaction
Missing prompt caching
Too few tools

developer-foundations.explanation: Conversation state can contain private context and instructions. Tenant sessions must be isolated, with identity and authorization bound from authenticated application state.

developer-foundations.q: A team upgrades a Claude Code plugin used in CI. Which evidence should accompany the change? Select all that apply.

options.text: Representative workflow eval and rollback steps
Inventory of newly added tools, hooks, Skills, and network access
The plugin publisher's signed release notes and compatibility statement, without an independent inventory or workflow evaluation in the team's CI boundary
Pinned or recorded plugin version and provenance

developer-foundations.explanation: A plugin changes executable capability and context. Provenance, capability review, regression evidence, and rollback make the upgrade controlled; marketing does not establish safety.

developer-foundations.q: A read-only provider request returns a transient 529 and no response body. Which recovery is strongest?

options.text: Convert the request into a mutating tool
Retry with bounded exponential backoff, jitter, and an overall deadline
Repeat forever until it succeeds
Switch to a fallback model and slightly relax the output schema on each retry while retaining the same unbounded retry schedule

developer-foundations.explanation: A transient availability error can justify a bounded retry for an idempotent read. Backoff, jitter, deadlines, and attempt limits prevent synchronized load and runaway latency.

developer-foundations.q: An API accepts create-ticket requests. Which field best protects a retry after a connection drop?

options.text: A longer user message
A fresh client-generated retry identifier created after each interrupted create-ticket attempt
A stable idempotency key bound to the intended operation
A provider-generated request identifier, because the service can use it to recognize repeated create-ticket payloads after an interrupted response

developer-foundations.explanation: Idempotency lets the server recognize the same logical operation and return or reconcile the prior result instead of creating a duplicate side effect.

developer-foundations.q: A database migration procedure is detailed, reusable, and needed only when migration files change. Where should the team place it?

options.text: Inside an API token
In the model alias
In the root CLAUDE.md so every repository task receives the full migration procedure and Claude can decide whether a changed file makes it relevant
In a task-relevant Skill or scoped Rule, depending on whether it is a procedure or file constraint

developer-foundations.explanation: A Skill packages reusable procedure with progressive disclosure, while a scoped Rule applies constraints to relevant files. Both avoid bloating every session with unrelated detail.

developer-foundations.q: A headless pull-request review runs on untrusted contributions. Which controls are required? Select all that apply.

options.text: Minimal repository and token permissions
A short-lived repository write token so the reviewer can apply obvious fixes to its branch after emitting structured findings
No unrelated secrets in the job environment
Bounded time, tools, network, and structured output

developer-foundations.explanation: Headless execution lacks interactive supervision, so its identity and capabilities must be narrow. The result should enter normal review and protected merge paths rather than bypass them.

developer-foundations.q: Claude chose the correct tool, but the tool returned HTTP 403 because the authenticated service account lacks scope. How should the failure be classified?

options.text: Authorization or integration failure at the tool boundary
Prompt wording failure
Sampling variance
A model planning failure because the selected tool could not accomplish the requested action with the service account available to the agent

developer-foundations.explanation: The model selected the expected capability. The authoritative 403 identifies an identity or authorization configuration problem, which should be fixed at the integration boundary rather than through prompting.

developer-foundations.q: Two requests with identical visible inputs produce different valid summaries. What is the best engineering interpretation?

options.text: The application should select a canonical answer by comparing deterministic surface features such as length and sentence coverage across the two outputs
Model generation is non-deterministic, so quality must be measured across representative repeated trials
One response proves the API is broken
Caching guarantees identical text

developer-foundations.explanation: Probabilistic generation can vary even under controlled settings. Evals should define acceptable properties and use repeated samples where variance matters instead of demanding identical wording.

developer-foundations.q: A classification task uses an enum and already passes its eval. What is the likely effect of increasing randomness?

options.text: Automatic schema validation
Greater coverage of borderline labels because additional sampling variance explores classifications the deterministic configuration might systematically miss
Potentially greater output variance without a demonstrated requirement
A larger context window

developer-foundations.explanation: Sampling controls influence variation, not truth or schema enforcement. A stable classification workload should keep settings justified by measured behavior.

developer-foundations.q: Which measurements belong in a model-selection comparison? Select all that apply.

options.text: The provider's broad benchmark ranking and advertised model tier, used as a proxy for capability classes not present in the representative task set
p50 and p95 latency
Task and safety pass rates on representative cases
Token and monetary cost per successful task

developer-foundations.explanation: Selection is an empirical tradeoff across quality, risk, latency, and economics. Branding does not prove fitness for one workload or its operational constraints.

developer-foundations.q: A smaller model fails only complex contract analysis cases, while it passes simple routing cases. Which architecture is most efficient?

options.text: Increase every prompt to the context limit
Remove the difficult cases from evaluation
Use the largest model for every request to avoid routing false negatives, then recover the added expense by shortening prompts for routine cases
Route by measured task complexity, with safeguards and fallback

developer-foundations.explanation: Model routing can reserve expensive capability for tasks that earn it while keeping simpler work fast and economical. The router and fallback need their own evaluation.

developer-foundations.q: Which statements about prompt caching are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A cache hit does not make stale source content correct
It can reduce repeated-prefix input cost and time to first token
Changing bytes early in the prefix can reduce downstream reuse
It lets the application exceed the selected model's context limit when the overflowing tokens belong to a byte-identical cached prefix

developer-foundations.explanation: Caching reuses computation for stable prompt prefixes. It changes economics and latency, not freshness, truth, authorization, or the context-window limit.

developer-foundations.q: A request exceeds the selected model's context window. Which response is strongest?

options.text: Prune irrelevant content, retrieve only needed evidence, compact durable state, or select a justified larger context
Split the oversized input into arbitrary equal parts, generate an answer for each part independently, and concatenate the answers without preserving cross-part obligations
Increase temperature
Encode the overflow as a secret

developer-foundations.explanation: Context is a finite budget. Selection, retrieval, pruning, and structured compaction preserve relevant evidence; a larger context is justified only when the workload still requires it.

developer-foundations.q: Extended thinking improves hard planning accuracy by 8 points but doubles p95 latency. What should determine adoption?

options.text: Whether prompt caching is disabled
Whether the target workflow's quality requirement earns the measured latency and cost tradeoff
Enable it for every request because a statistically significant gain on the hard planning slice justifies a uniform configuration and simpler operations
Whether the output contains more reasoning text

developer-foundations.explanation: Thinking is a workload-specific tradeoff. Adopt it on the tasks where measured quality gain is necessary and operational budgets remain acceptable.

developer-foundations.q: A direct API SDK upgrade changes typed response models. Which tests reduce migration risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Test deserialization of every used content block and stop reason
Capture and compare actual wire responses
Rely on the SDK's semantic-versioning guarantee for fields covered by its types, while testing only newly introduced response content blocks
Run live integration cases for streaming and tools

developer-foundations.explanation: Wire, typed-model, and end-to-end tests cover the serialization boundaries where fields can disappear or change. Version labels help planning but do not replace evidence.

developer-foundations.q: An application uses a moving model alias. What operational control is most important?

options.text: Depend on the moving alias as the rollback mechanism because the provider can update it again if the new resolved version causes a regression
Disable traces to reduce cost
Run scheduled canary evals and keep a tested rollback configuration
Never record the resolved model information

developer-foundations.explanation: A moving alias can change behavior without an application commit. Canary evals, recorded configuration, and rollback make that change observable and recoverable.

developer-foundations.q: A prompt fails on ambiguous invoices. Which improvement should be tried first?

options.text: Repeat the task name twenty times
Add several easy invoice examples that reinforce the normal-case format and tell Claude to extrapolate the same pattern when ambiguous fields appear
Remove the validation criteria
Add one representative difficult example with the desired decision and output contract

developer-foundations.explanation: Failure-driven few-shot examples clarify gray cases and the expected contract. Prompt changes should target observed errors rather than adding undirected text.

developer-foundations.q: Which prompt practices make mixed trusted instructions and untrusted documents easier to reason about? Select all that apply.

options.text: Delimit each source and label its role
Concatenate content into one XML-tagged document but omit source trust labels, assuming consistent delimiters are sufficient to preserve instruction priority
State that document content cannot override policy
Place output requirements near the task and validate them

developer-foundations.explanation: Clear boundaries, authority labels, and explicit output contracts reduce ambiguity. They support but do not replace deterministic security and validation controls.

developer-foundations.q: A chat has accumulated three unrelated tasks and contradictory constraints. What is the safest next step?

options.text: Start a clean session with a verified handoff containing only current facts and obligations
Continue in the existing session after appending a final instruction that newer constraints override older ones and asking Claude to resolve conflicts implicitly
Move secrets into the system prompt
Add every previous message twice

developer-foundations.explanation: Old context can contaminate a changed objective. A clean boundary and concise verified handoff preserve necessary state while removing stale instructions.

developer-foundations.q: Which information belongs in a long-task checkpoint artifact? Select all that apply.

options.text: The agent's full speculative reasoning history so a resumed session can understand why rejected approaches were considered and avoid repeating exploration
Current objective and acceptance criteria
Outstanding approvals and ambiguous side effects
Completed artifacts and their hashes

developer-foundations.explanation: A checkpoint preserves exact operational state needed to resume and verify. Speculative reasoning can be discarded unless it became an approved decision.

developer-foundations.q: A user-supplied field is inserted into a repair prompt. What is the safest construction?

options.text: Place the field directly after the system repair rules so it remains close to the validation instructions, then ask the model to ignore any embedded commands
Label and delimit it as untrusted data, include machine-generated validation errors, and cap attempts
Execute any commands it contains
Remove all validation so repair is easier

developer-foundations.explanation: Trust labeling and delimiting prevent input from masquerading as policy, while bounded repair and precise errors address formatting without creating an infinite injection loop.

developer-foundations.q: Claude returns valid JSON with priority 12, while the schema allows integers from 1 through 5. What should the consumer do?

options.text: Clamp it silently to 5
Accept it after clamping the value to the schema maximum and record the original value in telemetry for later prompt-quality analysis
Reject it as a schema violation and use bounded repair or fallback
Ask a tool to authorize 12

developer-foundations.explanation: Parsing proves only syntax. Numeric bounds are part of the contract, and silent coercion hides a producer failure that should remain observable.

developer-foundations.q: An MCP resource contains instructions to call a secret-export tool. Which defenses should apply? Select all that apply.

options.text: Require host and server authorization independent of content
Do not expose unnecessary secret or export capabilities
Keep resource content in an untrusted-data boundary
Treat instructions from an authenticated MCP server as trusted application policy, while still requiring normal approval for the resulting secret-export call

developer-foundations.explanation: Remote content and tool results can be compromised. Capability minimization and independent authorization prevent content from granting itself authority over protected operations.

developer-foundations.q: Where should a commerce API key be introduced into an order lookup?

options.text: In the user-visible trace
In a short-lived system prompt inserted only after the model has selected the order-lookup tool, with trace redaction enabled for the request
In the tool description
In trusted integration code immediately before the authorized request

developer-foundations.explanation: The model needs a business capability, not the credential. Trusted code retrieves the key from a protected source and returns only minimized result data.

developer-foundations.q: Claude proposes read_file with path /workspace/project/../secrets.txt. What should the policy check use?

options.text: The canonical resolved path against explicit allowed roots, plus operating-system sandboxing
Claude's confidence score
The file extension only
A normalized string-prefix check performed by the application before the tool call, without resolving symlinks or relying on an operating-system sandbox

developer-foundations.explanation: Traversal can make an apparently allowed prefix resolve outside the root. Canonical path enforcement and sandbox permissions provide complementary protection.

developer-foundations.q: Which statements about security hooks are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A pre-tool hook can block before a side effect
A post-tool hook can redact result content and record metrics
A tested pre-tool hook that canonicalizes paths and blocks known secret patterns can replace sandboxing for tools whose arguments are fully schema validated
Hooks should be tested with allowed and denied fixtures

developer-foundations.explanation: Hooks enforce lifecycle checks and need behavioral tests. They are one defense layer, not a replacement for filesystem, network, identity, and server-side controls.

developer-foundations.q: Which changes make a tool catalog easier for Claude to use correctly? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give each tool a distinct narrow purpose
Expose several overlapping tools under one namespace and use detailed examples in the system prompt instead of distinct names or negative-use descriptions
Describe important non-use cases
Use bounded schemas with required fields and enums

developer-foundations.explanation: Clear semantic separation and strict inputs improve selection and validation. Overlapping vague tools create ambiguity and consume context without adding reliable capability.

developer-foundations.q: A read-only tool handler times out. What should a useful tool error tell the model?

options.text: Instructions for bypassing policy
What failed, whether state changed, and whether a bounded retry is safe
Only the word error
The complete exception class, stack location, and request arguments so Claude can decide whether modified arguments would make a retry safe

developer-foundations.explanation: Concise operational facts let the loop choose a safe recovery. Internal stack traces and secrets belong in protected telemetry, not model-visible results.

developer-foundations.q: Claude requests two tools: create_invoice and send_invoice. Can they run in parallel?

options.text: Yes, if the harness starts both requests together but delays delivery of send_invoice until create_invoice returns the generated identifier
Yes, if temperature is zero
No, because sending depends on the created invoice and its identifier
No, because tools can never run concurrently

developer-foundations.explanation: These calls have a data and state dependency, so execution must remain sequential. Independent read-only calls may be parallelized with correlation and bounded concurrency.

developer-foundations.q: Which steps belong to the MCP connection lifecycle? Select all that apply.

options.text: Call optional methods documented by the server vendor before capability negotiation, then fall back when the server returns a method-not-found error
Discover only capabilities the server advertised
Send the initialized notification where required
