architect-foundations.explanation: Few-shot examples work by enabling the model to generalize the underlying judgment to novel patterns rather than matching pre-specified cases, and 2-4 targeted examples showing the reasoning for why one action was chosen over plausible alternatives is the documented approach. Option B misunderstands the mechanism — you can't enumerate every scenario, and volume doesn't teach a principle. Option C strips out exactly the reasoning that makes generalization possible, leaving surface pattern-matching. Option D covers the case you least needed help with.

architect-foundations.q: A batch of 500 documents completes, but 12 failed because they exceeded context limits. What's the most efficient way to handle this?

options.text: Identify the 12 failures by custom_id and resubmit only those, chunked so they fit within context limits.
Resubmit the entire batch of 500 with chunking applied to every document.
Switch the 12 failed documents to the real-time API without modification, since batch clearly can't handle them.
Discard the 12 failures — a 97.6% success rate is within normal tolerance for batch processing.

architect-foundations.explanation: custom_id fields correlate batch requests with their responses, which is exactly what lets you identify failed documents and resubmit only those with appropriate modifications such as chunking. Option B re-pays for 488 documents that already succeeded. Option C changes the API without addressing the cause — an oversized document exceeds context limits on the real-time API too. Option D silently drops data because of a fixable formatting issue.

architect-foundations.q: You must guarantee a 30-hour turnaround SLA on documents that arrive continuously, using the Message Batches API (up to 24-hour processing). What submission strategy meets the SLA?

options.text: Submit batches every 4 hours, so a document's maximum wait (up to 4 hours queued plus up to 24 hours processing) stays within 30 hours.
Submit one batch daily at midnight, since batches usually complete much faster than 24 hours.
Submit each document individually the moment it arrives, to minimize queue time.
The 30-hour SLA cannot be met with the Batches API under any submission schedule.

architect-foundations.explanation: Calculating submission frequency from SLA constraints is a documented skill: with up to 24 hours of processing and a 30-hour promise, the queue wait must stay under 6 hours, so a 4-hour submission window bounds the total safely. Option B allows nearly 24 hours of queueing before processing even starts, blowing the SLA — and "usually faster" is the exact reasoning the no-SLA caveat forbids. Option C forfeits the batching that makes the discount possible. Option D is defeatist: the math works comfortably at a 4-hour cadence.

architect-foundations.q: Your extraction pipeline uses tool_use with a strict JSON schema. Which two error types will the schema NOT prevent? (Select 2)

options.text: Invoice line items that don't sum to the stated total.
Malformed JSON with a trailing comma.
The invoice date placed in the due_date field.
An enum field containing a value outside the allowed set.

architect-foundations.explanation: Strict schemas via tool use eliminate syntax and structural errors but not semantic ones. Line items that don't sum to the total, and a correctly-typed date in the wrong field, are both perfectly valid schema-compliant JSON that happens to be wrong — catching them requires separate validation (e.g., extracting calculated_total alongside stated_total). Options B and D are exactly what the schema does prevent: syntax errors are eliminated by construction, and an out-of-range enum value violates the schema itself.

architect-foundations.q: Developers keep dismissing findings from your review bot, but you can't tell which kinds of code are triggering the bad findings. Which design change best enables systematic analysis?

options.text: Add a detected_pattern field to each structured finding recording which code construct triggered it, so dismissals can be analyzed by pattern.
Ask developers to write a free-text explanation each time they dismiss a finding.
Log the full prompt and response for every review run and read through them manually.
Increase the confidence threshold until dismissals drop to an acceptable rate.

architect-foundations.explanation: Tracking which code constructs trigger findings via a detected_pattern field is the documented mechanism for enabling systematic analysis of false-positive patterns when developers dismiss findings — it turns scattered anecdotes into aggregate data pointing at a specific prompt fix. Option B relies on busy developers writing prose and yields nothing aggregable. Option C doesn't scale and produces no structured signal. Option D suppresses the symptom while hiding the very evidence you need, and leans on poorly-calibrated self-reported confidence.

architect-foundations.q: An extraction schema needs to categorize expenses, but you know new categories will appear that you can't enumerate today. Which schema design handles this best?

options.text: An enum of known categories plus an "other" value, paired with a detail string field for the unenumerated case.
A free-text string field, so any category can be expressed.
An enum of known categories only, with required: true, forcing every expense into the closest match.
A boolean field per known category, so multiple can be set.

architect-foundations.explanation: The enum + "other" + detail string pattern is the documented approach for extensible categorization: it keeps the constrained, machine-parseable set for known cases while giving genuinely novel ones an honest escape hatch. Option B abandons constraint entirely, so the same category arrives spelled three ways. Option C forces novel cases into the nearest wrong category — the same fabrication pressure that required fields create. Option D changes the shape of the data without solving extensibility, since unknown categories still have no representation.

architect-foundations.q: Your document extraction returns empty values for required fields on a subset of documents. Investigation shows those documents structure their information differently — narrative prose rather than the structured tables in your examples. What's the most effective fix?

options.text: Add few-shot examples demonstrating correct extraction from documents with the varied formats, including the narrative-prose structure.
Mark the affected fields as nullable, since extraction clearly isn't possible from those documents.
Add a retry loop that re-requests the extraction when required fields come back empty.
Filter out narrative-format documents and route all of them to human review.

architect-foundations.explanation: Adding few-shot examples showing correct extraction from documents with varied formats is the documented fix for empty/null extraction of required fields caused by structural variety — the information is present, the model just hasn't been shown that layout. Option B misdiagnoses a solvable format problem as absent data, and would silently drop information that's actually there. Option C retries without new guidance, so the model repeats its misread. Option D abandons automation for documents the pipeline could handle with better examples.

architect-foundations.q: A team proposes adding "review your own output carefully and correct any errors before responding" to their code-generation prompt, instead of running a separate review instance. What's the flaw?

options.text: A model retains its reasoning context from generation, making it less likely to question its own decisions in the same session — self-review instructions don't remove that bias.
Self-review instructions cause the model to exceed max_tokens.
Self-review only works when tool_choice is set to "any".
There's no flaw — self-review instructions are equivalent to an independent review instance and cost less.

architect-foundations.explanation: Self-review is limited by the generating session's retained reasoning context: it already concluded its approach was right, so asking it to check invites re-deriving the same conclusion. Independent review instances without that context are documented as more effective at catching subtle issues than either self-review instructions or extended thinking. Option B invents an unrelated failure. Option C conflates structured-output configuration with review architecture. Option D asserts the equivalence the guide specifically rejects.

architect-foundations.q: Which two practices correctly describe designing a self-correcting extraction validation flow? (Select 2)

options.text: Extract a calculated_total alongside the document's stated_total so discrepancies are flagged automatically rather than silently trusted.
Add a conflict_detected boolean so internally inconsistent source data is surfaced instead of quietly resolved.
Mark every field required, so the model is never permitted to omit data.
On validation failure, resend the original request unchanged so the model gets a fresh attempt.

architect-foundations.explanation: Extracting calculated_total alongside stated_total and adding conflict_detected booleans for inconsistent source data are both documented self-correction validation designs — they catch the semantic errors strict schemas structurally cannot. Option C creates fabrication pressure: a required field the source lacks pushes the model to invent a plausible value. Option D omits the specific validation errors that make retry work at all; an unchanged request usually reproduces the same output.

architect-foundations.q: Your extraction pipeline handles several document types (invoices, receipts, purchase orders), each with its own schema, and the type isn't known until the document is read. You need guaranteed structured output on every call. Which tool_choice configuration fits?

options.text: tool_choice: "any" — the model must call one of the extraction tools but selects which schema fits the document it sees.
tool_choice: "auto" — let the model decide whether structured extraction is warranted.
Forced selection naming the invoice tool, since invoices are the most common type.
tool_choice: "any" combined with a required document_type parameter on every schema.

architect-foundations.explanation: tool_choice: "any" guarantees the model calls a tool rather than returning conversational text, while leaving the choice open — exactly right when multiple extraction schemas exist and the document type is unknown ahead of time. Option B permits a text response, forfeiting the guarantee. Option C forces the wrong schema onto receipts and purchase orders. Option D adds a redundant parameter: choosing the tool already declares the type, and making it required just adds a field the model must restate.

architect-foundations.q: A reviewer asks why your CI review prompt includes a few-shot example of code that *looks* like a bug but is an accepted local pattern, arguing the examples should only show real issues. What's the strongest justification for keeping it?

options.text: Examples distinguishing acceptable patterns from genuine issues reduce false positives while still letting the model generalize to novel cases.
It pads the prompt so the model spends more time reasoning about each finding.
Negative examples are required whenever tool_use enforces a JSON schema.
It demonstrates the output format, which positive examples cannot do.

architect-foundations.explanation: Providing few-shot examples that distinguish acceptable code patterns from genuine issues is documented as a way to reduce false positives while enabling generalization — and false positives in one category erode trust in the accurate ones, so this is high-leverage. Option B invents a mechanism; prompt length doesn't buy reasoning depth. Option C conflates few-shot prompting with schema enforcement, which are unrelated. Option D is false — any example demonstrates format; what this one uniquely teaches is the boundary between acceptable and problematic.

architect-foundations.q: A document analysis agent processes a long report and its findings summary mentions strong results in the opening and closing sections, but omits a significant caveat that appeared in the middle of the document. What effect does this most likely illustrate?

options.text: A hallucination.
The "lost in the middle" effect — models reliably process information at the start and end of long inputs but may under-weight content buried in the middle.
A tool-selection error.
A schema validation failure.

architect-foundations.explanation: This is the classic "lost in the middle" pattern: content at the beginning and end of a long input gets attended to reliably, while material buried in the middle is more likely to be omitted or underweighted.

architect-foundations.q: A customer explicitly says "I want to talk to a human" partway through a conversation the agent could otherwise resolve on its own. What should the agent do?

options.text: Continue attempting to resolve the issue autonomously since it's within its capability.
Honor the explicit request and escalate immediately, without first forcing another resolution attempt.
Ask the customer to rate their satisfaction before deciding whether to escalate.
Ignore the request unless the agent's own confidence score is below a threshold.

architect-foundations.explanation: An explicit customer request for a human is one of the clearest, most reliable escalation triggers and should be honored immediately — capability to resolve the issue autonomously isn't the deciding factor once the customer has explicitly asked for a person.

architect-foundations.q: A web-search subagent returns the generic status "search unavailable" after a failure, with no other detail. Why is this a problem for the coordinator?

options.text: It isn't a problem; "search unavailable" is sufficient information.
The generic status hides the context (failure type, attempted query, partial results) the coordinator would need to make an intelligent recovery decision.
The coordinator will crash on any string status.
It means the subagent used too many tokens.

architect-foundations.explanation: A generic status collapses potentially very different failure situations into one undifferentiated signal, preventing the coordinator from deciding intelligently whether to retry, try an alternative, or proceed with partial results.

architect-foundations.q: A support conversation runs long, and the agent periodically compresses earlier turns into a summary. Which detail is most at risk of being lost in that process?

options.text: The overall topic of the conversation.
Specific numbers, dates, and customer-stated expectations — progressive summarization tends to condense these into vague language.
The identity of who is speaking in each turn.
The language the conversation is conducted in.

architect-foundations.explanation: Progressive summarization is especially risky for transactional specifics — amounts, percentages, dates, and stated expectations — precisely because summarization tends to smooth these into vaguer language, losing exactly the details that matter for follow-up actions.

architect-foundations.q: What's the purpose of maintaining a persistent "case facts" block (order ID, amount, status) in every prompt, kept separate from the summarized conversation history?

options.text: To reduce token usage to zero.
To ensure key transactional facts survive summarization instead of being condensed into vague language over a long conversation.
It's required by the Claude API for all conversations.
To replace the need for tool calls entirely.

architect-foundations.explanation: A dedicated, unsummarized case-facts block guarantees that critical numbers, IDs, and statuses stay exact and available throughout a long conversation, immune to the vagueness that progressive summarization introduces elsewhere.

architect-foundations.q: A customer support agent's identity-lookup tool returns three customers matching the name and city provided. What should the agent do?

options.text: Pick the most recently active account, since that's statistically most likely to be correct.
Ask the customer for an additional identifier (e.g., order number or email) rather than selecting one match heuristically.
Proceed with the first match returned by the tool.
Escalate immediately without attempting to resolve the ambiguity.

architect-foundations.explanation: When a lookup returns multiple matches, the correct pattern is to request additional identifying information from the customer rather than guessing based on a heuristic — a wrong heuristic-based selection here risks acting on the wrong account entirely.

architect-foundations.q: During a long codebase-exploration session, the agent starts describing "typical patterns you'd expect" instead of referencing the specific classes it examined earlier in the same session. What does this most likely indicate, and what's a good mitigation?

options.text: Nothing unusual — this is expected behavior. No mitigation needed.
Context degradation — the earlier specific findings have effectively fallen out of usable context; persisting key findings in a scratchpad file mitigates this.
A tool-selection error that requires renaming the exploration tools.
A JSON schema validation failure in the exploration output.

architect-foundations.explanation: Falling back on generic "typical pattern" language instead of the specific things actually discovered is a hallmark of context degradation in long sessions. Scratchpad files that persist key findings, plus delegating verbose exploration to subagents, are the standard mitigations.

architect-foundations.q: A structured findings report shows 97% overall extraction accuracy. Is it safe to conclude accuracy is uniformly high across all document types and fields?

options.text: Yes, an aggregate accuracy number is always representative of every subgroup.
No — aggregate accuracy can mask much lower performance on specific document types or fields; accuracy should be validated by segment before reducing human review for any one of them.
Yes, as long as the sample size was large enough.
No, because aggregate accuracy metrics are never meaningful.

architect-foundations.explanation: A single aggregate number can hide a segment (a particular document type, or a particular field) performing far worse than the average. Segment-level validation is required before you can safely reduce human review for that segment specifically.

architect-foundations.q: Two credible sources report different statistics for the same metric during multi-source synthesis. Which two practices reflect the correct way to handle this? (Select 2)

options.text: Annotate the conflict, preserving both values along with their source attribution, rather than silently picking one.
Arbitrarily select the value from whichever source was processed first and discard the other.
Check whether the sources have different publication or collection dates that would explain the discrepancy rather than indicating a genuine contradiction.
Average the two values together and report only the average.

architect-foundations.explanation: The correct pattern preserves both values with source attribution and checks for a temporal explanation (different collection dates) before treating the discrepancy as a genuine conflict. Silently discarding one value or averaging them both destroy information the reader needs to judge the claim themselves.

architect-foundations.q: You paused a codebase investigation on Friday; over the weekend a teammate refactored the module the agent had analyzed, splitting one class into three and renaming the entry point. What's the most reliable way to continue Monday?

options.text: Start a new session with a structured summary of the prior findings injected into the initial context.
Run --resume and continue — the session already has a detailed model of the module.
Run --resume and ask the agent to double-check anything that seems inconsistent as it goes.
Run --resume with fork_session so the stale branch is preserved for comparison.

architect-foundations.explanation: When prior tool results are stale, starting fresh with an injected structured summary is more reliable than resuming — a refactor this substantial invalidates the session's core model of the module. Option B resumes silently: the agent has no way to know the weekend happened and will confidently reason from Friday's now-wrong structure. Option C relies on the agent noticing drift it has no signal for; its stale results look exactly as authoritative as fresh ones. Option D preserves a branch built on invalid analysis, which addresses nothing.

architect-foundations.q: A teammate modified two of the fifteen files your paused session had analyzed. The rest of its context is still accurate. What's the most efficient way to continue?

options.text: Resume the session and explicitly inform it which files changed, so it re-analyzes those specific files.
Start a completely fresh session and re-explore all fifteen files from scratch.
Resume the session without comment — with only two files changed, the impact is negligible.
Resume and instruct the agent to re-read all fifteen files before continuing.

architect-foundations.explanation: When prior context is mostly valid, resuming and informing the session about specific file changes enables targeted re-analysis rather than full re-exploration — that's precisely the payoff of resuming. Option B discards thirteen files of still-accurate analysis. Option C is the resume-silently trap: the agent can't detect changes it wasn't told about, so it reasons from stale results for those two files. Option D pays the full re-exploration cost while resuming, getting the worst of both.

architect-foundations.q: Which two changes best mitigate the "lost in the middle" effect when a coordinator aggregates findings from several subagents into one long input? (Select 2)

options.text: Place a key-findings summary at the beginning of the aggregated input.
Organize the detailed results under explicit section headers.
Sort all findings alphabetically so the ordering is predictable.
Compress the middle sections more aggressively than the beginning and end.

architect-foundations.explanation: The documented mitigations are positional and structural: key findings placed at the beginning where attention is reliable, and explicit section headers so structure compensates for position. Option C imposes an ordering unrelated to importance — material still lands in the middle, just alphabetically. Option D actively destroys the middle content instead of making it findable, converting a position problem into a summarization-loss problem.

architect-foundations.q: An order-lookup tool returns 40+ fields per order, of which about 5 matter for refund decisions. Over a long support conversation these results accumulate. What's the recommended approach?

options.text: Trim the tool output to the relevant fields before it accumulates in context.
Keep all 40+ fields — discarding data risks losing something needed later.
Summarize the accumulated tool results periodically once context pressure appears.
Stop passing conversation history in subsequent requests to make room.

architect-foundations.explanation: Tool results consume tokens disproportionately to their relevance, and trimming verbose output to relevant fields before it accumulates is the documented fix — nothing errors as the context quietly fills with warehouse codes, which is what makes it insidious. Option B is the behavior causing the problem. Option C waits until the damage is done and then applies summarization, which is itself lossy for exactly the numeric details that matter. Option D is actively harmful: passing complete conversation history is what maintains conversational coherence — you trim what enters context, not the history already there.

architect-foundations.q: You want to reduce human review for extractions the model scores as high-confidence. What's the responsible way to monitor for errors you're no longer catching?

options.text: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions to measure error rates and detect novel error patterns.
Review only the low-confidence extractions, since high-confidence ones are by definition unlikely to be wrong.
Rely on downstream systems to surface errors when they cause visible problems.
Re-run each high-confidence extraction a second time and compare the two outputs.

architect-foundations.explanation: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions is the documented mechanism for ongoing error-rate measurement and novel error pattern detection — you sample where you believe things are fine precisely because that's where an unnoticed systematic failure would hide. Option B guarantees you never discover errors the model is confident about, the exact blind spot sampling exists to cover. Option C discovers errors only after they've caused damage. Option D checks self-consistency rather than correctness: a systematically wrong extraction reproduces itself reliably.

architect-foundations.q: During synthesis, the summarization step compresses subagent findings into prose conclusions, and the final report's claims can no longer be traced to sources. What's the root cause?

options.text: Structured claim-source mappings (source URL, document name, relevant excerpt) weren't required in subagent outputs and preserved through synthesis.
The synthesis agent's context window is too small to hold the source documents.
The subagents used too many tools during research.
The report needed a bibliography section appended at the end.

architect-foundations.explanation: Source attribution is lost during summarization when findings are compressed without preserving claim-source mappings; the fix is requiring subagents to output structured mappings that downstream agents preserve and merge. Once a mapping is gone, no downstream step can reconstruct it. Option B misattributes a data-modelling failure to capacity — attribution is lost at the compression step regardless of window size. Option C is unrelated. Option D adds a bibliography of sources with no way to link claims to them, which is the problem restated.

architect-foundations.q: A document analysis subagent finds two credible sources reporting different values for the same market-size statistic. What should it do before passing findings to synthesis?

options.text: Include both values with explicit conflict annotation and source attribution, letting the coordinator decide how to reconcile them.
Select the value from the more recently published source and pass only that forward.
Omit the contested statistic entirely to avoid introducing a contradiction.
Average the two values so downstream synthesis receives a single number.

architect-foundations.explanation: Document analysis should complete with conflicting values included and explicitly annotated, letting the coordinator decide how to reconcile before passing to synthesis — resolving silently at the analysis step destroys information the coordinator needed. Option B applies a reconciliation heuristic unilaterally at the wrong layer, and recency doesn't establish correctness. Option C silently drops a finding the report may need. Option D fabricates a number neither source reported.

architect-foundations.q:
A retailer's support system uses a coordinator agent that receives each customer conversation and delegates to three subagents: an order-lookup agent with read-only order tools, a refund agent that can issue refunds, and a policy agent that searches the returns-policy knowledge base. Company policy: refunds above $250 need a human's approval, and customers can come back to an open conversation within 7 days.

The refund agent needs the order total, the purchase date and the customer's stated reason to decide eligibility. What should the coordinator include when it delegates the task?

options.text: An instruction for the refund agent to ask the customer to repeat the details
The full raw transcript plus every prior tool output, so the refund agent misses nothing
The specific facts the refund agent needs, written into the delegation prompt: order id, total, purchase date and the customer's stated reason
Nothing extra, because subagents can read the coordinator's conversation history

architect-foundations.explanation: Subagents in a hub-and-spoke design start with their own context window and see only what the coordinator passes to them, so C is the working design: the minimum necessary context, stated explicitly. D assumes an inheritance that doesn't exist. B spends tokens and attention on material the decision doesn't need, which is where lost-in-the-middle errors start. A makes the customer pay for a gap the coordinator could close with facts it already has.

architect-foundations.q:
A retailer's support system uses a coordinator agent that receives each customer conversation and delegates to three subagents: an order-lookup agent with read-only order tools, a refund agent that can issue refunds, and a policy agent that searches the returns-policy knowledge base. Company policy: refunds above $250 need a human's approval, and customers can come back to an open conversation within 7 days.

Which TWO events should trigger a handoff to a human agent? (Select TWO)

options.text: Answering the customer's question takes three tool calls
The customer asks to speak to a person
The model reports a confidence score of 0.62 on its eligibility decision
The customer writes in capital letters and says they are furious about a covered $90 refund
The customer requests a $400 refund for an order the policy covers

architect-foundations.explanation: An explicit request for a human (B) is a standing escalation trigger, and the $400 refund (E) crosses the $250 approval threshold, which makes the handoff mandatory under policy. Sentiment alone (D) is no trigger when the request sits inside clear policy; the agent can resolve it while acknowledging the frustration. Self-reported confidence (C) is poorly calibrated and makes an unreliable trigger. Task complexity (A) is the agent's job.

architect-foundations.q:
A retailer's support system uses a coordinator agent that receives each customer conversation and delegates to three subagents: an order-lookup agent with read-only order tools, a refund agent that can issue refunds, and a policy agent that searches the returns-policy knowledge base. Company policy: refunds above $250 need a human's approval, and customers can come back to an open conversation within 7 days.

The policy agent's knowledge-base search sometimes fails because the search service times out, and sometimes finds nothing because no policy covers the case. Both situations currently return an empty list. How should the tool respond instead?

options.text: Keep returning an empty list in both cases and let the agent retry
Return a structured error for the timeout (error type, retryable: true, what was attempted) and a successful empty result for the no-match case
Return the closest-matching policy in both cases so the agent always has something to cite
Raise an exception in both cases so the coordinator ends the conversation

architect-foundations.explanation: B separates a transient failure from a valid empty result, and the two need different recovery: retry the search, or tell the customer no policy applies. With A, the agent can't tell an outage from a real answer and may report that no policy covers the case during an outage. D ends conversations over a recoverable timeout. C invents relevance, which leads the agent to cite a policy that doesn't apply.

architect-foundations.q:
A retailer's support system uses a coordinator agent that receives each customer conversation and delegates to three subagents: an order-lookup agent with read-only order tools, a refund agent that can issue refunds, and a policy agent that searches the returns-policy knowledge base. Company policy: refunds above $250 need a human's approval, and customers can come back to an open conversation within 7 days.

A customer returns four days later to continue a conversation about a pending refund. Separately, a supervisor wants to test a different resolution on a copy of that conversation without changing what the customer sees. Which pairing fits?

options.text: Start fresh sessions for both and paste the last assistant message into each system prompt
Fork the session for the customer and resume it for the supervisor
Resume the same session for both
Resume the customer's session so the full history is restored, and fork a separate copy for the supervisor

architect-foundations.explanation: Resuming continues a session with its history intact, which is what the returning customer needs. Forking creates an independent branch from the same history, and changes in the fork never flow back, which is what the supervisor needs. D matches both. B swaps the two. C lets the supervisor's experiment change the customer's conversation. A throws away most of the context and relies on one message to carry it.

architect-foundations.q:
A security team runs a nightly audit across 40 repositories. A coordinator spawns one scanner subagent per repository. Each scanner has `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` plus a dependency-check tool. The coordinator merges the findings into one report for the morning stand-up and opens tickets for new critical issues.

Which execution pattern fits the scanning stage and the report stage?

options.text: Fan out the 40 scans in parallel, because they are independent, then run one merge step that builds the report from normalized results
Run several report writers in parallel and concatenate their outputs
Use one agent that scans all 40 repositories in a single context so it can spot cross-repository patterns
Scan sequentially so each scanner can learn from the previous one's findings, then write the report in parallel sections

architect-foundations.explanation: Independent work runs in parallel and dependent work runs in sequence, so the hybrid in A matches the data dependencies: the scans don't need each other, and the report needs all of them. D serializes independent work and slows the audit for no gain. C pushes 40 repositories into one context, which degrades attention and turns one failure into a total failure. B produces a report with no single view of the findings, which is what the merge step exists for.

architect-foundations.q:
A security team runs a nightly audit across 40 repositories. A coordinator spawns one scanner subagent per repository. Each scanner has `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` plus a dependency-check tool. The coordinator merges the findings into one report for the morning stand-up and opens tickets for new critical issues.

Last night the audit crashed at repository 27. The rerun started again from repository 1 and opened duplicate tickets for findings already reported. Which TWO changes fix this? (Select TWO)

options.text: Checkpoint progress to a manifest file (completed repositories, pending repositories, results so far) and resume from it after a crash
Give the scanners larger context windows so they remember the previous run
Run the audit weekly instead of nightly
Make ticket creation idempotent, for example keyed by repository and finding id, so a replay can't create duplicates
Ask the coordinator at startup which repositories it already finished

architect-foundations.explanation: A manifest (A) lets the restarted coordinator continue from repository 27, and idempotent side effects (D) make any replayed step harmless; together they turn a crash into a delay. Context windows (B) don't survive a process crash, and the coordinator has no memory of the previous run to ask about (E), because the API is stateless. Running less often (C) leaves the failure in place.

architect-foundations.q:
A security team runs a nightly audit across 40 repositories. A coordinator spawns one scanner subagent per repository. Each scanner has `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` plus a dependency-check tool. The coordinator merges the findings into one report for the morning stand-up and opens tickets for new critical issues.

An engineer proposes giving every scanner the full tool set, including `Write`, `Bash` and the ticketing tool, 'in case they need it.' What is the best response?

options.text: Replace the scanner tools with Bash alone, since Bash can do everything the other tools do
Give the scanners every tool and add a system-prompt rule forbidding writes
Keep each scanner on the read-only tools its job needs, and let only the coordinator open tickets from the merged findings
Accept the proposal, because more tools make the scanners more capable

architect-foundations.explanation: Least privilege scopes each agent to what its responsibility requires. C also keeps tool selection accurate and stops a misbehaving scanner from changing code or opening tickets. D widens the blast radius and adds selection noise for capabilities nobody uses. B relies on a probabilistic instruction to restrain a capability that should never be there. A hands the scanners the broadest tool of all.

architect-foundations.q:
A security team runs a nightly audit across 40 repositories. A coordinator spawns one scanner subagent per repository. Each scanner has `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` plus a dependency-check tool. The coordinator merges the findings into one report for the morning stand-up and opens tickets for new critical issues.

The morning report said 'No critical issues found across all repositories.' The team later learns that six scanners hit their token budgets and skipped their largest files. What should the report format have required?

options.text: Nothing; the scanners needed a more capable model
A longer narrative summary from each scanner
A confidence score from each scanner
A coverage annotation from every scanner (files reviewed, files skipped with reasons, coverage counts) carried into the merged report

architect-foundations.explanation: Without explicit coverage, 'no issues found' can't be told apart from 'no issues found in the part that ran.' D makes the gap visible so the skipped files can be queued for a focused pass. Self-reported confidence (C) is poorly calibrated and says nothing about what was skipped. A longer summary (B) adds words without the counts. A stronger model (A) can still hit a budget, and the report would still hide it.

architect-foundations.q:
After the first tool call, every follow-up request in your agent loop fails with a 400 error. Here is how the loop builds the next request. What is wrong?

```python
response = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024,
                                  tools=tools, messages=messages)
if response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    call = next(b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use")
    result = run_tool(call.name, call.input)
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [{
        "type": "tool_result",
        "tool_use_id": call.id,
        "content": result,
    }]})
```

options.text: The loop should set `tool_choice` to `any` after the first call
The assistant turn containing the `tool_use` block is never appended, so the `tool_result` refers to a call the next request doesn't contain
`tool_result` blocks belong in the system prompt
`max_tokens` is too low for a tool loop

architect-foundations.explanation: The API is stateless, so each request must carry the whole exchange: the assistant message with the `tool_use` block comes first, then the user message with the matching `tool_result` (B). Without it, the `tool_use_id` points at nothing. C misplaces tool results, which go in a user turn. D and A change settings that have nothing to do with a malformed history.

architect-foundations.q: Your research agent uses the server-side web search tool. Some responses come back with `stop_reason` `pause_turn`, and the loop treats them as finished, returning half-done research. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Send a follow-up request with the paused assistant response appended as-is, so Claude can continue the server-side work
Raise `max_tokens` and send the original request again
Treat `pause_turn` the same as `end_turn`
Run the web search locally and return a `tool_result` for it

architect-foundations.explanation: `pause_turn` means a server-side tool loop reached its iteration limit mid-task. The documented handling is A: return the response as the latest assistant turn, and Claude picks up where it stopped. C is the bug in the question. D treats a server tool like a client tool; there is no `tool_use` for your code to answer. B restarts the work and pays for it twice.

architect-foundations.q: A team answers one-line FAQ questions from a two-page policy with a six-subagent pipeline: retriever, reader, drafter, tone checker, fact checker and formatter. Answers take 25 seconds and cost far more than expected. What is the best change?

options.text: Collapse it to a single model call with the policy in context, plus a lightweight validation step if needed
Move every subagent to the most capable model to cut retries
Run the six subagents in parallel under a coordinator
Cache each subagent's output

architect-foundations.explanation: This is over-decomposition: the task is small, single-domain and fits in one context, so the subagents add orchestration cost without any isolation benefit, and A removes the overhead. Parallelizing (C) doesn't fit a chain where each step needs the previous step's output. B raises the cost of a design that shouldn't exist. D helps only with repeated identical questions and leaves the latency of the chain in place.

architect-foundations.q: A payments service's error rate spiked. The cause could be in code, configuration, infrastructure or a third-party API, and what to check next depends on what each check finds. How should the coordinator decompose the investigation?

options.text: One prompt asking Claude for the root cause
A fixed pipeline that runs the four checks in a set order
Dynamic decomposition: plan the next subtasks from each finding, with a token budget and iteration cap enforced in code as safety nets
Run every conceivable check in parallel with no coordinator

architect-foundations.explanation: Open-ended investigations, where the next step depends on what you just learned, call for dynamic decomposition. Because that pattern costs more and can wander, C pairs it with limits enforced outside the model. A fixed pipeline (B) suits workflows that are known in advance. D wastes effort and leaves nobody to connect the findings. A asks for an answer without giving the model any way to gather evidence.

architect-foundations.q: Long research tasks sometimes use ten times the expected tokens. Which TWO belong in a reliable token-budget design? (Select TWO)

options.text: Setting `max_tokens` to 50 on every call
Asking Claude each turn how many tokens it has used so far
A system-prompt instruction asking Claude to stay under 50,000 tokens
Track cumulative input and output tokens from each response's usage field inside the loop
Stop the loop in code when the budget is reached, with a wrap-up instruction injected at about 80% of the budget

architect-foundations.explanation: Budgets are enforced from outside the model: measure from the usage field (D) and act on the measurement with a soft warning and a hard stop (E). An instruction (C) and the model's own estimate (B) are probabilistic and unmeasured. A tiny `max_tokens` (A) truncates every response, so turns end at the cap before they finish.

architect-foundations.q: A team's MCP server should (1) let Claude create Jira tickets, (2) expose the team's API schema files so a user can attach them as context, and (3) provide a reusable 'triage this incident' template with the team's severity rubric. Which MCP primitives fit, in that order?

options.text: Tool, tool, tool
Resource, tool, prompt
Prompt, resource, tool
Tool, resource, prompt

architect-foundations.explanation: Creating a ticket is an action, so it's a tool. Schema files are read-only data for the client to browse and attach, so they're a resource. The packaged triage template is a prompt. D matches action, data and know-how in that order. A turns data and a template into callable functions. B and C put the action in the wrong primitive.

architect-foundations.q: Every developer on a team should get the same internal MCP server in Claude Code, and the server needs an API token. Which TWO choices are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Put the token in `CLAUDE.md` so Claude can pass it to the server
Paste the raw token into `.mcp.json` so setup is a single step
Define the server in the project's `.mcp.json` and commit it to the repository
Reference the token in `.mcp.json` as `${INTERNAL_API_TOKEN}` and have each developer set that environment variable
Have each developer add the server with local scope by following a wiki page

architect-foundations.explanation: Project scope (C) is the configuration that reaches the whole team through version control, and environment variable expansion (D) keeps the secret out of the repository. B commits a credential. E relies on every developer repeating a manual step, and local scope never propagates. A puts a secret into the model's context, where it can leak through outputs or logs.

architect-foundations.q: When users ask to change their email address, Claude often calls `get_customer` instead of `update_customer`, then tells the user the change is done. Both tools exist. What is the first fix?

options.text: Add a system-prompt line telling Claude to use `update_customer` for updates
Rewrite both descriptions: what each tool does, when to use it, and when to use the other one instead, with `get_customer` described as read-only
Rename `get_customer` to `fetch_customer`
Remove `get_customer` from the agent

architect-foundations.explanation: Claude selects tools mainly from their descriptions, so overlapping or vague descriptions are the first thing to fix (B), and the boundary statements ('to change a record, use `update_customer`') are what resolve this confusion. A rename (C) changes little while the descriptions stay vague. A system-prompt patch (A) is weaker than fixing the routing signal itself. Removing the read tool (D) breaks every legitimate lookup.

architect-foundations.q: Your team wants every file Claude edits to be formatted with Prettier immediately after each edit, for everyone working in the repository. Which configuration does that?

options.text: A hook in each developer's `~/.claude/settings.json`
A `CLAUDE.md` line: 'Run Prettier after every edit'
A `PostToolUse` hook in the committed `.claude/settings.json`, matching `Edit|Write`, that runs Prettier on the edited file
A `PreToolUse` hook on `Edit` that runs Prettier

architect-foundations.explanation: Formatting has to run after the file changes, which is `PostToolUse`, and the committed project settings file shares the hook with the whole team, so C covers both requirements. D runs before the edit exists. B is guidance Claude may skip, while a hook runs every time. A works only for developers who set it up themselves.

architect-foundations.q: A team requires that Claude never ends its work while the test suite is failing. Which hook enforces this?

options.text: A `SessionEnd` hook that runs the tests
A `Stop` hook that runs the tests and exits with code 2, printing the failures to stderr, when any test fails
A `PostToolUse` hook that runs the tests after every file read
A `UserPromptSubmit` hook that runs the tests before each prompt

architect-foundations.explanation: Exit code 2 from a `Stop` hook prevents Claude from stopping and feeds the stderr text back, so Claude keeps working on the failures (B). `SessionEnd` (A) fires as the session closes and can't block anything. D tests before the work happens. C runs constantly at the wrong moment and can't stop Claude from finishing.

architect-foundations.q: A `PostToolUse` hook on `Write` scans each file Claude writes. It finds an API key in a file Claude just wrote and exits with code 2. What happens?

options.text: The file has already been written; Claude receives the hook's stderr message and can act on it, for example by removing the key
Claude Code shuts down the session
Nothing happens, because exit code 2 is ignored for `PostToolUse`
The write is cancelled and the file is never created

architect-foundations.explanation: `PostToolUse` fires after the tool has run, so it can't undo the write; exit code 2 shows its stderr to Claude (A). To stop the write itself, the check belongs in a `PreToolUse` hook, where exit code 2 blocks the call, which is the behavior D describes. B and C describe behaviors that don't exist.

architect-foundations.q: A developer asks Claude Code to migrate 40 files from a callback-based API client to async/await. The change touches shared types, and there are two reasonable migration strategies. What is the best way to start?

options.text: One prompt for the whole change, then review the final diff
Direct execution, file by file, fixing problems as they appear
A `CLAUDE.md` rule saying 'use async/await'
Plan Mode: let Claude explore the codebase and propose a migration plan to review before any file changes

architect-foundations.explanation: Multi-file, cross-cutting changes with more than one valid approach are Plan Mode's case (D): the strategy gets agreed before 40 files move. B and A commit to an approach before anyone has compared the options, and a wrong choice is expensive to unwind. C states a preference without planning the migration.

architect-foundations.q: A team's dependency-audit skill prints thousands of lines of output, and teammates complain it floods the main conversation. Which frontmatter change fixes this?

options.text: `context: fork`, so the skill runs in an isolated subagent and returns its result
`disable-model-invocation: true`
`allowed-tools: Read`
`model: haiku`

architect-foundations.explanation: `context: fork` (A) runs the skill in its own subagent context, so the verbose work stays out of the main conversation. B only stops Claude from invoking the skill automatically; the output still floods the conversation whenever someone runs it. C changes which tools are pre-approved and D changes the model, and neither moves the output.

architect-foundations.q: In a monorepo, files under `services/payments/` follow strict rules (all amounts in integer cents, no floats). The rules confuse Claude when it works on the frontend. Which TWO placements load these rules only when Claude works in the payments code? (Select TWO)

options.text: A section titled 'Payments only' in the root `CLAUDE.md`
A `CLAUDE.md` file inside `services/payments/`
A file in `.claude/rules/` with `paths: ["services/payments/**"]` in its frontmatter
Each developer's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`
The project's `.mcp.json`

architect-foundations.explanation: A path-scoped rule (C) loads when Claude reads or edits a matching file, and a subdirectory `CLAUDE.md` (B) loads on demand when Claude works with files in that directory. The root `CLAUDE.md` (A) loads in every session, frontend work included. D is personal and reaches nobody else. E configures MCP servers and holds no instructions.

architect-foundations.q: A code-review prompt says 'Be thorough but avoid nitpicks.' Reviews flag style issues inconsistently and miss SQL injection. Which rewrite fixes the cause?

options.text: 'You are a world-class senior security engineer.'
'Be extremely thorough and never miss anything.'
'Be conservative with your comments.'
'Report only these issues: SQL injection, XSS, authentication bypass and secrets in code. Report high or critical severity only. Do not comment on formatting or naming.'

architect-foundations.explanation: Vague instructions produce inconsistent behavior because the model has to guess the threshold. D names the categories, the severity floor and the exclusions, and anyone reading a review can check whether it followed them. B and C push the same vague guidance in two directions. A role line (A) without criteria leaves the same guesswork.

architect-foundations.q: A classifier should flag support tickets that mention a physical safety risk. In testing it flags every ticket containing the word 'fire', including 'firewall rules reset after update.' What is the best few-shot improvement?

options.text: An instruction: 'Don't be fooled by keywords.'
Two to four examples that include the firewall ticket labeled not-safety with a one-line reason, a genuine safety ticket, and an ambiguous case
Twenty examples of genuine safety tickets
A lower temperature

architect-foundations.explanation: Few-shot examples teach reasoning and edge cases best when they include something the model should leave alone, so the tricky negative in B is the example that matters. C piles on positives and teaches nothing about the false positives. A is vague guidance. Temperature (D) changes randomness and leaves the misunderstanding in place.

architect-foundations.q: Your team plans to use structured outputs (a JSON schema in `output_config.format`) for invoice extraction. Which TWO statements about this feature are true? (Select TWO)

options.text: It guarantees the extracted values are correct for the source document
It works only when `tool_choice` forces a specific tool
It removes the need to validate business rules, such as totals matching line items
Constrained decoding makes the response valid JSON that matches the schema's structure and types
A refusal or a `max_tokens` cutoff can still produce output that doesn't match the schema, so check `stop_reason`

architect-foundations.explanation: Structured outputs guarantee format: valid, schema-compliant JSON (D), with the documented exceptions of refusals and truncation (E). Format says nothing about whether the values are right, so semantic checks such as totals and dates stay in your pipeline, which rules out A and C. B confuses the feature with forced tool use; structured outputs are requested through `output_config.format`.

architect-foundations.q: An extraction fails validation because `invoice_date` came back as 2026-04-31, a date that doesn't exist. What should the retry request contain?

options.text: The failed output and the words 'try again'
The original document again with no other changes
The original document, the failed output, and the specific error ('`invoice_date` 2026-04-31 is not a valid date'), with an instruction to correct only that field
The same request sent to a more capable model

architect-foundations.explanation: A useful retry tells the model exactly what failed and gives it the source to fix it against (C). B repeats the conditions that produced the error. A removes the source the model needs to correct the date. D changes the model without telling it what went wrong.

architect-foundations.q: A product team wants to move its live chat assistant to the Message Batches API to cut costs in half. What is the right assessment?

options.text: Reject it, because batch requests can't include a system prompt
Approve it: the same quality at half the price
Approve it, provided the app polls for results every second

Reject it: batches carry no latency guarantee (most finish within an hour, some take up to 24), so a waiting user can't be served; cut costs with prompt caching or by routing routine messages to a cheaper tier

architect-foundations.explanation: The batch discount comes with asynchronous processing and no latency guarantee, which rules it out for anyone waiting on an answer (D). B ignores the latency. Polling (C) doesn't speed up processing. A is false: batch requests take the same parameters as regular Messages requests.

architect-foundations.q: One prompt asks Claude to extract 30 fields from a contract, normalize every currency, classify the risk clauses and write an executive summary. Results vary from run to run, and errors are hard to trace. What is the best restructuring?

options.text: A chain of focused prompts (extract, validate, normalize, classify, summarize), each with its own instructions and checks
The same single prompt on a more capable model
Ask for the executive summary first, then the fields
The same single prompt with each requirement marked IMPORTANT

architect-foundations.explanation: Prompt chaining gives each stage one job and a validation point, so a failure shows up in the stage that caused it (A). Emphasis (D) doesn't reduce the number of jobs in one prompt. A stronger model (B) may help a little and leaves errors untraceable. Reordering (C) builds the summary on fields nobody has checked yet.

architect-foundations.q: A knowledge-base Q&A agent receives 40 retrieved passages per question. The passage with the answer usually lands near the middle, and answers often miss it. Which TWO changes address this? (Select TWO)

options.text: Retrieve 80 passages instead of 40
Re-rank the passages and pass only the most relevant few
Raise the temperature
Put the passages first and the question and instructions at the end of the prompt
Switch to a model with a larger context window

architect-foundations.explanation: Attention is weakest in the middle of long contexts, so the fixes shrink the middle and move what matters to the edges: fewer, better passages (B), and long material first with the question last, which Anthropic's long-context guidance recommends (D). A bigger window (E) and more passages (A) make the middle longer. Temperature (C) affects randomness and does nothing for attention.

architect-foundations.q: Two internal documents disagree about the warranty period: a 2024 policy says 12 months and a 2026 update says 24 months. What should the agent's answer do?

options.text: Decline to answer until someone fixes the documents
State 24 months without mentioning the conflict, because the newer document wins
Give the answer with attribution: both values, their documents and dates, the newer one identified as likely current, and the conflict flagged for review
Average the two and state 18 months

architect-foundations.explanation: Provenance keeps each claim tied to its source and surfaces conflicts instead of settling them silently (C). Silently picking one value (B) is the tested anti-pattern even when the choice happens to be right, because nobody learns that the documents disagree. D produces a number neither source supports. A withholds an answer the agent can give with a caveat.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

Your resolution agent occasionally calls `process_refund` before `get_customer` has returned a verified identity, even though the system prompt says identity verification is mandatory first. What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Rewrite the system prompt in bold, capitalized text
Add a programmatic prerequisite that blocks `process_refund` until `get_customer` returns a verified ID
Lower the model's temperature
Add five few-shot examples showing correct ordering

architect-foundations.explanation: Deterministic ordering guarantees for high-stakes operations (money, identity) need programmatic enforcement, not stronger prompt wording. This is the exam's single most-repeated lesson.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

`get_account_status` and `get_account_details` have nearly identical one-line descriptions. The agent frequently calls the wrong one for billing questions. What's the most effective first step?

options.text: Merge the two tools into one
Expand both descriptions with input formats, example queries, and explicit "use this vs. that" boundaries
Add a keyword pre-router in front of the agent
Force `tool_choice` to a single named tool

architect-foundations.explanation: Tool description quality is the primary, lowest-effort lever for fixing tool-selection confusion. Always fix descriptions before reaching for few-shot examples or architectural changes.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

A lookup for "Utkarsh Agarwal" returns three matching customer records. What should the agent do?

options.text: Pick the most recently active account
Pick the account with the most orders
Ask the customer for an additional identifier (email, order number, zip code)
Process the request against all three accounts and let the customer confirm afterward

architect-foundations.explanation: Multiple ambiguous matches should never be resolved heuristically; ask for another identifier to disambiguate safely.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

A customer says, "I want to speak to a human right now," about a routine, easily resolvable issue. What should the agent do?

options.text: Attempt to resolve the issue first, and escalate only if the customer repeats the request
Escalate immediately, honoring the explicit request
Explain why a human isn't necessary and continue autonomously
Ask the customer to describe the issue in more detail before deciding

architect-foundations.explanation: An explicit request for a human should be honored immediately, not investigated around. Offering to resolve first is correct only when the customer *hasn't* explicitly demanded escalation.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

A case is escalated to a human agent who cannot see the prior conversation. The handoff contains only a ticket number and the words "customer upset." What's missing?

options.text: A sentiment classification score
A structured summary: customer details, root cause, recommended action
The full unedited transcript
A timestamp of when escalation occurred

architect-foundations.explanation: A structured handoff (customer details, root cause, recommended action) lets a human act without re-investigating from zero; a sentiment score or bare transcript don't solve that gap.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

Your team wants to block any refund over $500 from being auto-approved, regardless of what the model decides. What's the most reliable mechanism?

options.text: A system prompt clause stating the $500 limit
A pre-call tool-interception hook that blocks `process_refund` above $500 and redirects to escalation
A few-shot example showing a refund being denied at $501
Reducing `max_tokens` so large numbers can't be generated

architect-foundations.explanation: A pre-call tool-interception hook gives a deterministic guarantee. Prompt clauses and few-shot examples are probabilistic and can fail.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

Multiple heterogeneous MCP tools return dates in different formats (Unix timestamps, ISO-8601, and localized strings). This is causing the agent to misinterpret order age. What's the best fix?

options.text: A `PostToolUse` hook that normalizes all date formats before the model sees them
A system prompt instructing the model to "convert dates carefully"
Removing date fields from tool responses entirely
Asking the customer to always state dates in ISO-8601 format

architect-foundations.explanation: A `PostToolUse` hook normalizes heterogeneous data formats before the model reasons over them — a hook problem, not a prompting problem.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

A customer has two unrelated concerns in one message: a billing dispute and a shipping delay. What's the best approach?

options.text: Address only the first concern mentioned and ask the customer to submit the second separately
Decompose into distinct concerns, investigate each with shared context, then synthesize one unified response
Escalate immediately since multi-concern messages are inherently too complex
Pick whichever concern seems more urgent and ignore the other

architect-foundations.explanation: Multi-concern requests should be decomposed into distinct items, investigated with shared context, then synthesized into one unified response.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

Your team currently escalates cases when the model's self-reported confidence score falls below 6/10. First-contact resolution remains far below target, with easy cases escalated and hard cases handled autonomously. What's wrong with this design?

options.text: The threshold is set too high and should be lowered
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated — the model is often confidently wrong on exactly the hardest cases
Confidence scores should be averaged over the whole conversation, not per-turn
The threshold should instead be based on the number of tool calls made

architect-foundations.explanation: Self-reported model confidence is a poorly calibrated proxy for actual case complexity; it fails precisely on the hardest cases, which is what's happening here.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

An MCP tool returns `{"isError": true, "message": "Operation failed"}` for every kind of failure — timeouts, invalid input, and policy violations alike. What's the problem, and the fix?

options.text: No problem; `isError: true` is sufficient signal
The agent can't distinguish retryable from non-retryable failures; add `errorCategory` and `isRetryable` fields
Replace `isError` with an HTTP status code instead
Log the error server-side only, since the agent doesn't need to see it

architect-foundations.explanation: Generic error responses hide information the agent needs to react correctly. Structured fields (`errorCategory`, `isRetryable`) let it distinguish retryable, validation, and business-rule failures.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A new engineer joins the team and doesn't seem to follow the team's established code style, even though it's documented. Investigation shows the conventions live in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the tech lead's machine. What's the fix?

options.text: Ask the new engineer to manually copy the file
Move the conventions to a project-level `CLAUDE.md` committed to the repo
Repeat the conventions verbally in stand-up each day
Add the conventions to the README instead

architect-foundations.explanation: User-level `CLAUDE.md` files are personal and not shared via version control. Team-wide conventions belong in a project-level file.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

Testing conventions need to apply to every `*.test.tsx` file in a large monorepo, regardless of which directory it lives in. What's the most maintainable approach?

options.text: A `CLAUDE.md` file in every directory containing tests
A `.claude/rules/testing.md` file with `paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]` frontmatter
One giant root `CLAUDE.md` with a "Testing" section
A skill that must be manually invoked before writing any test

architect-foundations.explanation: Glob-scoped `.claude/rules/` apply based on file path pattern, independent of directory — exactly the "convention tied to file type, not location" problem.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

You're building a skill that performs deep dependency tracing and produces very long, noisy output. You don't want this output cluttering the main conversation. Which `SKILL.md` frontmatter option addresses this?

options.text: `argument-hint`
`allowed-tools`
`context: fork`
`paths`

architect-foundations.explanation: `context: fork` runs a skill in an isolated sub-agent context so verbose output doesn't pollute the main conversation.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A task involves restructuring a monolithic service into 3 microservices, touching 50+ files, with multiple valid ways to draw service boundaries. What's the right approach?

options.text: Direct execution, refining the boundary as you go
Plan mode, to explore and design boundaries before committing to changes
A single, extremely detailed upfront prompt specifying every file change
Direct execution, switching to plan mode only if something unexpected comes up

architect-foundations.explanation: Multi-file architectural decisions with several valid approaches are exactly plan mode's use case — explore and design before committing.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A developer asks Claude to "clean up this data transformation function," and across three attempts, the definition of "cleaned up" varies each time (sometimes renaming variables, sometimes restructuring logic, sometimes both). What's the most effective fix?

options.text: Repeat the same instruction more forcefully
Provide 2–3 concrete before/after examples that pin down what "cleaned up" means here
Lower `max_tokens`
Request five attempts and pick the best one manually

architect-foundations.explanation: Inconsistent interpretation of a prose instruction is fixed with concrete before/after examples, not stronger wording.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A code review surfaces three interacting bugs in a module — fixing bug 1 changes what the correct fix for bug 2 should be. How should this be communicated to Claude?

options.text: One bug per message, sequentially
All three interacting issues together in one detailed message
Only the most severe bug; let Claude find the rest
A summary count of bugs without describing any of them

architect-foundations.explanation: Interacting issues need to be described together in one message; sequencing them risks contradictory or wasted fixes.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

Before implementing a rate-limiting layer in an unfamiliar service, a developer wants Claude to first surface design questions (burst handling, per-user vs. global limits, failure behavior) rather than jump straight to code. What technique fits best?

options.text: Test-driven iteration
The interview pattern
Prompt chaining
Direct execution with a longer prompt

architect-foundations.explanation: The interview pattern surfaces design considerations before implementation — well-suited to unfamiliar domains where not every consideration has been anticipated.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A project-scoped `/deploy-checklist` command should be available to every developer who clones the repo. Where should it live?

options.text: `.claude/commands/`
`~/.claude/commands/`
`CLAUDE.md`
`.claude/config.json`

architect-foundations.explanation: Project-scoped commands in `.claude/commands/` are version-controlled and shared with everyone who clones the repo.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

You want Claude to write a test suite, then iteratively improve an implementation based on which tests fail. What should you feed back after each attempt?

options.text: Only the original instructions, repeated
The actual test failures from that attempt
A new, unrelated set of instructions each time
Nothing — Claude should be able to infer failures without being told

architect-foundations.explanation: Test-driven iteration works by sharing actual test *failures* after each attempt, not just the original test suite once.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A developer is unsure whether to use `.claude/rules/` or a subdirectory `CLAUDE.md` for a convention that applies to all files under `src/api/`. Which favors `.claude/rules/`?

options.text: The convention only ever applies within that one directory
The convention needs to apply based on file path patterns that might extend beyond one directory in the future
The convention is short enough to fit in one line
There's no meaningful difference between the two options

architect-foundations.explanation: `.claude/rules/` with glob `paths` scales to conventions that might extend across directories; a subdirectory `CLAUDE.md` is bound to one location.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

A coordinator decomposes "renewable energy policy trends" into three subtasks, all focused on solar policy in a single country. Each subagent executes its assigned task correctly, but the final report is extremely narrow. Where's the defect?

options.text: The synthesis agent's summarization quality
The coordinator's task decomposition
The web search agent's query construction
The document analysis agent's relevance filtering

architect-foundations.explanation: Every subagent executed correctly; the narrow coverage comes from how the coordinator decomposed the topic in the first place.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

Which statement about subagent context is correct?

options.text: Subagents automatically inherit the coordinator's full conversation history
Subagents share memory across invocations by default
Subagents require context to be explicitly included in their invocation prompt
Subagents inherit context if invoked within the same API call

architect-foundations.explanation: Subagents do not automatically inherit context; it must be explicitly included in their invocation prompt.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

A coordinator needs both a web search subagent and a document analysis subagent to run concurrently rather than one after another. How should the coordinator invoke them?

options.text: Two separate Task tool calls made in two separate coordinator turns
Multiple Task tool calls emitted in a single coordinator response
One combined subagent that does both jobs
Sequential invocation is the only supported pattern

architect-foundations.explanation: Emitting multiple Task tool calls in a single coordinator response runs subagents concurrently rather than sequentially.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

A search subagent times out. What should it report back to the coordinator?

options.text: An empty result set marked as a success
Structured error context: failure type, what was attempted, any partial results, possible alternatives
A generic "search unavailable" string
Nothing — silently retry indefinitely without reporting

architect-foundations.explanation: Structured error context (failure type, attempted action, partial results, alternatives) lets the coordinator make an informed recovery decision. Silently succeeding (A) or vague strings (C) hide information; runaway retries (D) risk resource exhaustion without reporting.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

The synthesis subagent needs to verify simple facts (dates, names, statistics) very frequently — 85% of verification needs are simple, 15% require deep investigation. Routing every check through the coordinator adds significant latency. What's the best fix?

options.text: Give the synthesis agent full access to all search tools
Give the synthesis agent one scoped `verify_fact` tool for the common case; keep coordinator routing for complex cases
Batch all verifications to run at the very end of the pipeline
Remove verification entirely to save time

architect-foundations.explanation: Giving the synthesis agent one scoped tool for the common, simple case follows least-privilege while avoiding unnecessary coordinator round-trips; the rare complex case still routes through the coordinator.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

Two credible sources report different figures for the same statistic. What should the synthesis output do?

options.text: Use whichever source is more recent, silently
Average the two figures
Preserve both values with source attribution and flag the discrepancy
Omit the statistic entirely

architect-foundations.explanation: Conflicting credible sources should be preserved with attribution and flagged, never silently reconciled by picking or averaging one value.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

A subagent's findings are passed to the synthesis agent as a single block of unstructured prose, and the final report loses track of which claim came from which source. What's the fix?

options.text: Have the coordinator manually re-attribute claims after the fact
Require subagents to output structured claim-source mappings (claim, excerpt, source, date) that synthesis preserves
Reduce the number of subagents to avoid attribution complexity
Have the synthesis agent guess the most likely source based on writing style

architect-foundations.explanation: Structured claim-source mappings preserve provenance through synthesis; unstructured prose loses which claim came from which source.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

A coordinator's `allowedTools` list does not include `"Task"`. What happens when it tries to delegate to a subagent?

options.text: It works normally; `Task` is always available
It cannot spawn subagents at all
It spawns subagents but without passing context
It falls back to a built-in tool automatically

architect-foundations.explanation: The `Task` tool must be in `allowedTools` for a coordinator to spawn subagents at all.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

After a subagent crash mid-run, the coordinator needs to resume without losing prior progress. What's the recommended pattern?

options.text: Restart the entire pipeline from scratch every time
Each agent exports state to a known location; the coordinator loads a manifest on resume and re-injects it
Rely on the model's memory of the prior session
Manually re-type a summary of progress into the next prompt

architect-foundations.explanation: Structured state exports plus a coordinator-loaded manifest on resume is the recommended crash-recovery pattern.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

A report needs to include findings from sources published a decade apart, describing what appear to be conflicting figures. What should the synthesis output require to avoid misinterpreting a genuine trend as a contradiction?

options.text: Publication or data-collection dates on each finding
A single averaged figure across all sources
Removal of the older sources entirely
A confidence score attached to the more recent figure only

architect-foundations.explanation: Publication/collection dates let genuine change over time be distinguished from an apparent contradiction between sources.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A developer needs to find every file matching `**/*.config.ts` across a large repository. Which built-in tool is correct?

options.text: `Grep`
`Glob`
`Read`
`Edit`

architect-foundations.explanation: `Glob` matches file paths/names by pattern.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A developer needs to find every place in the codebase that calls a specific function by name. Which built-in tool is correct?

options.text: `Grep`
`Glob`
`Write`
`Bash` with no arguments

architect-foundations.explanation: `Grep` searches file *contents*, which is what's needed to find function callers.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A connected MCP server exposes a `trace_dependencies` tool that's meaningfully more capable than manually chaining `Grep` and `Read`, but the agent keeps using `Grep` instead. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: MCP tools are always deprioritized versus built-ins and this can't be changed
The MCP tool's description doesn't make a strong enough case for its capability relative to the familiar built-in
