The MCP server is misconfigured at the network level
`Grep` needs to be removed from the tool list entirely

architect-foundations.explanation: A thin MCP tool description loses to a familiar built-in by default; enhancing the description (not removing the built-in) is the fix.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

An `Edit` call fails because the anchor text it's trying to match appears more than once in the file. What's the reliable fallback?

options.text: Retry `Edit` with the exact same input
Use `Read` to load the full file, then `Write` the corrected version
Use `Grep` to force a unique match
Skip the edit and ask the user to do it manually

architect-foundations.explanation: When `Edit`'s anchor text isn't unique, `Read` + `Write` is the reliable fallback for a full-file rewrite.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A productivity agent needs credentials for a shared, team-wide MCP server, and the token must never be committed to git. Where should this be configured?

options.text: `~/.claude.json` with the token hardcoded
`.mcp.json` with `${TOKEN_NAME}` environment variable expansion
Directly inside `CLAUDE.md`
A comment at the top of the relevant source file

architect-foundations.explanation: Project-scoped `.mcp.json` with environment-variable expansion keeps credentials out of version control while remaining shared team config.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A developer wants a personal, experimental MCP server that only they use, without affecting teammates. Where should it be configured?

options.text: `.mcp.json` in the repo
`~/.claude.json`
`.claude/rules/`
A shared team wiki page

architect-foundations.explanation: `~/.claude.json` is the user-scoped location for personal/experimental servers.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

After several hours of exploring a large, unfamiliar codebase, Claude starts giving vague answers about "typical patterns" instead of referencing the specific classes it found earlier. What's the most direct fix?

options.text: Restart with no context
Maintain a scratchpad file recording key findings for the agent to reference
Switch to a different model mid-session
Increase `max_tokens`

architect-foundations.explanation: A scratchpad file persisting key findings counters context degradation in long exploration sessions.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A developer wants to build understanding of an unfamiliar codebase efficiently, without reading every file upfront. What's the recommended exploration pattern?

options.text: Use `Read` on every file in the repository first
Start with `Grep` to find entry points, then `Read` to follow imports and trace flow
Use `Bash` to `cat` the entire repo into one context block
Ask the user to describe the codebase verbally instead of exploring it

architect-foundations.explanation: Starting with `Grep` for entry points, then `Read` to follow imports, builds understanding incrementally without reading everything upfront.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A generic tool named `process_data` is used for three very different jobs: extracting data points, summarizing content, and verifying claims — and the agent frequently uses it incorrectly. After improving the description doesn't fully resolve the confusion, what's the next step on the fix ladder?

options.text: Add ten few-shot examples immediately, skipping other options
Split `process_data` into purpose-specific tools: `extract_data_points`, `summarize_content`, `verify_claim`
Remove the tool entirely
Rename it without changing its scope

architect-foundations.explanation: Splitting an overly generic tool into purpose-specific tools is the next rung on the fix ladder once description improvements alone haven't fully resolved confusion.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A team wants to give a productivity agent both `Read`/`Write`/`Bash` and 15 additional MCP tools for various integrations, all available at once. Recent logs show increasing tool misuse. What's the likely cause and fix?

options.text: The model needs a larger context window
Too many available tools increases decision complexity and misuse risk; scope tools per task/role instead
`Bash` should be removed since it's the most dangerous tool
The system prompt needs to list all 18 tools more explicitly

architect-foundations.explanation: Too many available tools increases selection complexity and misuse; scoping tools per task/role is the fix, not a bigger context window or removing a single tool.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

A CI job runs `claude "Summarize the diff and flag risky changes"` and hangs indefinitely, waiting for input. What's the fix?

options.text: Add the `-p` (or `--print`) flag
Set an environment variable to disable interactivity
Pipe an empty file into the command as a workaround
Add a `--ci` flag

architect-foundations.explanation: `-p` / `--print` runs Claude Code non-interactively, which is required in automated pipelines. (B and D describe flags/variables that don't exist — a common distractor pattern.)

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

You want automated PR review findings posted as machine-parseable inline comments. What CLI options should you use?

options.text: `--verbose` and `--debug`
`--output-format json` combined with `--json-schema`
`--print` alone is sufficient
`--format text`

architect-foundations.explanation: `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` produces machine-parseable structured findings suitable for automated PR comments.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

The same Claude Code session that generated a bug fix is also used to review that fix before merge, and subtle logic issues are consistently missed. Why?

options.text: The context window is too small
The same session retains its generation reasoning, making it less likely to challenge its own prior decisions
`--output-format json` wasn't set
The model needs more few-shot examples of "good reviews"

architect-foundations.explanation: A session that generated code retains its own reasoning and is less likely to challenge its own decisions; an independent instance reviews more effectively.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

Automated code review is producing a 40% false-positive rate concentrated in one finding category. The prompt already instructs the model to "only report high-confidence issues." What's the most effective next step?

options.text: Add "be even more careful" to the prompt
Define explicit, categorical criteria for that finding type, and consider temporarily disabling the category while iterating
Lower the sampling temperature
Permanently disable all review categories

architect-foundations.explanation: Vague instructions like "be conservative" don't meaningfully reduce false positives; explicit categorical criteria do, and temporarily disabling a high-false-positive category protects trust while iterating.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

A team wants Claude Code's automated review to avoid duplicate comments across re-runs after new commits are pushed to a PR. What should be included in context on re-runs?

options.text: Nothing — each run should be fully independent
The prior review's findings, with instructions to report only new or still-unaddressed issues
The full git history of the repository
A count of how many times the PR has been reviewed

architect-foundations.explanation: Including prior findings and instructing the model to report only new/unaddressed issues avoids duplicate PR comments across re-runs.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

A single-pass review across a 15-file PR produces inconsistent depth — some files get thorough feedback, others get superficial comments, and the same pattern is flagged in one file but approved in another. What's the fix?

options.text: Use a model with a larger context window
Split into per-file local-analysis passes, plus a separate cross-file integration pass
Require developers to submit smaller PRs
Run the same single pass three times and vote on findings

architect-foundations.explanation: Splitting into per-file passes plus a separate cross-file integration pass avoids the attention dilution causing inconsistent, contradictory findings.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

A team wants to reduce API costs on two workflows: (1) a blocking pre-merge check developers wait on, and (2) an overnight technical-debt report. Which should move to the Message Batches API?

options.text: Both
Only the overnight report; keep the pre-merge check synchronous
Only the pre-merge check
Neither, since batch API doesn't support any CI use case

architect-foundations.explanation: The Batch API's lack of a latency SLA makes it unsuitable for blocking workflows; it's appropriate only for the latency-tolerant overnight report.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

Test generation is producing many low-value, duplicate tests that already exist in the suite. What's the most direct fix?

options.text: Increase `max_tokens` for the generation call
Provide existing test files in context, and document testing standards/fixtures in `CLAUDE.md`
Disable test generation entirely
Ask developers to write all tests manually going forward

architect-foundations.explanation: Providing existing test files in context and documenting standards/fixtures in `CLAUDE.md` reduces duplicate, low-value test generation.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

A CI review pipeline needs its findings to be reliably parseable by a downstream bot that posts PR comments. Which is the most robust approach?

options.text: Ask the model nicely in the prompt to "format your response as JSON"
Use `--output-format json` with a `--json-schema` to enforce structure
Parse the model's free-text output with regular expressions
Manually reformat the output after each run

architect-foundations.explanation: Enforced structured output via CLI flags is far more reliable than asking nicely in a prompt or parsing free text with regex.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

Documented testing standards live only in a senior engineer's head and aren't written anywhere the CI pipeline's Claude Code invocation can access. What's the fix?

options.text: Rely on the model's general knowledge of "good tests"
Document testing standards, valuable test criteria, and available fixtures in `CLAUDE.md`
Ask the senior engineer to review every PR manually instead
Add the standards to a Slack channel pinned message

architect-foundations.explanation: Documenting standards in `CLAUDE.md` makes them available to every Claude Code invocation, including CI, instead of living only in one person's head.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

An extraction pipeline using `tool_use` with a strict JSON schema never produces malformed JSON, but sometimes produces line items that don't sum to the stated total. What does this indicate, and what's the fix?

options.text: The schema itself is broken; add more `required` fields
This is a semantic error, not a syntax error; add a `calculated_total` field to compare against `stated_total`
Switch away from `tool_use` to plain text JSON
Reduce `max_tokens` to force shorter output

architect-foundations.explanation: `tool_use` with a schema eliminates syntax errors but not semantic ones; comparing a calculated total against the stated total catches this class of mismatch.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

You have three separate extraction schemas (invoice, receipt, contract) and don't know the document type in advance, but want to guarantee some structured extraction occurs. Which `tool_choice` setting is correct?

options.text: `"auto"`
`"any"`
A forced call to one specific schema's tool
Omitting `tool_choice`

architect-foundations.explanation: `tool_choice: "any"` guarantees a tool call happens while still letting the model choose which of several schemas fits.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

A required field, `purchase_order_number`, keeps failing validation because the source document genuinely never contains a PO number anywhere. What should you do?

options.text: Keep retrying with the same prompt
Make the field nullable/optional instead of required
Fabricate a placeholder value so validation passes
Increase `max_tokens` and try again

architect-foundations.explanation: When information is genuinely absent from the source, no amount of retrying will produce it; the field should be nullable instead of required.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

A retry is needed because a nested array of line items was incorrectly flattened into a single string on the first extraction attempt. What should the retry prompt include?

options.text: Only a repeated instruction to "format correctly this time"
The original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error describing the flattening problem
A completely different, unrelated example document
Nothing further — the model should self-correct silently

architect-foundations.explanation: This is a structural, retry-fixable error — the retry needs the specific validation error to correct against.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

Two tools have nearly identical descriptions, causing selection confusion, and you've already rewritten both descriptions with clear boundaries — but genuinely ambiguous edge cases still cause mistakes. What's the next lever?

options.text: 2–4 few-shot examples showing correct selection with reasoning for the ambiguous cases
Force `tool_choice` to always pick one tool
Merge the tools into one
Increase `max_tokens`

architect-foundations.explanation: Once description improvements are exhausted, few-shot examples with reasoning are the next lever for genuinely ambiguous residual cases.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

An extraction pipeline reports 97% overall field accuracy. A stakeholder wants to reduce human review before fully trusting this number. What should happen first?

options.text: Immediately reduce human review across the board, since 97% is high
Validate accuracy broken down by document type and field, since aggregate accuracy can mask segment-level failure
Round the accuracy up to 100% for reporting purposes
Stop measuring accuracy since it's already high enough

architect-foundations.explanation: Aggregate accuracy can mask segment-level failure; validating by document type and field is required before reducing review.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

You want to catch novel extraction error patterns that wouldn't normally be reviewed, since your review process currently only samples low-confidence extractions. What should you add?

options.text: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions
A rule to never review high-confidence extractions
A fixed weekly quota of 10 reviews regardless of confidence
Removing confidence scoring entirely

architect-foundations.explanation: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions is specifically designed to catch novel error patterns that a confidence-based review process would otherwise never see.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

Your team wants to move a blocking, pre-merge invoice-validation workflow to the Message Batches API to save 50% on cost. Is this appropriate?

options.text: Yes, always — batch API should be used wherever possible for cost savings
No — batch processing has no latency SLA and can take up to 24 hours, making it unsuitable for a blocking workflow
Yes, as long as `custom_id` is set correctly
Only if the invoices are small in size

architect-foundations.explanation: The Batch API's lack of a latency SLA (up to 24 hours) makes it unsuitable for any blocking, pre-merge/pre-approval workflow.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

An extraction schema needs to categorize expenses, but the fixed set of categories won't cover every real-world case that will eventually appear. What schema design pattern handles this best?

options.text: A required `category` string field with no constraints
An `enum` field with a defined set of categories plus an `"other"` value and a `category_detail` string field
A free-text field parsed later with regular expressions
Omitting the category field entirely

architect-foundations.explanation: An `enum` plus `"other"` and a detail string handles extensibility without over-fitting to a fixed list or silently misclassifying novel cases.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

After several extraction pipeline iterations, the team wants to systematically analyze which document patterns most often trigger validation errors or get dismissed as false positives by downstream reviewers. What should be added to each structured finding?

options.text: A random UUID per finding
A `detected_pattern` field describing what triggered the finding
A free-text comment box with no structure
Nothing — this requires a separate ML model to analyze

architect-foundations.explanation: A `detected_pattern` field enables systematic, aggregate analysis of which patterns trigger errors or get dismissed as false positives over time.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

Your support agent has tools `get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, and `escalate_to_human`. A customer says "I want to speak to a manager right now" partway through a routine return. What should the agent do?

options.text: Offer a discount to de-escalate before considering a transfer
Ask one clarifying question to see if the issue can still be resolved
Escalate immediately, without attempting further investigation
Continue investigating the return since it's already 80% resolved

architect-foundations.explanation: An explicit request to escalate must be honored immediately, without further investigation, since customer-requested escalation overrides progress-based reasoning. Continuing to investigate because the return is "80% done" (D) ignores the customer's stated preference.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

`lookup_order` returns three possible matches for the identifiers provided. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Select the most recently placed order
Select the order with the highest dollar value, since it's likely the one in dispute
Process against all three and let the customer confirm afterward
Ask the customer for an additional identifier to disambiguate

architect-foundations.explanation: Multiple ambiguous matches should never be resolved by a heuristic guess like recency or dollar value; the safe move is asking for one more identifier to disambiguate. Picking heuristically risks acting on the wrong customer's order entirely.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

A refund-authorization hook blocks `process_refund` for amounts over $500 and redirects to `escalate_to_human`. An engineer proposes removing the hook and instead adding "never approve refunds over $500 without escalation" to the system prompt, arguing it's simpler to maintain. What is the main risk?

options.text: Prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate; the guarantee becomes probabilistic instead of deterministic
Removing the hook would violate the MCP specification
None — a clear instruction is just as reliable as a hook
The system prompt has a hard character limit that would be exceeded

architect-foundations.explanation: Prompt instructions carry a non-zero, probabilistic failure rate, so removing the hook trades a deterministic $500 threshold guarantee for something the model can occasionally ignore. Neither MCP compliance nor prompt length is actually at issue here.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

A customer's message covers two unrelated concerns: a billing dispute and a shipping delay. What is the best decomposition strategy?

options.text: Escalate immediately since multi-concern messages are inherently too complex
Ask the customer to restate their message as two separate, single-issue messages
Resolve only the first concern mentioned and ask the customer to open a second ticket for the other
Decompose into the two distinct items, investigate each using shared context, then synthesize one unified response

architect-foundations.explanation: Decomposing into the two distinct concerns, investigating each with shared context, then synthesizing one reply mirrors the exam's decomposition pattern (like per-file-then-cross-file review). Deferring one concern to a separate ticket (C) needlessly fragments the interaction when the agent already has what it needs to handle both.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

When escalating a case the agent cannot resolve, what should the handoff to the human agent include?

options.text: Just the customer's most recent message, since the human can read the full transcript
A confidence score representing how hard the case is
A structured summary: customer details, root cause analysis, and a recommended action
Only the customer ID, so the human starts the investigation fresh

architect-foundations.explanation: Since the human has no transcript access, the handoff must substitute for that missing context with customer details, root-cause analysis, and a recommended action. A bare customer ID or last message (A/D) forces the human to re-investigate from zero.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

`get_customer` and `lookup_order` are frequently confused by the model when a customer says "check on order #12345." Descriptions are minimal ("Retrieves customer information" / "Retrieves order details"). What should you try first?

options.text: Expand each description with input formats, example queries, and explicit "use this vs. that" boundaries
Add 8–10 few-shot examples of correct routing
Merge the two tools into one generic `lookup` tool
Build a keyword pre-router that inspects the message before the model sees it

architect-foundations.explanation: Description quality is always the lowest-effort, highest-leverage first fix for tool-selection confusion — before few-shot examples or structural changes. Merging the tools (C) would erase the very signal that lets the model discriminate between customer and order lookups.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

After a 20-turn conversation about a $215 refund on order #4471, the conversation is summarized to save tokens. The summary says "customer wants a refund," and the agent later asks the customer to repeat the amount and order number. What's the most direct fix?

options.text: Maintain a persistent "case facts" block (amount, order ID, dates) carried in every prompt outside the narrative summary
Disable summarization entirely for all conversations
Ask the customer to always begin messages with their order number
Switch to a model with a larger context window

architect-foundations.explanation: A persistent case-facts block for the amount and order ID, carried outside the narrative summary, survives compression that plain-prose summarization won't. Disabling summarization outright (B) is a blunt fix that reintroduces the token-bloat problem it was solving.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

Your team wants the agent to self-report a 1–10 confidence score and auto-escalate anything below 6, replacing explicit escalation criteria. What is the concern with this approach?

options.text: Confidence scores require a separate fine-tuned model to produce
This approach violates MCP resource specifications
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated — the model is often confidently wrong on exactly the hardest cases
Confidence scores can only be produced when using extended thinking

architect-foundations.explanation: Self-reported confidence scores are poorly calibrated, and models tend to be most confidently wrong on exactly the hardest cases — the opposite of what an auto-escalation gate needs. This is a calibration problem inherent to self-assessment, not a tooling or fine-tuning limitation (A, D).

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

(Select TWO) Which two error-reporting practices should an MCP tool AVOID when `lookup_order` fails due to a backend timeout?

options.text: Returning an empty result set marked as a successful, valid query
Returning `isError: true` with `errorCategory: "transient"` and `isRetryable: true`
Returning a generic "Operation failed" string with no other metadata
Returning the timeout duration and the specific query attempted

architect-foundations.explanation: Masking a timeout as a successful empty result (A) hides a real failure from the caller, and a bare "Operation failed" string (C) strips away the category and retryability info needed to react. B and D are the recommended structured practices (categorized retryable errors, useful diagnostic detail), not things to avoid.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

The agent has grown to 18 available tools across support, billing, and shipping functions, and tool-selection accuracy has degraded noticeably. What is the most appropriate fix?

options.text: Force `tool_choice` to a single always-used tool
Add a 20-example few-shot block covering every tool combination
Scope each agent/role to only the 4–6 tools relevant to it
Increase `max_tokens` so the model has more room to reason about tool choice

architect-foundations.explanation: Scoping each agent/role to the 4–6 tools it actually needs directly reduces the decision surface causing misselection. Forcing a single tool (A) or adding more few-shot coverage (B) doesn't address the root cause of too many overlapping options in one place.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

Which best describes why a programmatic prerequisite (blocking `process_refund` until `get_customer` returns a verified ID) is preferred over prompt wording for identity verification?

options.text: It provides a deterministic guarantee instead of relying on probabilistic model compliance
It's the only way to satisfy MCP's `isError` requirement
It is required by the Message Batches API
It reduces the number of tokens used per turn

architect-foundations.explanation: A hard prerequisite gives a deterministic guarantee that refunds can never fire before identity is verified, whereas any prompt-based rule is only probabilistically followed. This is the exam's central "structural fix beats prompt fix" lesson, not an MCP or token-budget issue (B, D).

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

A customer explicitly states policy allows price matching only against the company's own past sales, but asks for a price match against a competitor — a case the policy doesn't address either way. What should the agent do?

options.text: Offer a partial discount as a compromise
Escalate, since the policy is silent/ambiguous on this specific request
Deny the request, since it wasn't explicitly permitted
Approve the request, since it wasn't explicitly denied

architect-foundations.explanation: Silence in policy is treated the same as ambiguity: escalate rather than let the agent invent a resolution either way. Approving (D) or denying (C) both assume an answer the policy doesn't actually give.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

Which is the correct interpretation of a `PostToolUse` hook's role, given `lookup_order` returns Unix timestamps and `get_customer` returns ISO 8601 dates?

options.text: It's used to route the request to a different subagent
It's used to normalize the two different date formats into one consistent format before the model reasons over them
It's used to cache results across sessions
It's used to block a tool call before it executes

architect-foundations.explanation: A PostToolUse hook is the right place to normalize disparate tool output formats (Unix timestamps vs. ISO 8601) into one consistent representation before the model reasons over them. It doesn't block calls before execution (D) — that's a pre-call/interception hook's job.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

Sentiment analysis is added to detect customer frustration and auto-escalate above a threshold. Escalation rates go up sharply, but first-contact resolution doesn't improve, and some genuinely simple cases now escalate unnecessarily just because the customer sounded annoyed. What does this indicate?

options.text: The sentiment threshold was simply set too low
The agent needs more few-shot examples of angry customers
Sentiment doesn't reliably correlate with actual case complexity, so it's a poor escalation signal on its own
Sentiment analysis should be paired with a larger model

architect-foundations.explanation: Rising escalations without improved resolution, plus simple cases escalating just for sounding annoyed, is the signature of a signal that doesn't track actual complexity. Retuning the threshold (A) or adding more examples (B) would just move the same unreliable signal around rather than fix the mismatch.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

A customer says "I already tried this, just send me to a person," after the agent offers to help resolve a straightforward issue. What's the appropriate next step?

options.text: Honor the reiterated request and escalate
Continue offering the same resolution path, since the issue is within the agent's capability
Provide a partial refund automatically without further discussion
Ask one more diagnostic question to confirm the issue is really unresolved

architect-foundations.explanation: A reiterated, explicit request for a human takes priority over the agent's belief that the issue is simple; explicit requests get honored immediately rather than re-litigated. Asking one more diagnostic question (D) directly contradicts the customer's stated preference.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

A coordinator delegates to a web-search subagent and a document-analysis subagent. For the coordinator to invoke either one, what must be true?

options.text: Both subagents must share the coordinator's full conversation history automatically
The subagents must be configured with `context: fork`
The coordinator must run in plan mode
The coordinator's `allowedTools` must include `"Task"`

architect-foundations.explanation: The coordinator can only invoke subagents through the Task tool, so it must appear in `allowedTools`; nothing about shared history, fork context, or plan mode is a real prerequisite for delegation.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

All subagents in a research pipeline complete successfully and report no errors, yet the final report covers only 30% of the requested topic. Where should you look first?

options.text: The web-search subagent's result ranking
The document-analysis subagent's summarization fidelity
The coordinator's task decomposition logs
The synthesis subagent's writing quality

architect-foundations.explanation: When every subagent succeeds at its assigned slice but overall coverage is narrow, the defect lives upstream in what the coordinator chose to assign, not in how well any individual subagent executed its own task.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

The synthesis subagent needs the findings gathered by the web-search and document-analysis subagents. What must happen for it to have that information?

options.text: Nothing — subagents automatically share a session-scoped memory pool
The synthesis subagent must call `fork_session` to inherit prior context
The coordinator must explicitly include the complete findings in the synthesis subagent's prompt
The findings are inherited automatically as long as all subagents share the same `AgentDefinition`

architect-foundations.explanation: Subagents don't automatically inherit the coordinator's history, so findings must be explicitly written into the synthesis subagent's prompt; there's no automatic memory pool (A, D), and `fork_session` branches a session's own context rather than transferring another subagent's output (B).

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

The coordinator needs to run a web-search subtask and a document-analysis subtask concurrently rather than one after another. How should it do this?

options.text: Send both subtasks in separate turns but with the same `tool_use_id`
Use `fork_session` to duplicate the coordinator into two parallel coordinators
Set `tool_choice: "any"` on the coordinator's next call
Emit both `Task` tool calls within a single coordinator response

architect-foundations.explanation: Real concurrency requires the coordinator to emit both Task calls within one response so they execute in parallel; reusing a `tool_use_id` (A) is invalid, `fork_session` (B) duplicates a session rather than dispatching two subtasks, and `tool_choice: "any"` (C) only forces some tool call, not simultaneity.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

Two credible sources report different figures for the same statistic during synthesis. What should the final report do?

options.text: Preserve both values with source attribution, distinguishing well-established from contested findings
Average the two figures and report the average as the value
Silently prefer whichever source was retrieved most recently
Omit the statistic entirely since it can't be verified

architect-foundations.explanation: Preserving both values with attribution keeps the reader informed of a genuine disagreement; averaging (B) invents a number neither source reported, and recency bias (C) or omission (D) both discard real information.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

During synthesis, a claim's supporting excerpt is compressed for brevity, and the source URL originally attached to it is dropped in the process. What principle was violated?

options.text: The excerpt should have been translated into a different content type
Structured claim-source mappings must be preserved and merged through synthesis, not summarized away
The claim should have been paraphrased more aggressively, not less
The claim needed a confidence score instead of a source

architect-foundations.explanation: The source-to-claim mapping is exactly the provenance information synthesis must carry forward intact, not compress away in the name of brevity.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

A web-search subagent times out mid-query. What should it return to the coordinator?

options.text: An empty result set marked as a successful query
A retry loop that continues indefinitely until it succeeds
Nothing — the coordinator should assume failure from a lack of response
Structured error context: failure type, what was attempted, any partial results, and possible alternatives

architect-foundations.explanation: Structured failure context (failure type, what was attempted, partial results, alternatives) lets the coordinator make an informed recovery decision; masking it as success (A), retrying forever (B), or going silent (C) all destroy that information.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

A statistic in one subagent's findings comes from a report published two years ago, while another subagent's finding on the same metric is from last month. Synthesis treats these as contradictory. What was missing from the subagents' structured output?

options.text: A `retryable` boolean
A `confidence` field
An `errorCategory` field
Publication or data-collection dates, which would show this is a change over time rather than a contradiction

architect-foundations.explanation: Without publication or data-collection dates, synthesis has no way to distinguish a genuine change over time from a contradiction between two sources measuring the same thing at different times.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

The synthesis subagent frequently needs simple fact-checks (dates, names, statistics) — 85% of verification needs are simple, 15% require deep investigation. Routing every check through the coordinator to the web-search agent adds significant latency. What is the most balanced fix?

options.text: Batch all verification requests to run once at the end of the pipeline
Have the web-search subagent pre-cache anything it speculates might later be needed
Give the synthesis subagent full, unrestricted access to all search tools
Give the synthesis subagent one scoped `verify_fact` tool for the simple 85%, keep coordinator-routed delegation for the complex 15%

architect-foundations.explanation: A narrowly scoped `verify_fact` tool handles the high-frequency simple case without ballooning the synthesis agent's tool surface (unlike C), while the rarer complex 15% still routes through the coordinator as before; batching (A) or speculative caching (B) don't fix the routing overhead itself.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

A coordinator decomposes "impact of remote work on urban commercial real estate" into three subtasks: "office vacancy rates downtown," "office vacancy rates in suburbs," and "office leasing trends." The resulting report never touches retail or residential conversion angles. What is the root cause?

options.text: The coordinator's task decomposition was too narrow, missing entire relevant sub-domains of the topic
The web-search subagent didn't search broadly enough
The document-analysis subagent filtered out irrelevant sources
The synthesis subagent lacked writing guidance on breadth

architect-foundations.explanation: All three subtasks are narrow slices of the same angle (vacancy/leasing), so no subagent was ever asked to look at retail or residential conversion — the gap originates in decomposition, not execution.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

After reviewing a first-pass synthesis output, the coordinator identifies that the "counterarguments" section is thin. What is the appropriate next action, consistent with iterative refinement of multi-agent research?

options.text: Publish the report as-is; thoroughness is the synthesis agent's sole responsibility
Lower the temperature and regenerate synthesis from the same inputs
Ask the user to manually supply counterarguments
Re-delegate to search/analysis subagents with targeted follow-up queries, then re-invoke synthesis

architect-foundations.explanation: A thin section reflects missing evidence, not bad prose, so the fix is gathering more findings via targeted follow-up delegation and re-synthesizing; regenerating at a different temperature (B) can't manufacture counterarguments that were never collected.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

Which best distinguishes a subagent's isolated context from the coordinator's context?

options.text: Subagents inherit context only during the first invocation of a session
Subagents do not automatically inherit the coordinator's conversation history; relevant context must be explicitly passed in
Subagents share the coordinator's memory but not its tool access
Subagents inherit context if and only if they use the same underlying model

architect-foundations.explanation: Isolation is the default behavior; relevant context must be explicitly passed in, not automatically shared via memory (C) or matched via model identity (D).

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

A research pipeline crashes mid-run due to an infrastructure failure. What design allows the coordinator to resume cleanly?

options.text: Each agent exporting state to a known location; the coordinator loads a manifest on resume and re-injects it
Relying on the model to recall its own prior progress from training data
Restarting from scratch and re-running every subagent regardless of prior progress
Keeping all state only in the coordinator's in-memory variables

architect-foundations.explanation: Externalized per-agent state plus a coordinator-read manifest is what makes clean resume possible after an infrastructure crash; relying on model recall (B) or blind full restarts (C) can't actually recover prior progress.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

The synthesis subagent is given tools for web search, document parsing, and fact verification "just in case it needs them for edge cases." What risk does this create?

options.text: It requires `fork_session` to function correctly
It has no real downside since unused tools cost nothing
Agents with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them (e.g., a synthesis agent attempting its own web searches)
It will always outperform a narrowly-scoped agent

architect-foundations.explanation: Tools outside an agent's specialization invite misuse (a synthesis agent wandering into its own web searches), which is the real cost — "unused tools cost nothing" (B) ignores exactly this selection risk.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

Structured findings from subagents should separate content from metadata. Which of these best exemplifies that separation?

options.text: Separate fields for `claim`, `evidence_excerpt`, `source_url`, and `publication_date`
A markdown-formatted paragraph with inline citations
A single string like `"Retail vacancy hit 18% (Source: CBRE, March 2026, cbre.com/report-2026)"`
A raw dump of the source webpage's HTML

architect-foundations.explanation: Separate fields for claim, excerpt, source, and date keep content and provenance metadata independently addressable through further processing; a formatted string (C) or prose paragraph (B) bakes metadata into content where it's easily lost or mis-parsed.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A developer wants to find every file that calls a specific exported function across a large codebase. Which built-in tool is the right starting point?

options.text: `Read`, applied to every file in the repo
`Bash` with no specific command needed
`Grep`, since it searches file contents for the function name
`Glob`, since it searches by pattern

architect-foundations.explanation: Grep searches file contents for the function name, which is exactly what's needed to find every call site; Glob only matches file paths/names, not the code inside them.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A developer wants to locate every test file in a monorepo matching `**/*.test.tsx` regardless of directory. Which tool is correct?

options.text: `Write`
`Grep`
`Glob`
`Edit`

architect-foundations.explanation: Glob does file-path pattern matching, which is precisely suited to a glob pattern like `**/*.test.tsx`; Grep searches file contents, not paths.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

`Edit` repeatedly fails on a file because the anchor text it's trying to match appears multiple times. What is the recommended fallback?

options.text: Switch to `Bash` with `sed` exclusively
Use `Read` to load the full file, then `Write` the corrected full content
Split the file into smaller files first
Increase `max_tokens` and retry `Edit`

architect-foundations.explanation: When an anchor string isn't unique, Edit can't reliably target the right occurrence, so loading the full file with Read and rewriting it with Write sidesteps the ambiguity entirely; switching to sed loses the model's understanding of context and isn't the documented fallback.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A team keeps a company-wide MCP server for Jira in `.mcp.json`, using `${JIRA_TOKEN}` for the credential. A developer also wants to experiment with a personal, unreleased MCP server without affecting teammates. Where should the personal server be configured?

options.text: It cannot be done without modifying the shared repo config
In `CLAUDE.md` as a code block
In `.mcp.json` with a different key
In `~/.claude.json`

architect-foundations.explanation: Personal/experimental MCP servers belong in the user-scoped `~/.claude.json`, keeping them invisible to teammates; putting it in `.mcp.json` (even under a different key) would land in the shared, version-controlled team config.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

Claude Code keeps preferring `Grep` over a connected MCP server's more powerful `search_codebase` tool, even though the MCP tool would give better results for the developer's query. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: MCP tools always lose to built-in tools by design and this can't be changed
The MCP tool is broken; disable `Grep` entirely
The MCP tool's description under-sells its capability relative to the well-known built-in tool; improve the description to clarify when and why to prefer it
Switch the MCP server from project scope to user scope

architect-foundations.explanation: Claude has a strong prior toward familiar built-ins like Grep, so an under-described MCP tool loses out by default; the fix is enhancing the description to make the capability advantage explicit, not disabling Grep or changing server scope.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A developer wants a "codebase exploration" skill whose verbose dependency-tracing output shouldn't clutter the main conversation. Which SKILL.md frontmatter option addresses this?

options.text: `argument-hint`
`paths`
`allowed-tools`
`context: fork`

architect-foundations.explanation: `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context so its verbose dependency-tracing output never pollutes the main conversation; `allowed-tools` restricts tool access, not output visibility.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A skill should be limited to file-write operations only, with no ability to run destructive `Bash` commands. Which frontmatter option enforces this?

options.text: There is no way to restrict a skill's tool access
`allowed-tools`
`argument-hint`
`context: fork`

architect-foundations.explanation: `allowed-tools` directly restricts which tools a skill can invoke, letting it be scoped to file-write only; `context: fork` isolates context/output, not tool permissions.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A new hire isn't receiving the team's established coding conventions, even though a senior engineer insists "it's all in CLAUDE.md." What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The conventions live in the senior engineer's user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which isn't shared via version control
CLAUDE.md files are cached and require a manual cache clear
The new hire's IDE isn't configured to load CLAUDE.md
The conventions are correctly placed in the project-level CLAUDE.md, and the new hire simply hasn't read it

architect-foundations.explanation: The classic failure mode is conventions living in the senior engineer's personal `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which never gets committed, so new hires cloning the repo never see them; this fits better than assuming the new hire simply skipped a file that was in fact correctly placed and shared.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A monorepo has React, API, and database-model layers, each with different conventions, plus test files scattered throughout every layer. What is the most maintainable way to apply testing conventions specifically, regardless of file location?

options.text: A `.claude/rules/testing.md` file with `paths: ["**/*.test.*"]` frontmatter
A skill that must be manually invoked before writing any test
Put a "Testing" section in the root CLAUDE.md and hope Claude infers when it applies
Add a CLAUDE.md to every directory that happens to contain a test file

architect-foundations.explanation: `.claude/rules/*.md` with `paths` frontmatter applies conventions by glob pattern regardless of directory, exactly matching test files scattered across layers; per-directory CLAUDE.md files don't scale and don't follow files that move.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A developer is asked to add comprehensive tests to a legacy codebase with no existing test coverage and unclear module boundaries. What task-decomposition approach fits best?

options.text: Map the codebase structure first, identify high-impact areas, then build a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered
A fixed, fully pre-specified sequential checklist decided before any exploration
Escalate to a human immediately since the task is too undefined for an agent
Write tests for every file in alphabetical order

architect-foundations.explanation: This is the textbook adaptive-decomposition case: with unclear module boundaries, mapping structure and prioritizing as dependencies are discovered beats any fixed upfront checklist, which can't account for what hasn't been explored yet.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A developer is debugging a single failing test with a clear stack trace pointing to one function. What's the appropriate mode?

options.text: Plan mode, to explore alternative architectures first
Fork the session to explore two different fixes in parallel
Direct execution, since the change is small and well-understood
Escalate to a second Claude instance for independent review before touching any code

architect-foundations.explanation: A clear stack trace pointing to one function is a well-understood, single-file fix, which is exactly when direct execution is appropriate; plan mode or parallel forking would be needless overhead for a task with no real ambiguity.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A developer describes a desired data-transformation function in prose, but Claude's implementation is inconsistent across attempts — sometimes handling edge cases differently. What is the most effective way to tighten the specification?

options.text: Lower `max_tokens` to force a more concise implementation
Provide 2–3 concrete input/output examples that pin down the exact expected transformation
Repeat the same prose instructions with more emphatic wording
Switch to a different model without changing the instructions

architect-foundations.explanation: Inconsistent handling across attempts signals genuine ambiguity in the prose spec, and concrete input/output examples pin down the exact expected behavior; repeating the same instructions more emphatically doesn't resolve ambiguity, it just restates it.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

Before implementing a caching layer in an unfamiliar part of the codebase, a developer wants Claude to surface considerations they might not have thought of — invalidation strategy, failure modes, TTL choices — before writing any code. What technique does this describe?

options.text: Plan mode is not applicable here since this is a single feature, not an architecture-wide task
The interview pattern — having Claude ask clarifying questions before implementation
Test-driven iteration
Prompt chaining

architect-foundations.explanation: The interview pattern — having Claude surface open design questions before implementing — is designed for exactly this kind of unfamiliar-domain uncertainty; test-driven iteration assumes you can already specify expected behavior, which is what's missing here.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A code-review request surfaces three findings that interact with each other (fixing one changes the correct fix for another). What's the better way to communicate them to Claude?

options.text: Ignore the interactions and let Claude discover them on its own
Provide all three interacting issues together in a single detailed message
Fix them one at a time in separate messages, waiting for each fix before mentioning the next
Ask Claude to pick which one to fix first

architect-foundations.explanation: Because the three findings interact, fixing one changes the correct fix for another, so they must be communicated together in one message; addressing them sequentially risks rework when an earlier "fix" is invalidated by a later one.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A team is restructuring a monolith into microservices — changes will span 45+ files, and there are multiple valid ways to draw service boundaries. What's the correct approach, and which subagent helps avoid exhausting context during the investigation phase?

options.text: Direct execution; no subagent is needed since this is primarily a refactor
Plan mode to explore and decide on an approach first, using the Explore subagent to isolate verbose discovery output
Direct execution with an extremely long, fully-detailed upfront prompt describing every service boundary
Plan mode, but skip subagents entirely to keep everything in one context

architect-foundations.explanation: Dozens of files with multiple valid service-boundary designs is squarely plan mode's use case, and the Explore subagent isolates the noisy discovery phase so it doesn't burn the main session's context; skipping subagents (D) forfeits that context-isolation benefit for no real gain.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

An extraction schema marks `contract_end_date` as a required field, but many contracts in the corpus are open-ended with no end date. What happens, and what's the fix?

options.text: Switch from `tool_use` to plain-text JSON output to avoid the issue
This is expected behavior and requires no change
The model may fabricate a plausible end date to satisfy the required constraint; make the field nullable/optional instead
Extraction will simply fail validation every time; the schema is unusable

architect-foundations.explanation: With no end date anywhere in many source contracts, forcing `contract_end_date` as required pressures the model to invent a plausible-looking date rather than admit absence; making it nullable/optional removes that pressure. D overstates the failure mode (validation wouldn't fail "every time" — it would silently succeed with fabricated data, which is the more dangerous outcome).

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

An extraction pipeline using `tool_use` with a strict JSON schema never produces malformed JSON, but sometimes produces line items that don't sum to the stated total. What does this indicate?

options.text: This is a semantic error, not a syntax error — add a `calculated_total` field to compare against `stated_total` and flag mismatches
Lowering `max_tokens` will resolve the inconsistency
The schema itself is broken and needs stricter typing
`tool_use` cannot guarantee numeric fields and should be abandoned for this use case

architect-foundations.explanation: `tool_use` with a schema guarantees syntactic validity but not semantic correctness, so line items can still fail to sum correctly; adding a `calculated_total` field to diff against `stated_total` catches exactly this class of error downstream. D is the tempting-but-wrong take — the tool is working as designed, so abandoning it throws out a mechanism that's already solving the syntax problem.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

You have three extraction schemas (invoice, receipt, contract) and don't know in advance which document type will arrive, but you want to guarantee some structured extraction occurs. Which `tool_choice` setting is correct?

options.text: `"auto"`
Omitting `tool_choice`
`{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"}`
`"any"`

architect-foundations.explanation: `"any"` forces the model to call some tool (guaranteeing structured output) while still letting it pick which of the three schemas fits the incoming document. `"auto"` (the tempting alternative) would let the model bail out with plain text on an ambiguous document, defeating the stated goal of guaranteeing extraction.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

An extraction validated against a JSON schema fails because a required field, `vendor_tax_id`, is missing. On investigation, the source document never contained a tax ID anywhere. What should happen next?

options.text: Recognize that retrying is unlikely to help since the information is genuinely absent from the source; the field should have been optional
Fabricate a placeholder value so the schema validates
Increase `max_tokens` and retry
Retry the extraction with the same prompt; retries usually resolve missing-field errors

architect-foundations.explanation: Since the tax ID is confirmed absent from the source document, no retry can manufacture data that was never there; the correct move is to accept the gap and make the field optional going forward. D is the trap: it assumes missing-field errors are generically retry-fixable, but that's only true for structural/formatting mistakes, not genuine source-data absence.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

A validation-retry loop for extraction failures should include which of the following in the follow-up request?

options.text: The original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error(s) that occurred
Only the original document, without reference to the prior failed attempt
A completely new document as a substitute
Only a generic instruction to "try again more carefully"

architect-foundations.explanation: An effective retry needs the original document, the prior failed output, and the specific validation error so the model has something concrete to correct against. A bare "try again" (D) or a fresh document with no error context (B, C) gives the model no signal about what actually went wrong.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

A finding-tracking system for a review pipeline adds a `detected_pattern` field to every flagged issue. What is this field's purpose?

options.text: To determine `isRetryable` status
To enable systematic analysis of which code constructs trigger findings, useful for spotting false-positive patterns developers repeatedly dismiss
To select which `tool_choice` mode to use next
To store the model's confidence score

architect-foundations.explanation: Tagging findings with `detected_pattern` turns individual fixes into aggregate data, letting you spot which constructs or patterns developers repeatedly dismiss as false positives and target prompt fixes at them. It's a tracking/analytics field, not a routing or scoring mechanism, so A/C/D misattribute its purpose.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

A code-review prompt already says "only report high-confidence findings," yet developers report 40% of flagged issues in the "style consistency" category are false positives. What's the most effective next step?

options.text: Lower the model's temperature setting
Permanently remove the category so it never generates findings again
Add "be even more conservative" to the prompt
Define explicit, categorical criteria for what specifically counts as a style issue vs. what doesn't, and consider temporarily disabling the category while iterating

architect-foundations.explanation: "Only report high-confidence findings" is already vague, and 40% false positives shows vague conservatism instructions don't work; the fix is explicit categorical criteria for what counts as a style issue, with temporary category suppression while iterating. C repeats the same failed pattern (more vague conservatism language) rather than fixing the underlying ambiguity.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

Few-shot examples are added to help a model select between two visually similar tools in ambiguous cases. What makes few-shot effective here, beyond simply showing input/output pairs?

options.text: Few-shot examples eliminate the need for good tool descriptions entirely
Showing the reasoning for why one tool was chosen over a plausible alternative helps the model generalize judgment to novel, unseen cases
Few-shot examples work only because they increase total prompt length
Few-shot examples are only useful for formatting, not for judgment calls

architect-foundations.explanation: Showing the reasoning behind choosing one tool over a plausible-but-wrong alternative teaches the model the underlying judgment, so it generalizes to new ambiguous cases rather than just memorizing the shown pairs. A overreaches — few-shot supplements good descriptions, it doesn't make them unnecessary.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

Your organization wants to move two workloads to the Message Batches API for its 50% cost savings: (a) an overnight technical-debt report and (b) a blocking pre-merge security gate that developers actively wait on. What's the correct call?

options.text: Batch both, with a real-time fallback triggered if the batch takes too long
Keep both synchronous, since batch correlation via `custom_id` is too error-prone
Batch both workloads
Batch only the overnight report; keep the pre-merge gate on synchronous calls

architect-foundations.explanation: The overnight report is latency-tolerant and fits batch's non-blocking, no-SLA processing window, but a pre-merge gate developers are actively waiting on needs real-time responsiveness batch can't guarantee. A's "real-time fallback" is tempting but adds complexity for a workflow that should never have been batched in the first place.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

A batch submission of 200 documents returns some failures. What's the correct remediation approach?

options.text: Switch failed documents to a completely different extraction schema
Identify the failed documents by `custom_id`, and resubmit only those, adjusting for the specific cause (e.g., chunking oversized documents)
Resubmit the entire batch of 200 documents from scratch
Discard the failed documents permanently since batch jobs cannot be retried

architect-foundations.explanation: Batch failures should be triaged individually via `custom_id`, with the specific cause addressed (e.g., splitting an oversized document) before resubmitting just those items. C wastes cost/time reprocessing 198 documents that already succeeded, which defeats the point of batch's cost savings.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

An extraction system reports 97% aggregate accuracy across all processed documents. A stakeholder asks whether this is sufficient to reduce human review. What should you check before answering?

options.text: Whether the model used `tool_choice: "auto"` or `"any"`
Only the accuracy of the single most common document type
Nothing further — 97% aggregate accuracy is sufficient on its own
Accuracy broken down by document type and by field, since aggregate metrics can mask poor performance on specific segments

architect-foundations.explanation: A 97% aggregate can mask a document type or field with much worse accuracy, so the honest answer requires breaking the metric down before making a review-reduction call. B is the near-miss — checking only the most common type still hides poor performance on rarer-but-consequential types/fields.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

To catch novel extraction error patterns that wouldn't normally be caught by reviewing low-confidence outputs, what technique should be applied to high-confidence extractions?

options.text: Re-run the same extraction twice and average the two outputs
Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions for ongoing error-rate measurement
Apply a stricter required-fields schema only to high-confidence cases
Skip reviewing them entirely, since they're already high-confidence

architect-foundations.explanation: Since low-confidence outputs get reviewed by default, novel error patterns hiding in *high*-confidence outputs are only caught by proactively sampling them (stratified random sampling) for ongoing measurement. D is the failure mode this technique exists to prevent — skipping high-confidence review entirely is exactly how these errors go undetected.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

Field-level confidence scores are being used to route extractions to human review. What should calibrate the routing thresholds?

options.text: An arbitrary fixed cutoff, e.g., always exactly 80%
The number of fields in the schema
Thresholds calibrated using labeled validation sets, so the confidence score maps to actual accuracy
The document's file size

architect-foundations.explanation: Thresholds are only meaningful if calibrated against labeled validation data so a given confidence score actually corresponds to a known accuracy rate; otherwise the score is just an arbitrary number. A's fixed 80% cutoff is the tempting-but-ungrounded choice — with no calibration, 80% could mean anything from 60% to 99% real accuracy.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

The same Claude session that generated a code fix is also used to review that fix before merge, and subtle logic errors are consistently missed. What's the underlying cause and the fix?

options.text: `--output-format json` needs to be enabled for accurate review
The session retains its generation reasoning and is less likely to challenge its own decisions; use an independent review instance without that prior context
The context window is too small for review tasks; use a larger model
The prompt lacks a sufficient number of few-shot examples of bugs

architect-foundations.explanation: The session carries its own generation-time reasoning, so it's biased toward defending its prior work rather than genuinely scrutinizing it — fresh independent instances lack that baggage and catch subtle issues more reliably. A stronger self-critical prompt can't overcome context the model already holds, since the bias is structural, not a wording problem.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

(Select TWO) Which two practices are appropriate when reviewing a 16-file pull request to avoid the attention dilution seen in single giant review passes?

options.text: Run one single-pass review across all 16 files simultaneously for maximum context
Split into focused per-file passes for local issues
Require exactly three independent full-PR passes and keep only majority-vote findings
Run a separate cross-file integration pass for data-flow issues spanning files

architect-foundations.explanation: Per-file passes give each file focused attention for local issues, while a separate cross-file pass specifically targets data-flow/integration issues that span files — together avoiding the attention dilution of one monolithic pass. A is the exact anti-pattern being guarded against, and C substitutes brute-force repetition and majority voting for a structurally sound decomposition.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A developer asks Claude to "clean up this parsing function" with no further detail. Three separate attempts produce three meaningfully different refactors, each reasonable in isolation but inconsistent with each other. What is the most effective way to converge on a consistent result?

options.text: Reduce `max_tokens` so the model has less room to improvise
Ask for five more attempts and pick the best one
Repeat the same request with stronger emphasis ("please be consistent this time")
Provide 2–3 concrete before/after examples showing exactly what "cleaned up" means for this codebase's style

architect-foundations.explanation: Three inconsistent refactors from the same vague instruction is a definitional-ambiguity problem, not a randomness problem, so 2–3 concrete before/after examples pinning down what "cleaned up" means fixes the actual cause. Reducing `max_tokens` or repeating the request with more emphasis doesn't resolve what "clean" means for this codebase.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

Before implementing a rate-limiting feature in a service Claude hasn't seen before, a developer wants Claude to first ask about traffic patterns, failure behavior under load, and whether limits should be per-user or global. What technique does this describe, and when is it most valuable?

options.text: Prompt chaining — valuable for any multi-step task regardless of familiarity
Plan mode — but only for single-file changes
Test-driven iteration — valuable only when a test suite already exists
The interview pattern — most valuable in unfamiliar domains where the developer may not have anticipated key design considerations

architect-foundations.explanation: Asking Claude to surface traffic-pattern, failure-mode, and scoping questions before writing any code is the interview pattern, and it earns its keep specifically in unfamiliar domains where the developer hasn't already anticipated every design consideration. Prompt chaining (A) sequences already-known steps rather than surfacing unknown design questions.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A team wants Claude to build a data-migration script and has already written a test suite covering expected behavior, edge cases (including null values), and performance constraints. What is the recommended way to use these tests during development?

options.text: Show Claude the tests once at the start, then ignore test results during implementation
Iterate by sharing test failures with Claude after each attempt, letting it progressively correct the implementation
Convert the tests into prose requirements instead of running them
Withhold the tests until the implementation is "done" so Claude isn't biased toward passing them narrowly

architect-foundations.explanation: With tests already covering behavior, edge cases, and performance up front, the recommended loop is to hand Claude the actual failures after each attempt so it can progressively converge. Showing tests once and then ignoring results (A), or withholding them until "done" (D), both break the feedback loop that makes test-driven iteration work.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A pull request fixes three bugs that interact — fixing bug 1 changes the correct approach to fixing bug 2. Which approach to communicating these to Claude is better?

options.text: Report each bug in a separate message, waiting for a fix before mentioning the next
Only describe the most severe bug and let Claude discover the other two independently
Ask Claude to guess which bugs might be related before describing any of them
Describe all three interacting issues together in one detailed message

architect-foundations.explanation: Because fixing bug 1 changes the correct approach to bug 2, the issues interact, and interacting issues must be described together in one detailed message so Claude reasons about them jointly. Reporting them one at a time (A) risks Claude fixing bug 2 in a way bug 1's fix later invalidates, forcing rework.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A team is deciding between a single-file bug fix (clear stack trace, one obvious cause) and a cross-service authentication redesign (multiple valid approaches, dozens of files). Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Direct execution for the bug fix; plan mode for the authentication redesign
Plan mode for both, since plan mode is always safer
Direct execution for both, since Claude Code doesn't meaningfully benefit from planning
Plan mode for the bug fix; direct execution for the redesign

architect-foundations.explanation: A single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace is the well-understood, low-ambiguity case direct execution suits, while a cross-service redesign with multiple valid approaches and dozens of files benefits from planning before committing to changes. Treating plan mode as "always safer" (B) ignores the needless overhead it adds on trivial, unambiguous fixes.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A `/deploy-check` slash command should run the team's pre-deployment checklist and be available to every developer immediately after cloning the repo. Where should it live?

options.text: `.claude/commands/deploy-check.md` in the repository
A `.claude/config.json` commands array
`~/.claude/commands/deploy-check.md`
Inside the root `CLAUDE.md` file as a named section

architect-foundations.explanation: A command every developer needs immediately after cloning must be version-controlled and project-scoped, which is exactly what `.claude/commands/deploy-check.md` provides. The personal `~/.claude/commands/` location (C) is never shared via git, so a fresh clone wouldn't have it.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A "brainstorm alternative approaches" skill tends to produce long, exploratory output that isn't useful to keep in the main conversation once a decision is made. Which frontmatter setting addresses this?

options.text: `context: fork`
`allowed-tools`
`paths`
`argument-hint`

architect-foundations.explanation: `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context, keeping the long exploratory brainstorm output out of the main conversation once a decision is made. `allowed-tools` (B) restricts which tools a skill can call, not where its output lands.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

Two engineers on the same team have different personal preferences for commit-message style, but the team's actual required conventions live correctly in the project-level CLAUDE.md. One engineer also has their personal preferences saved in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. What's true about this setup?

options.text: It's broken — user-level and project-level CLAUDE.md files cannot coexist
It's fine — the user-level file applies only to that engineer and doesn't affect teammates via version control
Only one CLAUDE.md file can be active per repository
The user-level file will silently overwrite the project-level file for everyone

architect-foundations.explanation: User-level and project-level CLAUDE.md files are designed to coexist and stack; the personal file at `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is never checked into version control, so it only affects that one engineer's own sessions. Claiming it "silently overwrites" the project file for everyone (D) misreads the hierarchy — personal preferences layer on top of, rather than replace, shared team conventions.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A large monorepo has different testing conventions for unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests, each identifiable by filename pattern but scattered across many directories. What's the best way to load the right convention automatically based on which file is being edited?

options.text: Three separate skills that must be manually invoked before editing each test type
Three separate directory-level CLAUDE.md files, duplicated into every directory containing tests
One root CLAUDE.md with three sections and hope Claude infers the right one
Three separate `.claude/rules/*.md` files, each with `paths` frontmatter matching the relevant filename pattern

architect-foundations.explanation: Because each convention is tied to a filename pattern rather than a single directory, three `.claude/rules/*.md` files with `paths` frontmatter load automatically based on which file is being edited, regardless of location. Duplicating directory-level CLAUDE.md files into every test directory (B) doesn't scale and invites drift.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A developer wants to compare two different caching strategies starting from the same point in their investigation of a codebase, without redoing the initial exploration twice. What capability supports this?

options.text: `--resume` with two different session names created independently
`/compact` run twice
`fork_session`, branching two parallel explorations from the shared baseline
Restarting from scratch for each strategy

architect-foundations.explanation: `fork_session` is built for exactly this: branching two parallel explorations from a shared baseline so the initial investigation isn't redone. Using `--resume` with two independently created session names (A) doesn't share a common starting point the way a fork does.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A developer resumes a two-day-old session to continue a refactor, but teammates modified several of the files Claude had already analyzed in that session. Claude's suggestions reference outdated function signatures. What should have been done?

options.text: Used `fork_session` instead of `--resume`
Started an entirely new session with zero context
Informed the resumed session explicitly about which files changed, prompting targeted re-analysis
Increased `max_tokens` for the resumed session

architect-foundations.explanation: Resuming a session doesn't make Claude aware that files changed since last time; the fix is explicitly telling it which files changed so it can do targeted re-analysis. Switching to `fork_session` (A) solves a different problem (parallel branching), not stale context in a resumed session.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A skill for generating boilerplate files should never be allowed to run destructive shell commands, even accidentally. Which frontmatter field enforces this restriction directly?

options.text: `argument-hint`
`paths`
`context: fork`
`allowed-tools`

architect-foundations.explanation: `allowed-tools` frontmatter directly restricts which tools a skill can invoke, so scoping it away from shell/`Bash` access structurally prevents destructive commands. `context: fork` (C) isolates output/context, it doesn't restrict tool access.

architect-foundations.q:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

A developer needs to trace how a specific exported utility function is used across a codebase, including through re-export wrapper modules with different names. What's the most effective approach?

options.text: First identify all exported names for the function (including wrapper re-exports), then `Grep` for each name across the codebase
`Read` every file in the repository upfront to build full context before searching
`Glob` for `**/*.ts` and manually scan the output
Ask the user to supply the call sites manually

architect-foundations.explanation: Wrapper re-exports mean the function may be called under several different names, so all of them must be enumerated before `Grep` can find every call site; grepping only the original name would miss usages through renamed re-exports.
