architect-professional.explanation: Modular instruction architecture reduces context cost and conflict. The team should preserve core policy, load specialized procedure only when relevant, enforce invariants outside the prompt, and validate behavior through evals.

architect-professional.q: A claims classifier performs well on obvious cases but confuses borderline exclusions. Which prompting intervention is most targeted?
architect-professional.domain: D2 Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering

options.text: Increase output length to 5,000 words
Add few-shot examples drawn from the difficult boundary cases with correct rationale and labels
Add a larger balanced sample of routine approved and denied claims so the model sees the overall label distribution, without emphasizing borderline exclusions
Tell the model it is a world-class classifier

architect-professional.explanation: Few-shot examples are most valuable where category boundaries are ambiguous. Representative hard cases teach the intended distinction, while easy repetition and personas do not address the observed failure.

architect-professional.q: A research agent repeatedly includes 200 pages of source material even though each question needs only a few sections. What is the best architecture?
architect-professional.domain: D2 Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering

options.text: Pre-summarize each source into a short paragraph, concatenate all summaries into a stable context, and retrieve from that compressed corpus without source-level provenance
Always select the largest context window
Retrieve and rank relevant sections, preserve provenance, and keep durable state outside the prompt
Drop source citations to save tokens

architect-professional.explanation: Context should carry the evidence needed for the current decision, not the entire corpus by default. Retrieval and durable state reduce bloat while provenance preserves verification.

architect-professional.q: A service repeats a long stable policy and tool catalog across requests. Which choices improve cache economics? Select all that apply.
architect-professional.domain: D2 Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering

options.text: Place the stable prefix before customer-specific content
Put tenant metadata first to bind every cached prefix
Measure cache creation, hit rate, latency, and cost
Keep reusable prefix bytes stable where practical

architect-professional.explanation: Prompt caching benefits from stable shared prefixes and empirical measurement. Volatile content near the beginning prevents reuse for everything that follows it.

architect-professional.q: Which content is best packaged as an Agent Skill instead of always placed in the root prompt? Select all that apply.
architect-professional.domain: D2 Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering

options.text: A universal safety rule that loads only after model risk detection
Reference files and scripts used by one specialized workflow
A domain playbook that should load when its task is detected
A reusable incident-analysis procedure needed only during incidents

architect-professional.explanation: Skills support progressive disclosure for reusable specialized procedure and assets. A safety invariant needed every time belongs in trusted core policy and deterministic controls.

architect-professional.q: Extended thinking improves one architecture-planning eval but causes the interactive service to miss its latency objective. What is the strongest response?
architect-professional.domain: D2 Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering

options.text: Keep extended thinking on the synchronous route and stream a generated progress explanation to users, because perceived responsiveness may offset the measured latency miss
Disable all reasoning features permanently
Ignore the latency objective
Use the measured gain only in an asynchronous or high-complexity route whose service objective can absorb it

architect-professional.explanation: Reasoning budget must fit the service and task. Routing difficult or asynchronous work to a higher-effort configuration preserves quality without violating the primary interactive path.

architect-professional.q: An enterprise agent loads 140 overlapping tools on every turn. Which redesigns are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Group capabilities into coherent domain surfaces
Use progressive discovery so detailed tools load only when relevant
Remove or merge overlapping tools based on trajectory evals
Keep all tools but shorten each description to one sentence

architect-professional.explanation: Capability bloat consumes context and increases selection ambiguity. Domain scoping, progressive discovery, and evidence-driven consolidation preserve useful reach with a smaller active surface.

architect-professional.q: An MCP tool accepts tenant_id and user_role directly from model arguments. Which corrections are required? Select all that apply.

options.text: Authorize the specific operation and resource on the server
Bind tenant and identity from the authenticated session
Trust schema-validated tenant and role arguments from the model
Treat model-provided role as advisory only, never proof of authority

architect-professional.explanation: Schema validity does not establish identity or permission. Authentication comes from trusted session state, and server-side authorization must constrain every resource and action.

architect-professional.q: A corpus contains long legal documents whose meaning depends on sections, clauses, and cross-references. Which chunking strategy is strongest?

options.text: Structure-aware chunks that retain section metadata, overlap where needed, and preserve document and clause identifiers
Fixed five-character chunks
Sentence-level chunks grouped into fixed windows after shuffling boilerplate clauses away, with the parent document ID retained for reconstruction
Uniform token-sized chunks with generous overlap and document IDs, because consistent embedding units simplify indexing and cross-document retrieval at scale

architect-professional.explanation: Structure-aware chunking preserves semantic units and provenance while keeping retrieval granular. Metadata and controlled overlap support cross-reference resolution and later citation checks.

architect-professional.q: A support assistant retrieves an obsolete cancellation policy even though the new policy is indexed. Which system change most directly addresses the defect?

options.text: Increase semantic-ranking weight for cancellation queries and ask the generator to compare any retrieved policy dates before choosing which passage to cite
Add version, effective-date, and authority metadata; filter or rank to the active policy and test freshness
Increase generation temperature
Remove all document identifiers

architect-professional.explanation: This is a retrieval-governance failure. Explicit authority and temporal metadata let the retriever select the active source and make freshness observable in tests and operations.

architect-professional.q: A product search must handle exact part numbers and natural-language descriptions. Which retrieval design is appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lexical retrieval for exact identifiers
Recall likely catalog entries before retrieval
A reranking stage evaluated on representative queries
Semantic retrieval for paraphrased needs

architect-professional.explanation: Exact and semantic queries have different strengths, so hybrid retrieval plus reranking can serve both. Product availability and identifiers require current authoritative data, not model memory.

architect-professional.q: A large internal platform has hundreds of APIs. Which progressive-discovery design is strongest? Select all that apply.

options.text: Put compressed summaries for every API in root context
Record discovery and selection in the trace
Expose a small capability index with concise domain descriptions
Load detailed schemas only after a domain is selected

architect-professional.explanation: Progressive discovery keeps initial context small while retaining access to deeper capability. Tracing makes routing errors diagnosable; monolithic schemas increase cost and confusion.

architect-professional.q: One service makes one stable, high-volume call to an internal risk API. No other host needs discovery. Which integration is the best default?

options.text: A public MCP registry entry
A small MCP server deployed beside the service so the internal risk capability can later be discovered by additional hosts without changing the client contract
A direct typed API client with authentication, timeouts, and contract tests
A new multi-agent protocol

architect-professional.explanation: A direct typed client is the smallest reliable boundary for one stable high-volume integration. MCP or agent-to-agent protocols add value only when interoperability or delegated coordination justifies their lifecycle cost.

architect-professional.q: A desktop host and two IDEs need the same governed repository tools and reusable resources. Which option best fits?

options.text: Duplicate bespoke connectors in each host
A spreadsheet copied into every session
Three host-specific connectors generated from one shared integration package, all calling the same governed repository API and consent service
A reviewed MCP server with negotiated capabilities and host-specific consent

architect-professional.explanation: MCP standardizes discovery and invocation across compliant hosts while preserving one governed server boundary. Authentication, authorization, consent, and versioning remain necessary.

architect-professional.q: A request crosses an API gateway, Claude call, MCP server, and database. Which telemetry is needed for diagnosis at scale? Select all that apply.

options.text: Latency and result class for each boundary
Versioned model, prompt, tool, and policy identifiers
A propagated correlation or trace ID
Log bearer-token fingerprints in every trace span

architect-professional.explanation: Correlation and versioned boundary telemetry reconstruct the request path and identify regressions. Credentials and unrestricted sensitive content should be redacted or omitted from observability.

architect-professional.q: A RAG pipeline improves recall by issuing five query expansions, but p95 latency exceeds the user objective and answer quality improves only 0.4 points. What should the architect do?

options.text: Use eval evidence to reduce or condition expansion, then measure quality and latency by query slice
Remove retrieval entirely
Hide the latency metric from stakeholders
Keep all five expansions for every query but run them concurrently and cache repeated candidates, optimizing transport latency before changing retrieval behavior

architect-professional.explanation: The small average quality gain may not earn the latency cost. Conditional expansion for difficult query slices can preserve value while meeting the service objective.

architect-professional.q: A third-party model platform is proposed for regulated regional workloads. What must be verified before approval?

options.text: Only whether it exposes a compatible chat method
Identity, data processing and residency, model and feature availability, network path, logging, retention, and contractual controls
Whether its SDK preserves the existing method names, streaming events, and error classes so the application can migrate without code changes
Whether a demo completes once

architect-professional.explanation: API compatibility does not establish compliance or operational suitability. The architect must verify the full data and identity boundary and document which controls remain the customer's responsibility.

architect-professional.q: A tool times out after it may have created a customer record. Which integration controls are required before retry? Select all that apply.

options.text: A stable idempotency key
A bounded retry policy based on failure class
Ask a model whether the timed-out write succeeded
Authoritative reconciliation of the operation outcome

architect-professional.explanation: Ambiguous side effects require transaction-level evidence. Idempotency, reconciliation, and classified retry policy prevent duplicates; generation settings cannot determine whether the first write completed.

architect-professional.q: Which measures form a balanced production scorecard for an account-support agent? Select all that apply.

options.text: Cost per successful resolution and human-review minutes
Track response length and model confidence
P50 and P95 latency plus availability
Task success and unsupported-claim rate

architect-professional.explanation: A balanced scorecard covers quality, reliability, economics, and operational burden. Stylistic counts matter only if tied to a validated user requirement.

architect-professional.q: A team builds an evaluation set from production traffic. Which practices improve validity? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tune prompts against held-out failures until those cases pass
Represent common, boundary, high-impact, and adversarial slices
Preserve provenance and label quality while minimizing sensitive data
Separate development cases from held-out release cases

architect-professional.explanation: Representative slices and trustworthy labels make the set useful, while a held-out partition limits overfitting. Repeated tuning on release cases converts them into development data.

architect-professional.q: An LLM judge gives a helpfulness score. How should the team establish whether the judge is reliable enough for a release gate?

options.text: Ask the judge to score its own accuracy
Use the same model and prompt as the generator
Calibrate it against independently labeled human examples and inspect false positives, false negatives, and slice disagreement
Accept it after prompt-level consistency tests show stable JSON scores across repeated samples, using disagreement with human labels only to refine the judge prompt

architect-professional.explanation: Judge validity is empirical. Human calibration and disagreement analysis reveal rubric ambiguity and shared blind spots that structured output or self-assessment cannot remove.

architect-professional.q: A RAG answer cites the wrong policy. Which tests isolate the cause? Select all that apply.

options.text: Evaluate reranker ordering independently
Measure whether the correct document appeared in the retrieved top-k set
Give Claude the correct source directly and test answer faithfulness
Change prompt, reranker, and model together before retesting

architect-professional.explanation: Separate retrieval, ranking, and generation tests localize the failure. Changing every component together may improve one run but destroys causal evidence.

architect-professional.q: Variant B raises offline answer quality by 3 points but increases live abandonment. What should determine rollout?

options.text: Offline score alone
The offline score if it was measured on a representative dataset, while treating abandonment as a temporary interface-adaptation effect after release
The architect's personal preference
A predeclared decision rule combining guardrails and the primary live outcome, followed by slice analysis

architect-professional.explanation: Offline quality is one signal. A production experiment should use predeclared business and safety metrics, ensure valid assignment, and inspect important slices before deciding.

architect-professional.q: One evaluation run passes all 50 cases. What can the architect conclude?

options.text: Only that one sampled run passed; higher-variance or high-risk cases need repeated measurement and confidence analysis
The model is deterministic
The system will always pass those cases
The current prompt-model combination is ready for launch on the represented cases, provided deterministic checks pass, without estimating run-to-run uncertainty

architect-professional.explanation: Probabilistic model behavior and changing integrations make one run insufficient evidence of stability. Repeated trials and production monitoring quantify variance and detect distribution shift.

architect-professional.q: The provider wire response contains a citation field, but the application trace and UI do not. What should the team inspect first?

options.text: The UI rendering component and browser compatibility layer, because the trace may intentionally omit provider-only citation metadata before display
SDK deserialization and each application serialization boundary
The retrieval and citation-generation prompts, because a citation visible on the provider wire may still have been produced from a malformed evidence chunk
The system prompt

architect-professional.explanation: The field existed at the provider boundary, so the likely defect is integration mapping. Comparing wire, SDK object, service DTO, and UI payload locates where the field disappeared.

architect-professional.q: Prompt caching cuts input cost by 35 percent, but a stale policy prefix causes incorrect decisions. What is the correct optimization response?

options.text: Increase cache lifetime without measurement
Remove correctness from the scorecard
Restore source freshness and versioned invalidation, then evaluate cache economics on correct outputs
Keep caching enabled but shorten the cache lifetime and add a prompt instruction to prefer newer retrieved policy when it conflicts with the stable prefix

architect-professional.explanation: Optimization is subordinate to correctness. Stable prefixes need explicit content ownership and invalidation so cost savings do not preserve obsolete policy.

architect-professional.q: Which release gates protect against a misleading average improvement? Select all that apply.

options.text: No regression beyond threshold in high-impact slices
Zero new unauthorized side effects
Gate only on a significant aggregate improvement
Cost and latency within approved budgets

architect-professional.explanation: Non-negotiable safety failures, critical slices, and operational budgets prevent aggregate gains from hiding unacceptable regressions. Averages cannot express every risk boundary.

architect-professional.q: Which information belongs in a production trace for a tool-using Claude workflow? Select all that apply.

options.text: Model, prompt, schema, tool, and policy versions
Encrypted full prompts, retrieved documents, and tool arguments in a restricted trace store so investigators can reproduce any result without source lookups
Stop reason and redacted tool-decision events
Correlation IDs and final-state verification result

architect-professional.explanation: Versioned and correlated decision events support reproduction and incident analysis. Sensitive payloads and credentials should be minimized, redacted, and protected rather than copied into general telemetry.

architect-professional.q: A coding agent can read files, execute commands, and access a package registry. Which layered controls are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: A system instruction that assigns Claude the role of a security-conscious senior engineer and requires explicit reasoning before any tool with side effects
Prompt-level trust-boundary instructions
Pre-tool policy hooks and explicit approval for consequential actions
Filesystem and network sandboxing with least privilege

architect-professional.explanation: Defense in depth combines behavioral guidance, deterministic gates, human authority, and infrastructure isolation. Capability claims do not constrain execution or replace enforceable boundaries.

architect-professional.q: Which properties make a human-review step meaningful? Select all that apply.

options.text: A qualified reviewer with evidence and authority
A defined trigger based on impact, uncertainty, or policy
A time objective and safe fallback when review is unavailable
A post-action reviewer checkpoint that can reverse most outcomes and records whether the original model action should remain in effect

architect-professional.explanation: Human review needs a trigger, accountable role, evidence packet, time budget, and fallback. Review after an irreversible action cannot serve as preauthorization.

architect-professional.q: A European customer-service assistant is being designed. Which GDPR-aligned architectural questions should be answered? Select all that apply.

options.text: What lawful basis and purpose govern processing
How data-subject rights and deletion propagate through stores and logs
Which optional customer fields could improve future personalization, provided the privacy notice describes broad service-improvement use and access is restricted
Which personal data is necessary and how long it is retained

architect-professional.explanation: Purpose limitation, data minimization, retention, and rights handling shape the data lifecycle. Speculative collection conflicts with minimization and increases risk. Legal counsel must confirm obligations for the deployment.

architect-professional.q: A healthcare workflow will send protected health information through Claude. What is the architect's strongest first governance action?

options.text: Assume encryption alone makes the workflow compliant
Ask Claude to certify compliance
Use the provider's encrypted transport and approved enterprise plan, send complete records to maximize clinical context, and rely on downstream access logs for compliance
Confirm the covered workflow, approved service configuration and agreements, minimum-necessary data, access controls, auditability, and organizational HIPAA review

architect-professional.explanation: HIPAA suitability depends on the complete administrative, technical, contractual, and data-minimization boundary. A model cannot declare the system compliant, and encryption is only one control.

architect-professional.q: A US government team requires a FedRAMP-authorized boundary. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The exact cloud service, deployment boundary, region, inherited controls, customer responsibilities, and data flow must be verified
A local prototype is sufficient evidence
Use the same model family through any government cloud region, provided encryption, identity federation, and agency logging meet the team's inherited control baseline
FedRAMP applies only to the user interface

architect-professional.explanation: Authorization attaches to a defined service and control boundary, not a model name in isolation. Architects must verify the approved offering and map inherited versus customer-operated controls.

architect-professional.q: A benefits-triage system has acceptable overall accuracy. Which fairness checks are still needed? Select all that apply.

options.text: Compare error and escalation rates across relevant groups
Use the acceptable aggregate score plus a balanced overall label distribution as evidence of fairness, then monitor complaints for group-specific problems
Test accessibility and language slices
Review whether labels and proxy variables encode historical inequity

architect-professional.explanation: Aggregate performance can conceal concentrated harm. Slice metrics, data and label review, and accessibility evaluation reveal distributional failures that require governance decisions.

architect-professional.q: Users receive recommendations that affect account access. Which transparency design is strongest?

options.text: Publish private chain-of-thought
Disclose the AI-assisted role, provide understandable factors and evidence where appropriate, and offer a challenge or escalation path
Disclose that AI generated the recommendation, show a calibrated confidence band, and direct users to ordinary customer support without exposing decision factors
Hide that AI contributed so users trust the result

architect-professional.explanation: Meaningful transparency explains the system's role, basis, limitations, and recourse without exposing private reasoning or sensitive controls. A bare confidence number is not an explanation.

architect-professional.q: An external document instructs a procurement agent to approve a new vendor and send credentials. Which controls should prevent harm? Select all that apply.

options.text: Treat the document as authenticated business intent when its signature image and vendor details match an approved record, then apply ordinary tool approval
Treat document instructions as untrusted content
Require authenticated human approval bound to the exact vendor action
Keep vendor approval and credential access outside automatic model authority

architect-professional.explanation: Indirect prompt injection exploits legitimate agent authority. Trust labeling, least privilege, and action-bound approval prevent content from authenticating or authorizing itself.

architect-professional.q: A secret appears in a model trace. What is the correct immediate response?

options.text: Restrict trace access, add the secret pattern to redaction, and monitor the credential for suspicious use before rotating it at the next maintenance window
Ask the model to forget it
Contain the affected capability, revoke or rotate the credential, preserve redacted evidence, and investigate actual access
Delete the trace and continue using the credential

architect-professional.explanation: Once exposed, a credential is no longer trustworthy. Containment and rotation reduce ongoing risk, while protected evidence and authoritative logs establish impact and support regression fixes.

architect-professional.q: A discovery workshop for an underwriting assistant is beginning. Which questions should the architect prioritize? Select all that apply.

options.text: Which data and systems are authoritative
Which action follows the output and what happens when it is wrong
What observable outcome should improve and who owns it
Which current model leads broad public benchmarks and has the strongest adoption among comparable underwriting teams

architect-professional.explanation: Outcome ownership, downstream consequence, and authoritative data define the problem boundary. Model popularity is not a requirement and should not precede discovery.

architect-professional.q: Executives ask why the proposed architecture keeps human approval for refunds above a threshold. Which explanation is strongest?

options.text: The engineering team prefers more screens
The model is not intelligent enough
Human review is retained because refunds are external financial actions, so a uniform approval rule across all values is simpler to audit and explain than a calibrated risk threshold
The threshold balances handling-time benefit with the financial impact, reversibility, policy obligation, and measured uncertainty of higher-value cases

architect-professional.explanation: Tradeoff communication should connect the control to value, risk, evidence, and policy. It avoids vague capability claims and explains why the boundary is proportional.

architect-professional.q: A stakeholder says the agent must be 99 percent accurate. What should the architect ask next?

options.text: Which task population, label, evaluator, time window, error classes, and consequences define that target
Whether 99 is the stakeholder's favorite number
Which prompt is longest
Whether the target refers to offline model accuracy or end-to-end production success, then adopt the stricter definition to avoid understating performance

architect-professional.explanation: An accuracy target is meaningless without a denominator, measurement method, and error taxonomy. Operational commitments must name the population and response when objectives are missed.

architect-professional.q: Which sections belong in a useful architecture decision record? Select all that apply.

options.text: Options, decision, and rejected alternatives
Consequences, verification, and reversal conditions
The final architecture diagram plus implementation milestones and owners, with rejected options and reversal conditions retained in workshop notes
Context, constraints, and evidence

architect-professional.explanation: A decision record preserves why an option fit the evidence and how it will be validated or reversed. A diagram alone shows structure but not rationale or operational consequences.

architect-professional.q: Before handing a Claude system from the build team to operations, which artifacts are required? Select all that apply.

options.text: Runbooks, escalation paths, and rollback procedure
A signed build-team statement that the production-like demo passed its acceptance cases, with unresolved issues documented in the handoff meeting notes
Service objectives, dashboards, and alert ownership
Version inventory for model, prompt, tools, data, and policy

architect-professional.explanation: Operations needs measurable service behavior, response procedures, ownership, and versioned dependencies. A successful demo does not define how to detect, contain, or recover from production failure.

architect-professional.q: A high-impact assistant is ready for rollout. Which pilot design is strongest? Select all that apply.

options.text: Grant production authority to a small expert-user cohort with a global kill switch, using rapid incident response instead of draft-only or read-only boundaries
Collect structured reviewer feedback and failure traces
Use a bounded population and read-only or draft-only authority
Define success, safety gates, review load, and rollback before launch

architect-professional.explanation: A bounded pilot tests the riskiest assumptions while limiting harm. Predeclared gates and structured evidence make the decision to expand or stop defensible.

architect-professional.q: Reviewers complain that too many safe cases are escalated. What should the lifecycle owner do?

options.text: Raise the escalation confidence threshold immediately based on reviewer complaints, then compare queue volume and incident counts during the next release window
Measure false-escalation slices, review the trigger and evidence quality, test a candidate change, and monitor safety guardrails
Tell reviewers to work faster
Remove human review entirely

architect-professional.explanation: Feedback should become a classified, measurable improvement hypothesis. The team can reduce unnecessary review only while preserving the high-impact safety boundary.

architect-professional.q: How should the same architecture change be communicated to an executive sponsor and an on-call engineer?

options.text: Give both audiences the architecture decision record and full sequence diagram so each receives the same authoritative details and can extract what matters
Send both the complete source code only
Explain business outcome, risk, and cost to the sponsor; give dependencies, signals, failure modes, and recovery steps to the engineer
Hide tradeoffs from the sponsor

architect-professional.explanation: Stakeholders need different levels of detail while the underlying decision remains consistent. Communication should support each audience's decisions and responsibilities.

architect-professional.q: A source system is being retired. Which lifecycle actions are required for the Claude application? Select all that apply.

options.text: Migrate or remove data with retention and deletion controls
Identify prompts, retrieval indexes, tools, evals, and runbooks that depend on it
Re-run acceptance and failure tests before cutover
Keep the old connector disabled but deployable as an emergency fallback, without including it in routine runbooks, tests, or dependency inventories

architect-professional.explanation: Decommissioning is an architectural change across data, integration, evaluation, and operations. Undocumented stale access increases security risk and can silently reintroduce obsolete information.

architect-professional.q: A team standardizes Claude Code across repositories. Which configuration belongs in reviewed project scope? Select all that apply.

options.text: Repository-specific constraints and approved hooks
Versioned team settings needed for consistent safe behavior
References to production secret names together with sample resolved values so every repository can validate credential format during setup
Canonical build and test commands

architect-professional.explanation: Shared commands, constraints, hooks, and settings create repeatable behavior. Credentials belong in protected environment or secret-management boundaries, never committed project instructions.

architect-professional.q: A headless Claude Code job reviews untrusted pull requests. Which controls are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Minimal repository and token permissions
A short-lived protected-branch token limited to reviewer-generated fixes, allowing the headless job to apply high-confidence findings after tests pass
Bounded tools, network, time, and structured report output
No unrelated secrets in the environment

architect-professional.explanation: Headless automation lacks interactive supervision, so capability and identity must be narrower. Findings should enter normal review and protected merge paths instead of bypassing them.

architect-professional.q: An on-call engineer uses Claude to investigate a latency incident. Which inputs and boundaries are most useful? Select all that apply.

options.text: Short-lived read credentials copied into a protected system prompt so Claude can reproduce failing dependency requests directly from the incident context
Redacted correlated traces and recent version changes
Read-only diagnostic tools before any remediation authority
Service objectives, dependency health, and runbook steps

architect-professional.explanation: Correlated evidence, objectives, dependency state, and safe diagnostic tools support fast causal analysis. Credentials add exposure and should remain inside trusted integrations.

architect-professional.q: A team upgrades Claude Code, a plugin, and an MCP server in one release. Which practices reduce operational risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Run representative canary workflows with rollback instructions
Inventory changes to tools, hooks, permissions, and network access
Record and pin versions where supported
Rely on successful installation and protocol negotiation as compatibility proof, then monitor production canaries instead of running representative workflows before release

architect-professional.explanation: Behavior depends on the combined tool and configuration surface. Version records, capability review, canaries, and rollback turn upgrades into controlled operational changes.

architect-professional.q: A stakeholder asks for an autonomous support agent. What should the architect establish first?

options.text: The number of specialist subagents and the handoff protocol between them
The orchestration framework, hosting topology, and preferred deployment region
The model family, context window, and token budget that fit the expected support volume
The business outcome, baseline, authority boundary, and cost of error

architect-professional.explanation: Discovery must define the decision, desired outcome, current baseline, authority, and consequences before a technical pattern can be evaluated. Model and framework choices follow those requirements.

architect-professional.q: Which statement is a service-level indicator rather than an objective or agreement?

options.text: The percentage of evaluated drafts with a valid active-policy citation
The team will approve launch only if citation quality improves during the pilot
Eligible customers receive a first response within the contracted four-hour window
At least 98 percent of drafts should cite the active policy

architect-professional.explanation: An SLI is the measured signal. The 98 percent target is an SLO, while the contractual response promise is an SLA. Choosing a tool is neither.

architect-professional.q: A proposed workflow automates refund execution, but policy requires approval above a threshold. Which requirement class makes the architecture conflict explicit?

options.text: Service-level performance requirement
Safety and authority requirement
Model quality and evaluation requirement
Functional automation requirement

architect-professional.explanation: The approval threshold limits action authority and prevents a high-impact outcome. It is a safety and authorization constraint, not a presentation or model preference.

architect-professional.q: Why should a pilot measure human review time as well as model quality?

options.text: Review time proves whether the approval policy must cover every generated draft
Review time determines the context size and model tier needed for each request
Human review can move the bottleneck instead of reducing total work
Review time directly measures model quality

architect-professional.explanation: A system can generate good drafts yet fail the business goal if review cost erases the time saved. Human review is an operational step with latency, capacity, and quality of its own.

architect-professional.q: A stable claims workflow has known steps and strict latency targets. Which starting architecture is most defensible?

options.text: A single Claude call with structured output and validation after every completed claim
A bounded agent that selects the next step dynamically within explicit tool limits
A planner-executor pair with bounded handoffs
A deterministic workflow with Claude used only where judgment is required

architect-professional.explanation: Known steps and strict latency favor deterministic orchestration. Claude can handle bounded judgment tasks while the workflow keeps sequence, permissions, and failure handling explicit.

architect-professional.q: What makes an architecture decision record useful during later review?

options.text: It records context, alternatives, the decision, consequences, and verification plan
It records the final component diagram and deployment owner
It stores the operational metrics, alerts, and traces needed to verify the architecture
It freezes the original rationale so later maintainers cannot reverse the approved design

architect-professional.explanation: An ADR preserves why the choice fit the evidence and constraints at the time, including rejected alternatives and consequences. That context makes future reversal or revision rational.

architect-professional.q: A process has stable, known steps and strict audit requirements. Which pattern is the strongest default?

options.text: A tool-enabled single prompt
A planner-executor agent pair
A deterministic workflow
A bounded agent

architect-professional.explanation: Known steps and audit needs favor code-owned transitions, narrow permissions, and explicit recovery. An agent is justified only when adaptive path selection is a real requirement.

architect-professional.q: When is a multi-agent design most justified?

options.text: When redundant agents independently vote on every output
When an agent framework supports handoffs and parallel execution without additional application code
When a task has distinct stages that can each receive a specialized prompt and dedicated tool set
When context isolation, independent review, or parallel work measurably improves the outcome

architect-professional.explanation: Multiple agents add coordination, cost, and handoff risk. They earn that complexity when isolation, independence, parallelism, or specialization addresses a measured requirement.

architect-professional.q: Which control should be enforced outside the model?

options.text: Whether a requested refund exceeds the caller's authorized limit
Whether a clause creates material business risk under the available evidence
Whether a summary preserves the decision-critical nuance of the source material
Whether a draft is sufficiently persuasive

architect-professional.explanation: An authorization limit is a stable predicate over trusted identity and transaction data. Code must enforce it. Semantic judgments can use Claude with evaluation and review.

architect-professional.q: Why can the cheapest model per token be more expensive per successful task?

options.text: Low unit price always lowers task cost
Higher retry and human-review rates can outweigh the lower call price
Its token price changes the authorization boundary for costly or high-impact tool calls
Its lower capability tier requires every tool operation to be confirmed by a human reviewer

architect-professional.explanation: Architecture economics include retries, tool calls, review labor, and corrections. Lower unit price does not guarantee lower expected cost for an accepted outcome.

architect-professional.q: A contract pipeline returns polished redlines with unsupported conclusions. Which change best addresses the structural failure?

options.text: Retrieve the highest-ranked clauses, generate the full redline in one step, and keep the version with the strongest confidence score
Run a second verifier prompt over each completed redline and accept it when the verifier reports no unsupported claims
Separate retrieval, clause analysis, evidence review, redline generation, and approval with explicit contracts
Add the full contract and policy library to one longer prompt, then require citations in the returned redline

architect-professional.explanation: The failure comes from collapsed responsibilities and missing provenance. Decomposition with contracts localizes errors and prevents generation from bypassing evidence review.

architect-professional.q: What should a feedback record include so it can guide an architecture change?

options.text: The final answer, its cited evidence, and the model confidence reported for each conclusion
A task-level rating, reviewer identity, and timestamp attached to the final response
Token usage, latency, retry count, and total cost for the completed model trajectory
Input class, versions, evidence, trajectory, validation, human edits, and downstream outcome

architect-professional.explanation: A useful feedback loop connects outcome to the system state and trajectory that produced it. That evidence distinguishes prompt, retrieval, tool, routing, and scope failures.

architect-professional.q: A RAG system becomes confidently wrong immediately after a document refresh while the model and latency are unchanged. What should be investigated first?

options.text: Ingestion, index versions, filters, and retrieved chunks
An output-formatting rule that may suppress qualifying language from otherwise grounded answers
A temperature setting that now makes generation less deterministic for the refreshed documents
A model-weight regression near the refresh

architect-professional.explanation: The timing points to the data and retrieval boundary. Inspect active source versions, parsing, chunking, filters, and candidate ranking before changing the model.

architect-professional.q: Which retrieval method is especially useful for exact error codes and product identifiers?

options.text: Dense semantic retrieval
Sparse term-based retrieval
Generative query expansion
Cross-encoder reranking

architect-professional.explanation: Sparse retrieval preserves exact lexical matches and is strong for codes, names, and policy phrases. Dense retrieval can complement it for paraphrases.

architect-professional.q: Why must access-control filtering happen before retrieved text reaches Claude?

options.text: Post-generation filtering enforces the same boundary
Filtering before context preserves the retriever's original relevance order across users with different permissions
Prompt instructions are not an authorization boundary
Access-control metadata is unavailable to Claude once a retriever serializes document chunks into prompt text

architect-professional.explanation: Forbidden content should never enter model context. A request to ignore unauthorized text does not enforce confidentiality or least privilege.

architect-professional.q: What does recall at K measure in a retrieval evaluation?

options.text: What fraction of the top K candidates is labeled relevant to the evaluation query
What fraction of cited source URLs remain reachable when the evaluation is replayed
Whether the answer cites all K candidates
Whether required evidence appears among the top K candidates

architect-professional.explanation: Recall at K measures candidate coverage for labeled relevant evidence. It isolates retrieval quality before generation is evaluated.

architect-professional.q: Two active policy chunks conflict. What is the most reliable system behavior?

options.text: Apply an explicit precedence rule if one exists; otherwise report the conflict and escalate
Prefer the chunk from the most recently refreshed index because freshness establishes policy authority
Ask the model to reconcile both chunks into one conservative rule and flag its answer as low confidence
Use the chunk with the highest semantic score, then cite the lower-ranked chunk as supplementary context

architect-professional.explanation: Similarity does not establish authority. The system needs a trusted precedence rule or an explicit conflict result that routes to a qualified owner.

architect-professional.q: Which refresh design best prevents old and new chunks from mixing in production?

options.text: Clear the model and retrieval caches before updating documents in the currently active index
Build and validate a versioned index, then switch the active pointer atomically
Upsert every new chunk into the active index, then delete stale chunks after retrieval smoke tests pass
Increase overlap between refreshed chunks so both old and new policy wording remain retrievable during rollout

architect-professional.explanation: A versioned build plus validation and atomic activation keeps the serving index consistent and retains a rollback path if retrieval quality regresses.

architect-professional.q: Support staff only read tickets and draft replies, but their agent also has refund and account-deletion tools. What best reduces risk?

options.text: Route sensitive tool calls to a larger model that can reason more reliably about authorization
Keep the capabilities visible but require each tool description to repeat the role's policy limits
Remove the unnecessary tools and scopes from that role
Keep every tool but log sensitive calls

architect-professional.explanation: Least privilege removes capabilities the role does not need. Logging and warnings can support controls but leave the unnecessary authority and attack surface intact.

architect-professional.q: Why are capability discovery and execution authorization separate controls?

options.text: Discovery is evaluated when a session begins, so authorization is only required for tools reached outside the advertised catalog
Discovery limits context, so execution authorization is redundant
Discovery filters capabilities at the host, while the integration protocol automatically authorizes every advertised operation
Hiding tools reduces exposure, while execution authorization prevents direct or stale unauthorized calls

architect-professional.explanation: A narrow catalog improves selection and exposure, but a caller may still reach an endpoint or permissions may change. The service must authorize every execution.

architect-professional.q: When is MCP a stronger fit than a direct API?

options.text: When multiple hosts need standardized dynamic discovery of capabilities across server boundaries
When one stable service needs the lowest latency
When an integration needs the protocol layer to infer user identity and grant permissions without a separate policy service
When any Claude application needs tool calls and wants one protocol to replace service-specific authorization

architect-professional.explanation: MCP earns its extra boundary through standardized capability discovery and integration across hosts. A known low-overhead service call may remain clearer as a direct API.

architect-professional.q: What must a reliable approval bind to?

options.text: The model's confidence, risk classification, and stated reason for selecting the proposed capability
Exact action, parameters, requester, approver authority, and expiration
The tool name and approving tenant
The current prompt and conversation identifier so all tool calls within that model turn inherit approval

architect-professional.explanation: Approval is valid for a specific proposed effect under a specific identity and time window. Changed parameters require a new decision.

architect-professional.q: A tool returns an authorization error. How should an agent harness classify it?

options.text: Route the request to a stronger model so it can revise the tool parameters until authorization succeeds
Retry with the same credentials after exponential backoff because authorization services can be temporarily inconsistent
Non-retryable unless access or approval state changes, with a safe escalation action
Record the failure as a tool warning, omit the restricted effect, and continue as though the workflow succeeded

architect-professional.explanation: Repeating the same unauthorized request cannot succeed. A structured error should explain the safe next step without leaking secret details.

architect-professional.q: Why is an application-wide service API key insufficient for per-user authorization?

options.text: It prevents downstream audit logs from recording the application identity or the requested service operation
It authenticates only the client transport and therefore cannot invoke downstream service endpoints directly
It expires at application scope, so a user request can outlive the credential before authorization is checked
It identifies broad application authority but may not carry the human principal, tenant, or current scopes

architect-professional.explanation: The downstream service needs trusted claims about the actual principal and requested action. Broad application credentials can collapse user boundaries into unenforceable prompt instructions.

architect-professional.q: A dashboard shows 99.9 percent successful API calls, but users report wrong answers. What is missing?

options.text: A lower generation temperature recorded as an attribute on every successful model span
Task-quality and trajectory evaluation connected to system traces
A larger model for semantic errors
A transport retry metric that separates transient HTTP failures from successful first-attempt requests

architect-professional.explanation: Transport success only proves the protocol completed. The system needs evidence about retrieval, tools, validation, final-state quality, and downstream outcomes.

architect-professional.q: Why should a team monitor P95 latency as well as P50?

options.text: P95 combines response time and model accuracy so a team can detect quality degradation in slow requests
P95 approximates the slowest request
P95 exposes slow paths such as retries, large contexts, and tool timeouts that the median hides
P50 is unstable at production traffic volumes, while P95 remains comparable across any sample size

architect-professional.explanation: The median describes the ordinary path. Tail percentiles reveal a slower cohort that can dominate user complaints and timeout behavior.

architect-professional.q: Which cost comparison best supports model routing decisions?

options.text: The average provider charge per model call, including cached and uncached input tokens
The monthly application infrastructure spend allocated across all attempted tasks, regardless of acceptance
The output-token price for each model multiplied by the median completion length
Total model, tool, retry, review, and correction cost per accepted task outcome

architect-professional.explanation: A cheaper call can create more retries and review. Cost per successful outcome incorporates the full trajectory and enables a fair architecture comparison.

architect-professional.q: What is the primary purpose of a distributed trace in a Claude application?

options.text: Connect model, retrieval, tool, validation, retry, and approval spans for one trajectory
Store complete user inputs and credentials so every production failure can be reproduced from one record
Guarantee task correctness by proving that every required model, retrieval, and tool span completed successfully
Replace aggregate service metrics

architect-professional.explanation: A trace reveals where time and failure occurred across the end-to-end path. Metrics aggregate behavior, while evaluations determine correctness.

architect-professional.q: After a release, P95 latency and cost rise while P50 stays stable. Which investigation is most useful?

options.text: Treat the stable median as evidence that the release is healthy and wait for the tail to converge with more traffic
Inspect slow-path retries, rate limits, large inputs, tool timeouts, and cache misses by release version
Disable detailed tracing because added span collection is the most likely cause of the higher cost and tail latency
Shorten all prompts with higher median token use

architect-professional.explanation: The shape points to a slow cohort rather than a universal slowdown. Versioned traces and strata can identify retries, tools, input size, and cache behavior in that cohort.

architect-professional.q: Which rollout policy is strongest for a new architecture variant?

options.text: Canary the variant while monitoring transport errors and latency, then evaluate task quality after reaching full traffic
Route all low-risk traffic to the cheapest variant first, then add quality evaluation if user complaints increase
Shadow, canary, guarded expansion, and automatic rollback using quality, safety, latency, and cost gates
Release to all users after the offline suite and one production demo pass, then compare aggregate metrics with the prior release

architect-professional.explanation: Progressive exposure limits harm while collecting live evidence. Multiple gates prevent an economic improvement from hiding quality or safety regression.

architect-professional.q: A team says a sensitive-data workflow is compliant because every output receives human review. What is the main problem with that claim?

options.text: The only missing evidence is a benchmark proving reviewers outperform the model on average cases
The review stage should be replaced by a second model because automated consistency is easier to audit than reviewer judgment
Compliance follows from an enterprise plan and encrypted transport, so the team only needs to document those product settings
It omits the data flow, feature configuration, reviewer design, control evidence, and authorized compliance decision

architect-professional.explanation: Review is one possible control. Governance requires the exact data boundary, obligations, technical controls, owners, tests, residual risk, and decisions by qualified authorities.

architect-professional.q: Which action follows data minimization?

options.text: Remove identity fields that the task does not require before sending data
Pseudonymize identifiers after the provider response while leaving the original request payload unchanged
Log every input field, encrypted, for future incident reconstruction
Send every available field but instruct the model to ignore attributes unrelated to the current task

architect-professional.explanation: Minimization prevents unnecessary data from entering the system. Encryption and access controls then protect the data that remains necessary.

architect-professional.q: What makes human review a real control?

options.text: Two reviewers approve every output, regardless of risk, evidence quality, queue capacity, authority, or reversibility
A defined trigger, qualified reviewer, evidence packet, authority, service level, fallback, and audit record
Use model confidence alone to route low-scoring outputs to an available reviewer
Every output enters a general review queue, where any available reviewer chooses what evidence and escalation are needed

architect-professional.explanation: Review reduces risk only when the person can detect and act on the failure within an operationally viable process. The design must specify each boundary.

architect-professional.q: Why should an architect verify retention for each enabled feature?

options.text: Feature retention determines model accuracy and context capacity even when the deployed data path remains unchanged
Prompt wording selects the provider retention tier, and each feature accepts a different retention instruction
Files, batch, hosted sessions, tools, and standard requests can cross different storage and eligibility boundaries
All hosted features inherit one retention policy, so the team must verify that shared policy only once for the account

architect-professional.explanation: The concrete data flow depends on the features and agreement in use. Governance must evaluate the deployed combination against current official documentation.

architect-professional.q: A high-impact workflow has an aggregate quality gain but a large regression for one affected group. What is the strongest response?

options.text: Replace the group slice with a larger overall sample and apply the same aggregate threshold to every future release
Route the affected group to a larger model while keeping the rollout open, since model capacity is the most likely cause
Deploy the aggregate improvement, monitor the affected group in production, and wait for a larger sample before deciding on a separate control later
Investigate the slice, assess harm and uncertainty, involve the proper owner, and block or constrain rollout until the risk decision is made

architect-professional.explanation: Aggregate performance cannot average away a material group harm. The team needs contextual fairness analysis, evidence, authority, and a controlled deployment decision.

architect-professional.q: Which event should trigger governance reassessment?

options.text: A material change to use case, model, data, tool authority, scale, policy, or observed risk
Any documentation-format change, because every editorial revision invalidates the architecture's approval boundary
Wait for the annual governance review unless a highest-severity production incident occurs
Only a change to the base model, because prompts, data, tools, scale, and policy do not alter approved risk

architect-professional.explanation: Approval applies to a specific architecture and risk profile. Material changes can alter affected people, data boundaries, controls, and residual risk, so the decision must be revisited.

architect-professional.q: An executive review receives only a detailed component diagram. What critical information is missing?

options.text: A dependency inventory showing whether the proposed design is technically feasible
A model benchmark and prompt transcript so the group can compare raw answer quality before discussing ownership
The business decision, options, consequences, residual risk, evidence, and owner
A line-by-line implementation plan so executives can estimate engineering effort without the delivery team's input

architect-professional.explanation: Executives need to decide whether expected value justifies investment and residual risk. Components matter only as evidence for that decision.

architect-professional.q: Why should an ADR include rejected alternatives?

options.text: To make every considered option appear equally credible
To stop future teams revisiting the decision after constraints change
To replace implementation tests with the written decision record
To preserve which constraints and evidence made other choices weaker

architect-professional.explanation: Rejected options preserve tradeoff context. Future teams can revisit the decision rationally when evidence or constraints change instead of repeating hidden analysis.

architect-professional.q: When is an operational handoff complete?

options.text: When the receiving owners can monitor, evaluate, recover, change, and support the system under agreed acceptance criteria
When the implementation team stays on call indefinitely, so the receiving team never needs independent recovery or change capability
When the deck, runbook, and repository have been delivered, even if receiving owners have not exercised them
When one production request succeeds and the implementation team has documented the nominal workflow

architect-professional.explanation: Handoff transfers demonstrated operating ability and responsibility. Dashboards, runbooks, evaluation, rollback, access, review capacity, and ownership must be ready.

architect-professional.q: What is the strongest way to assign lifecycle ownership?

options.text: Wait until the first incident reveals which team has the operational access and expertise to respond
Name owners and approvers for each decision, artifact, control, metric, and operational response
Give one AI team end-to-end ownership so fewer groups must coordinate lifecycle decisions
Assign ownership to the model-routing service so changes to prompts, knowledge, controls, and policy stay synchronized

architect-professional.explanation: Specific assets and decisions change at different rates and require different authority. Concrete ownership prevents silent decay and unclear escalation.

architect-professional.q: A pilot has high login counts but reviewer time and correction rate doubled. What should the steering group conclude?

options.text: Expand the pilot immediately so a larger user sample can determine whether the correction rate is statistically stable
Treat the login growth as proof of adoption because reviewer effort is an implementation cost that should fall after scale
Usage alone is insufficient; evaluate outcome, rework, review burden, quality, and cost per accepted result
Exclude reviewer time from the scorecard because human correction sits outside measured AI performance

architect-professional.explanation: The workflow may have shifted work instead of reducing it. Adoption must connect to the intended business and quality outcomes without hidden operational burden.

architect-professional.q: What is a useful reversal condition in an architecture decision?

options.text: A scheduled date when the team must reconsider the decision, regardless of whether any relevant evidence has changed
A general quality-improvement goal used as the condition that triggers future architecture reconsideration
Any stakeholder question about the architecture, even when the question does not challenge a constraint or outcome
A measurable event, such as P95 latency or review load exceeding an agreed bound, that triggers reconsideration

architect-professional.explanation: A reversal condition turns uncertainty into a planned response. It identifies evidence that invalidates the current tradeoff and prompts a controlled decision review.

architect-professional.q: What is the capstone's primary deliverable?

options.text: A connected, evidence-linked architecture packet covering requirements, design, validation, rollout, and operations
A model-feature inventory mapping every available capability to the component where it could be enabled
An exam-alignment report linking architecture patterns to blueprint domains and practice scores
A comprehensive multi-agent diagram showing every available role, model route, integration, and communication path

architect-professional.explanation: Professional readiness requires connected decisions, contracts, controls, tests, rollout, ownership, and recovery. Complexity and feature lists do not prove that.

architect-professional.q: A candidate architecture has excellent average quality but one unverified authorization hard gate. What is the release decision?

options.text: Release because aggregate quality demonstrates that the remaining authorization risk is unlikely to affect most requests
Block release until the authorization control is implemented and verified at the execution boundary
Lower the authorization gate's weight so stronger aggregate quality can offset the missing evidence
Add a system instruction telling the model to avoid unauthorized actions, then monitor the pilot for violations

architect-professional.explanation: A hard gate represents a constraint that cannot be averaged away. Authorization must be proven at the execution boundary before exposure.

architect-professional.q: Why must a model or agent call trace back to a requirement?

options.text: Every requirement needs a model call because deterministic components are insufficient
A one-to-one mapping makes architecture ownership and implementation review easier across teams
Unjustified calls add cost, latency, attack surface, and maintenance without proven value
Each requirement should receive equal model-token allocation across capabilities

architect-professional.explanation: Architecture spends complexity to satisfy constraints and outcomes. A call with no requirement is capability bloat and should be removed or justified.

architect-professional.q: What makes a capstone evaluation representative?

options.text: It measures API availability, request latency, token use, and error rate because operational metrics are objective and comparable
It reproduces one successful end-to-end demonstration with the exact prompt, model, tools, and data intended for launch
It uses a large synthetic set of well-formed inputs so every component receives enough statistically consistent success cases
It covers task distribution, risk strata, ambiguity, stale data, attacks, dependency failures, quality, trajectory, latency, cost, and review

architect-professional.explanation: Representative evidence covers ordinary work and the failures the architecture must control, across both final outcomes and the trajectory that produced them.

architect-professional.q: Which statement best defends a deterministic workflow over an adaptive agent?

options.text: The path is known, strict latency and auditability are requirements, and evaluations show no value from adaptive planning
Deterministic workflows are categorically safer than agents, so requirements and evaluation evidence do not need to influence the choice
Adaptive agents consume more tokens in many trajectories, so token count alone establishes that a fixed workflow is the correct pattern
The team lacks Agent SDK experience, so a fixed workflow reduces implementation, testing, and delivery risk for this release

architect-professional.explanation: A strong defense connects the pattern to explicit requirements and evidence. It also leaves room to reverse the decision if the task distribution changes.

architect-professional.q: What proves an operational handoff in the capstone?

options.text: The pilot completes without a visible error, which demonstrates that the receiving owner will be able to handle future failures
The receiving owner can monitor, evaluate, contain, roll back, recover, and change the system using accepted evidence
The architect approves the final delivery packet and remains available to explain any undocumented operating assumption
The repository, architecture packet, dashboards, and runbooks exist in locations the receiving team can access

architect-professional.explanation: Handoff is demonstrated operating ability and accepted responsibility. Recovery drills, runbooks, access, evaluation, and ownership prove it.

architect-professional.q: A team wants Claude to handle open-ended customer research questions where the right sequence of searches can't be known in advance, and the number of tool calls needed varies per question. Which pattern fits best?

options.text: An augmented LLM — a single call enriched with retrieval and tools.
A fixed workflow with hardcoded steps.
An agent that dynamically decides which tools to call and when to stop.
A multi-agent pipeline with a rigid, unchanging three-step sequence.

architect-professional.explanation: An unpredictable, variable-length task with no enumerable path in advance is exactly where an agent's added autonomy is warranted. A fixed workflow can't flex to per-question variability, and a single augmented-LLM call can't span multiple dependent, dynamically-chosen tool calls.

architect-professional.q: A stakeholder insists on "the best possible" architecture without specifying what matters most. What's the right first move?

options.text: Build the most sophisticated multi-agent system available.
Ask which business pillar — efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, or SLA — matters most for this system, since that determines the tradeoffs.
Default to whatever pattern was used on the last project.
Pick the cheapest model tier and build up from there.

architect-professional.explanation: There is no single "best" architecture independent of what the business is optimizing for. Naming which pillar matters most is what lets the architect make and defend the actual design tradeoffs.

architect-professional.q: An architect decomposes "assess our exposure to the new privacy regulation" into three subtasks — EU customers, US customers, APAC customers. Each subtask returns a correct, well-researched answer, but the final assessment misses the regulation's reach into vendor sub-processors entirely. What went wrong?

options.text: The subtasks were executed incorrectly and need better prompts.
The decomposition itself was too narrow — the missing scope was never assigned to anyone, so no step could fail loudly and reveal the gap.
The model tier was too weak for regulatory analysis.
Decomposition was the wrong approach; this should have been one large prompt.

architect-professional.explanation: Every subtask succeeded at what it was assigned; the hole is in the assignment. Narrow decomposition fails silently precisely because correct execution of an incomplete breakdown produces confident, well-formed output. The fix is a coverage pass that checks the assembled result against the original question — not better subtask prompts (A), a bigger model (B), or abandoning decomposition (D), which would reintroduce the shallow-on-everything problem.

architect-professional.q: A single Claude call is asked to plan a multi-city trip, book flights, check budget constraints, and draft an itinerary document, all in one shot, and the results are inconsistent. What's the most likely architectural fix?

options.text: Add more examples to the single prompt.
Decompose the task into a workflow of separate, scoped steps — for example, budget check, then flight search, then itinerary drafting — each independently testable.
Switch to a larger, more capable model without changing the structure.
Reduce the temperature setting to zero.

architect-professional.explanation: Bundling several distinct, loosely related goals into one call produces shallow, inconsistent results because nothing forces the work to happen in a reliable order with clear inputs at each stage. Decomposing into a workflow creates checkpoints and testable steps; a bigger model doesn't fix a scope problem.

architect-professional.q: In a well-designed input → processing → output → feedback loop architecture, what is the purpose of the feedback loop specifically?

options.text: To let the system change its own goals without oversight.
To capture signal from real usage — corrections, outcomes, human review — and feed it back into prompts, tools, or evaluation so the system improves over time.
To intentionally increase latency for safety.
To bypass the need for evaluation entirely.

architect-professional.explanation: The feedback loop is what turns a static deployment into a system that improves — it routes real-world signal back into the parts of the architecture (prompts, tools, retrieval, evaluation) that can actually act on it.

architect-professional.q: Which two of the following are genuine signs that an agentic pattern is justified over a fixed workflow? (Select 2)

options.text: The number and order of steps needed varies unpredictably by input and can't be enumerated in advance.
The task is a fixed, five-step process that never changes.
The system needs to decide dynamically, based on intermediate results, which tool to call next.
Latency must be as low and predictable as possible.

architect-professional.explanation: Unpredictable step count/order and dynamic, results-dependent tool selection are the classic justifications for an agent loop. A fixed, unchanging process and a hard low-latency requirement both favor a predictable workflow instead.

architect-professional.q: Which of the following is a genuine cost of a multi-agent orchestration pattern compared to a single, well-scoped agent?

options.text: It always produces lower-quality answers.
More total tokens spent, since each agent re-establishes its own context, and a harder-to-debug failure surface across workers and the synthesis step.
It cannot be combined with tools at all.
It removes the need for evaluation.

architect-professional.explanation: Multi-agent orchestration's real costs are token overhead (repeated context per agent) and a wider failure surface to debug — a bad final answer could originate in any worker or in the synthesis step. It doesn't inherently lower quality or remove the need for tools or evaluation.

architect-professional.q: A company wants Claude to enable an entirely new customer offering that wasn't previously feasible with their existing team's capacity, rather than just speeding up an existing report. Which business value pillar does this best represent?

options.text: Efficiency
Transformation
Cost reduction alone
Performance SLA

architect-professional.explanation: Transformation is enabling work that wasn't previously possible or economical at all — distinct from efficiency, which speeds up or cheapens an existing process without changing what's possible.

architect-professional.q: An orchestrator-workers workflow is best suited to tasks where:

options.text: The subtasks are tightly coupled and must run in strict sequence with shared mutable state.
The subtasks are independent, can be explored in parallel, and their results synthesized afterward.
There is only ever one subtask to complete.
The task requires no tools at all.

architect-professional.explanation: Orchestrator-workers earns its overhead specifically when subtasks are independent enough to parallelize and later synthesize. Tightly coupled, strictly sequential work doesn't benefit from splitting across separate worker contexts.

architect-professional.q: A stakeholder asks for a Claude architecture to auto-approve small expense reports under $500 with no human review, citing "efficiency." Which tradeoff should the architect surface before proceeding?

options.text: None — efficiency justifies full automation regardless of the decision's stakes.
Whether the accuracy/risk profile of unreviewed financial approvals is acceptable given the SLA and the cost of an error, not just the time saved.
Whether the model in use is the newest available version.
Whether Opus or Haiku costs less per token.

architect-professional.explanation: Citing one pillar (efficiency) doesn't excuse skipping the tradeoff analysis against risk and cost-of-error — an architect's job is to surface that tradeoff explicitly, even for a seemingly low-value decision like small expense approvals.

architect-professional.q: A hospital network's COO says: "We want to use AI to reduce nurse burnout." Which response best reflects how an architect should translate a business problem into a solvable one?

options.text: Propose a multi-agent nursing assistant, since burnout is a complex, multi-faceted problem that needs a sophisticated architecture.

Ask what specific work is consuming nurses' time, what decision or artifact that work produces, what a wrong output would cost, and how quickly it's needed — then design against whichever of those is both burdensome and safely automatable.
Benchmark several model tiers on clinical reasoning and pick the highest scorer before proceeding.
Decline the engagement, since burnout is a management problem rather than a technical one.

architect-professional.explanation: "Reduce burnout" is a symptom, not a requirement — it names an outcome nobody has yet connected to a process. The four constraint questions (what decision it feeds, volume, cost of error, latency budget) are what convert it into something buildable, and will likely land on something narrow like shift-handoff note drafting. Jumping to a multi-agent design (A) picks a pattern before knowing the problem; benchmarking models (C) optimizes a decision that isn't yet on the table; declining (D) mistakes a badly-stated problem for no problem.

architect-professional.q: An architect reviews a two-year-old "fixed workflow" and finds it now contains 40+ conditional branches, added one edge case at a time, and no one on the team can fully describe its behavior. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: The workflow needs more branches to cover the remaining edge cases.
The task has outgrown the fixed-workflow pattern — the branching is approximating agent behavior badly, and the paths can no longer be enumerated, which was the pattern's whole justification.
The team should upgrade the model tier so the workflow makes fewer mistakes.
Nothing is wrong; branch count is not an architectural signal.

architect-professional.explanation: A workflow's justification is that its paths are enumerable, testable, and predictable. When branch growth destroys that property, the pattern is no longer earning its keep and is poorly imitating the dynamic decision-making an agent does natively. More branches (A) accelerates the problem; a stronger model (C) doesn't address control-flow complexity; and unbounded branch growth is precisely the signal the pattern choice needs revisiting (D).

architect-professional.q: An architect proposes replacing a client's requested agentic design with a fixed workflow. Which two arguments legitimately support that recommendation? (Select 2)

options.text: A workflow lets you state a latency SLA, because the step count is bounded rather than open-ended.
Workflows always produce higher-quality output than agents on any task.
A required compliance check can be guaranteed to run when it's a line of code, whereas an agent may skip a step it judges unnecessary.
Agents cannot be integrated with external tools or retrieval.

architect-professional.explanation: Bounded step count (enabling a real SLA) and hard guarantees on mandatory steps are the two concrete, defensible reasons to prefer a workflow where one suffices. Option B is false — on genuinely open-ended tasks an agent outperforms a workflow that can't express the task at all. Option D is simply wrong; tool use is central to agent patterns.

architect-professional.q: Two teams at the same insurer build Claude systems for claims. Team A auto-approves straightforward claims to cut cost per claim; Team B gives adjusters a drafting assistant so each closes more complex claims per week, with headcount unchanged. What best explains why their architectures share almost nothing?

options.text: One team is more technically skilled than the other.
They're optimizing different business value pillars — efficiency versus productivity — and the pillar determines the guardrails, the latency budget, and whether a human is in the loop at all.
Team B's approach is simply an earlier, less mature version of Team A's.
Insurance claims cannot be architected consistently, so divergence is expected.

architect-professional.explanation: Efficiency (A) removes the human, so it demands airtight guardrails, a confidence threshold, and an approval audit trail.
