Early course corrections and a working reporting cadence are the healthy pattern, not a warning sign.

architect-professional.q: An architecture document was accurate at handoff a year ago but has never been updated since, despite three significant changes to the system. What's the risk?

options.text: None, since it was accurate when written.
The document goes stale and becomes untrustworthy exactly when someone needs it most, the same way an unmaintained configuration confidently serves outdated information.
Architecture documents don't need to reflect changes after handoff.
The system will automatically update the document.

architect-professional.explanation: Documentation that isn't maintained through the iteration phase drifts from reality — and the moment someone relies on it (an incident, an onboarding, a redesign) is exactly when a stale document does the most damage.

architect-professional.q: Discovery on "automate our ticket triage" reveals the support director means priority assignment, the engineering manager means routing to the right team, and the funding VP means deflecting tickets from engineering entirely. All three approved the requirements document. What does this illustrate?

options.text: The stakeholders were not paying attention when they approved the document.

Consensus on an abstraction — an abstract noun like 'triage' lets each listener resolve the ambiguity in their own favor and hear their own answer, so agreement on the phrase masks disagreement on the thing.
The requirements document was too long for stakeholders to read carefully.
Ticket triage is inherently too vague to build a system for.

architect-professional.explanation: This is why discovery insists on concreteness: never leave without a written statement of what the system will output, to whom, and what they'll do with it. Approval of "automate ticket triage" is real approval — of three different systems. Attention (A) and document length (C) aren't the mechanism; each stakeholder read it and agreed with what they understood. And triage is perfectly buildable (D) once you know which one you mean.

architect-professional.q: A prototype answered in 600ms against 200 documents on a laptop. That number appeared in a slide, and "sub-second response" became the documented SLA. Production runs 40,000 documents with concurrency, a reranker, and a compliance audit write; p95 is 2.1s. What's the underlying failure?

options.text: The team should not have added the reranker or the audit write.

A prototype measurement escaped into a slide and hardened into a commitment nobody negotiated — the conditions that produced 600ms didn't survive to launch, and were never stated alongside the number.
The production infrastructure is under-provisioned and needs scaling.
The SLA should simply be deleted from the documentation.

architect-professional.explanation: Nothing went wrong technically — every addition was correct, and each one cost latency the original number never accounted for. The failure is that an observation became a promise by being written down. The defense is stating conditions with the number every time. Removing the reranker and audit write (A) discards correct work to protect an unnegotiated figure; scaling (C) can't recover a 3.5x gap caused by added work; deleting the SLA (D) evades the renegotiation.

architect-professional.q: An architect must explain to a non-technical CFO why adding a reranker raised p95 latency from 800ms to 1.4s while reducing wrong answers. Which two properties should the explanation have? (Select 2)

options.text: Confirm the complaint is accurate — it did get slower — rather than reframing it as normal variance.
Include the technical mechanism (cross-encoder over the top-50 candidate set) so the CFO understands the engineering.
State the tradeoff in units the CFO can weigh, and hand back the decision as one that's genuinely theirs to make.
Assert that the tradeoff was technically necessary so the decision doesn't get re-litigated.

architect-professional.explanation: Confirming the true complaint preserves credibility, and framing the tradeoff in decidable terms gives the sponsor a decision they're entitled to make. The mechanism (B) is the wrong altitude — accurate and unusable, which is performing rather than informing. Claiming necessity (D) is false: it was a judgment call, and dressing a judgment as a constraint removes the CFO's legitimate say.

architect-professional.q: A project is 10% behind on its accuracy target. Why is communicating this in week 2 categorically different from it surfacing at the milestone review, given identical facts?

options.text: It isn't different — the facts are the same, so the conversation should be the same.
In week 2 there are options, and at the review there's only an explanation. Alignment economics are nonlinear because early corrections arrive while the situation is still steerable.
Week 2 reports are less likely to be read by senior stakeholders.
The 10% gap will probably close on its own before the review.

architect-professional.explanation: The facts being identical is precisely the point: what changed is the option set. Early, the stakeholder can rescope, extend, or accept; at the review they can only be told. That's why small continuous corrections are cheaper in trust and in rework — not because they sound better, but because they arrive when something can still be done. Option C hopes for less scrutiny, and D is the reasoning that produces milestone surprises.

architect-professional.q: A design document states: "We used a fixed workflow." A better version states: "We used a fixed workflow rather than an agent because the four steps were known and the compliance check had to be guaranteed to run." What does the second version give a future reader that the first doesn't?

options.text: A longer document, which signals more thorough work.
The condition under which the decision should be revisited — when the steps stop being known — so the next architect can tell whether a constraint still applies rather than guessing.
Legal protection if the architecture later fails.
A record of who on the team preferred which option.

architect-professional.explanation: Rejected alternatives and their reasoning encode the decision's expiry conditions. Without them the next architect either preserves a constraint that no longer applies or removes one that still does, with no way to tell which. Length (A) isn't a virtue, legal protection (C) isn't the purpose, and individual preferences (D) are noise compared to the reasoning.

architect-professional.q: Which lifecycle phase does an architect most commonly abandon, and why is that specific gap costly?

options.text: Discovery — because stakeholders resist structured questioning.

Monitoring — architects often leave at handoff, which is exactly the phase with the least information and the most consequence: nothing has met real traffic, so every SLA is an estimate and every guardrail untested.
Design — because it's the phase most often delegated to engineering.
Iteration — because systems rarely change after launch.

architect-professional.explanation: Leaving at handoff means never learning which design decisions held under real conditions — the architect loses their own feedback loop, and the project loses the person who knows why each guardrail exists at the moment those guardrails first face traffic. Discovery (A) and design (C) are the phases architects are most present for, and systems change constantly after launch (D), which is why iteration matters.

architect-professional.q: An engineering team receives a handoff document describing what was built but not why each guardrail exists. Six months later they remove a confidence-threshold check during a latency optimization. What's the root cause?

options.text: The engineering team acted carelessly and should have asked before removing it.

The handoff documentation failed to record the guardrails that must be preserved and their purpose — a constraint whose reason isn't written down looks like unexplained overhead to whoever is optimizing.
Confidence thresholds should be enforced in infrastructure, not application code.
The team should not have been permitted to modify the system without the original architect.

architect-professional.explanation: Handoff's job is to let a team that wasn't in the room operate the system correctly, which means the guardrails and SLAs that must survive — with their reasons. An undocumented constraint is indistinguishable from dead weight to someone optimizing in good faith. Blaming the team (A) ignores that they had no way to know; the enforcement layer (C) is a separate question; and requiring the original architect forever (D) is what documentation exists to avoid.

architect-professional.q: A team lets each developer configure their own Claude Code permissions and available MCP servers independently, with no shared baseline. What's the risk?

options.text: None, since flexibility is always better.
Inconsistent guardrails across the team — one developer's environment might grant broader tool access or weaker permission checks than the team's actual policy intends.
Claude Code cannot be configured per-developer at all.
It will automatically synchronize settings across the team.

architect-professional.explanation: Without a shared baseline, team-scale tooling drifts the same way ad hoc configuration drifts anywhere else — some developers end up with broader access or weaker checks than the team's actual policy intends, purely by accident of individual setup.

architect-professional.q: An AI-assisted debugging tool is asked to root-cause a production incident, but the system has no structured logging or metrics, only unstructured free-text logs with no timestamps or request correlation. What limits the tool's usefulness here?

options.text: Nothing, AI tooling doesn't need structured data to be effective.
It has no better evidence to work from than a human would have — AI-assisted triage is only as good as the observability data underlying it.
It will fabricate the missing structure automatically and reliably.
Unstructured logs are actually preferred for AI-assisted debugging.

architect-professional.explanation: AI-assisted triage depends on the same observability investment a human investigator would need — structured logs and correlated metrics. Without them, the tooling has no better evidence to reason from than a person staring at the same raw logs.

architect-professional.q: An AI-generated test suite for a new module reports 90% coverage with every test passing. What should a reviewer check before treating that as meaningful?

options.text: Whether coverage can be pushed above 95%.
Whether the tests assert what the code should do rather than what it currently does — tests written from the implementation pass forever, including after someone breaks the intended behavior.
Whether the tests run fast enough to stay in CI.
Whether the test file naming matches team conventions.

architect-professional.explanation: Coverage measures what was executed, not what was checked. A test asserting current behavior is a snapshot, not a specification — it will pass through the exact regression it appears to guard against. Raising coverage (A) compounds the problem, and runtime (C) and naming (D) are real but minor next to tests that can't fail when they should.

architect-professional.q: What's the most reliable way to ensure every developer's Claude Code environment reflects the same permission policy and tool availability?

options.text: Ask each developer to configure it individually to their own preference.
Standardize the shared configuration — permissions, available MCP servers, conventions — at the team level rather than leaving it to individual setup.
Disable all tooling to avoid inconsistency.
Give every developer administrator-level access by default for convenience.

architect-professional.explanation: Team-level standardization is what keeps guardrails consistent across developers — individual configuration invites drift, and disabling tooling or granting broad default access both overcorrect in the wrong direction.

architect-professional.q: Which developer task is the strongest fit for AI-assisted tooling?

options.text: Deciding the final architecture for a critical security-sensitive component with no review.
Generating a first-pass test suite for a new module that a developer then reviews and refines.
Automatically merging code with no human review.
Making the final call on a production incident's root cause with no verification.

architect-professional.explanation: A first-pass test suite that a human then reviews and refines is exactly the pattern that earns AI-assisted tooling its place — fast to produce, cheap to verify, with a human still owning the final judgment. The other options remove human ownership from decisions that need it.

architect-professional.q: AI-assisted tooling drafts a full first-pass code review with several comments. What remains true regardless of how good the draft is?

options.text: The human reviewer still owns the merge decision and needs to verify the comments are actually correct.
No human review is needed once the AI has commented.
The review comments should be applied automatically without inspection.
The developer who wrote the code should not see the AI's comments.

architect-professional.explanation: AI-assisted tooling shifts where a developer's time goes, from drafting to review, but it doesn't remove the ownership step — a human reviewer still needs to verify the comments and owns the merge decision.

architect-professional.q: AI-assisted triage correlates a production error spike with a deploy that happened ten minutes earlier. What's the appropriate next step?

options.text: Automatically roll back the deploy with no further verification.
Treat the correlation as a hypothesis to verify, and have a human confirm the root cause before deciding the fix, especially if customer data is involved.
Ignore the correlation since AI-generated hypotheses are never useful.
Disable logging to reduce noise for next time.

architect-professional.explanation: AI-assisted triage is valuable for surfacing a hypothesis fast, but confirming the root cause and deciding the fix, especially with production or customer data at stake, remains a human responsibility.

architect-professional.q: Which two factors make AI-assisted debugging triage effective? (Select 2)

options.text: Structured logging and clear metrics that give the tooling real evidence to correlate against.
Removing all human verification of the AI's root-cause hypothesis.
A human who confirms the root cause and owns the fix decision.
Unstructured, uncorrelated free-text logs with no timestamps.

architect-professional.explanation: Effective AI-assisted triage depends on good observability data to reason from and a human who still confirms the conclusion — removing verification or relying on unstructured, uncorrelated logs both undermine it.

architect-professional.q: Eleven of twelve developers configure their Claude Code permissions sensibly. The twelfth, blocked late on a Friday, approves everything so the tooling stops prompting — and leaves it that way. No incident occurs. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Nothing — no incident means no problem, and the developer unblocked themselves efficiently.
Configuration drift produces no symptom until it produces an incident, so the team's real security posture is now set by its least patient member on their worst day, and nobody knows.
The eleven other developers configured their environments incorrectly.
Claude Code should not prompt for permission at all, since prompting causes this behavior.

architect-professional.explanation: The absence of an incident is exactly why this survives: there's no error, no alert, and no signal of any kind. That's the argument for a shared baseline rather than individual setup. Option A mistakes the absence of a symptom for the absence of a problem; the eleven did fine (C); and removing prompts entirely (D) discards the control instead of standardizing it.

architect-professional.q: A team argues that adopting AI-assisted debugging tooling will compensate for their lack of structured logging, since the AI can read raw logs quickly. What's wrong with this reasoning?

options.text: Nothing — reading large volumes of unstructured text quickly is a genuine strength.

The dependency runs the other way: AI-assisted triage is a multiplier on observability you already have, and multiplying zero gives zero. With no structured logs, the tooling has no better evidence than a human staring at the same text.
AI tooling cannot process log files at all.
The team should adopt the tooling first and add logging afterward if it proves insufficient.

architect-professional.explanation: AI-assisted triage isn't a workaround for missing observability — it accelerates correlation across evidence that exists. Without timestamps, request correlation, or structure, there's nothing to correlate. Speed of reading (A) doesn't create the causal links the evidence never captured, tooling can read logs (C), and adopting first (D) defers the investment the tooling depends on.

architect-professional.q: An architect reviews a proposal to give the team's AI coding tooling a service credential with production database write access, so it can help debug data issues — even though none of the developers have that access themselves. What's the objection?

options.text: The tooling will be slower with a broader credential.

A developer's AI tooling shouldn't default to broader permissions than the developer's own role has — a tool that reaches production when its operator can't is a privilege-escalation path with a helpful interface.
Production debugging should never involve AI-assisted tooling.
The credential should be shared across all teams for consistency.

architect-professional.explanation: This is the least-privilege principle from Integration applied to developer tooling, and the specific hazard is that the tool becomes a way to do what its operator is not authorized to do. Performance (A) is irrelevant; AI tooling can legitimately assist production debugging within the operator's own permissions (C); and broadening the credential's reach (D) worsens the exact problem.

architect-professional.q: A support team wants answers to product questions grounded in a 300-page manual. Questions are single-turn, and the manual is updated monthly. What is the simplest sufficient architecture?

options.text: An augmented LLM: retrieval over the manual feeding a single model call that cites the passages it used
An autonomous agent that browses the manual page by page
A multi-agent research system with a planner and three specialists
A model fine-tuned on the manual every month

architect-professional.explanation: One well-scoped, grounded call meets the requirement, so retrieval plus a single call is the simplest sufficient pattern (A). C and B add autonomy the task doesn't need, with the cost and latency to match. Monthly fine-tuning (D) is heavy, slower to update than re-indexing, and gives no citations.

architect-professional.q: Which architecture proposal for an invoice-processing assistant is complete?

options.text: Extraction with schema validation; posting to the ERP; a dashboard of monthly volume

Email intake and OCR; extraction with schema validation; posting to the ERP with an exceptions queue; per-field accuracy evals, user corrections and monitoring fed back into prompt and model decisions
Email intake and OCR; extraction with the most capable model; posting to the ERP
Email intake; a multi-agent extraction team; posting to the ERP; a launch announcement

architect-professional.explanation: A complete architecture has input, processing, output and a feedback loop that turns evals, user corrections and monitoring into design changes (B). C has no feedback loop. A has no input stage, and a volume dashboard measures activity without feeding quality back. D adds complexity and still has no feedback loop.

architect-professional.q: Two designs meet the accuracy target. Design 1 uses the top tier: p95 latency 6 seconds, $0.09 per request. Design 2 routes between the fast and balanced tiers: p95 latency 2 seconds, $0.02 per request. The client's stated constraint is a 3-second p95 SLA at 2 million requests a month. Which design, and why?

options.text: Run both in production indefinitely
Postpone the decision until a newer model is released
Design 1, for quality headroom
Design 2, because it meets the latency SLA and the cost pillar at the same accuracy

architect-professional.explanation: When both options meet accuracy, the stated business constraint decides, and only Design 2 meets the 3-second SLA, at about $40,000 a month against $180,000 (D). C breaks the SLA. A doubles cost and complexity for no reason. B ignores a decision the data already supports.

architect-professional.q: A due-diligence system must analyze each target company's financials, legal filings and press coverage. The three analyses are independent, and each needs different tools and sources. Which design fits?

options.text: Three separate systems whose reports nobody combines
One agent holding all the tools for all three analyses
An orchestrator with three scoped subagents running in parallel, followed by a synthesis step
One agent doing the three analyses in sequence

architect-professional.explanation: Independent subtasks with different tool needs are what justifies decomposition: each subagent gets a narrow toolset and its own context, and the orchestrator merges the results (C). B is capability bloat. D gives up parallelism and mixes three contexts. A skips the synthesis the client actually needs.

architect-professional.q: A global retailer's policy assistant covers 14 regions. Each region's policies differ and are owned by different teams. Answers mix rules from different regions. What is the best design change?

options.text: Put all 14 regions' policies in every request
Partition by data domain: tag documents with their region and filter retrieval by the user's region before semantic search
Fourteen agents that negotiate with each other on every question
Ask users to mention their region and change nothing else

architect-professional.explanation: The data has a clean partition, so filtering on region metadata keeps other regions' rules out of the context (B). C adds coordination machinery to a retrieval problem. A is context stuffing. D leaves the mixed retrieval in place.

architect-professional.q: Which TWO workloads benefit most from prompt caching? (Select TWO)
architect-professional.domain: D2 Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering

options.text: Single requests shorter than the minimum cacheable length
Requests whose first line is the current timestamp
An agent loop that resends the same 12,000-token system prompt and tool definitions on every turn
An endpoint where many users ask questions about the same 50-page policy within minutes of each other
A weekly job that sends one unique 3,000-token prompt

architect-professional.explanation: Caching pays off when a long, stable prefix repeats within the cache lifetime (C, D). A weekly unique prompt (E) never repeats in time. A timestamp at the start (B) breaks the prefix on every request. Prompts under the minimum length (A) are never cached.

architect-professional.q: An eligibility step must apply six interacting rules. Accuracy is the priority, and the latency budget is generous. Which prompting approach fits?
architect-professional.domain: D2 Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering

options.text: A lower temperature
Few-shot examples alone, with no stated rules
Have the model reason through the rules step by step (or enable thinking) before deciding, with each rule stated as an explicit criterion, then validate the decision
A zero-shot prompt kept as short as possible

architect-professional.explanation: Multi-step logic benefits from explicit reasoning before the answer, and the generous latency budget covers its cost (C). Zero-shot (D) suits simple, unambiguous tasks. Examples (B) teach format and edge cases, and six interacting rules still need to be stated. Temperature (A) adds no reasoning.

architect-professional.q: An enterprise assistant's system prompt has grown to 60,000 tokens of procedures for 40 business processes, and most requests need one or two of them. Latency and cost are high, and instruction-following has slipped. What is the best restructuring?
architect-professional.domain: D2 Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering

options.text: Build 40 separate assistants and make users choose
Move to a model with a larger context window
Mark the most important procedures in capitals
Keep the system prompt to the core role and rules, and package each procedure as a Skill or retrievable module that loads only when relevant

architect-professional.explanation: Loading procedures on demand keeps the context small and focused, which improves attention, cost and latency together (D). Emphasis (C) doesn't shrink the prompt. A bigger window (B) holds more of the same dilution. A moves the routing problem onto users.

architect-professional.q: Downstream systems consume the assistant's JSON, and occasional schema violations cause failed transactions. Which change addresses this at the source, and what still needs checking?
architect-professional.domain: D2 Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering

options.text: Structured outputs with the integration schema, which guarantees schema-valid JSON, plus semantic validation of the values and handling of the refusal and `max_tokens` stop reasons
A stronger instruction to follow the schema
A retry loop and nothing else
A regex that repairs broken JSON

architect-professional.explanation: Constrained decoding removes schema violations at the source, and semantic checks plus stop-reason handling cover what it doesn't guarantee (A). Retries (C) and instructions (B) reduce failures without eliminating them. Regex repair (D) guesses at intent and can corrupt data quietly.

architect-professional.q: A procurement agent must get quotes from a supplier's own AI agent, which runs on the supplier's systems with its own tools, policies and reasoning. Which integration mechanism fits?

options.text: Agent-to-agent delegation over a defined protocol, with explicit request and response contracts, authentication, and failure isolation
A direct API call to Claude with the supplier's price list pasted into the prompt
An MCP server that gives your agent direct access to the supplier's database
A shared system prompt that both companies edit

architect-professional.explanation: Two autonomous systems with separate owners, tools and policies call for delegation between agents, with contracts and isolation so either side can fail independently (A). C bypasses the supplier's agent and policies and assumes access you won't get. B works only if you already have current prices, which is what you're asking for. D merges two organizations' control into one prompt.

architect-professional.q: One internal app sends support tickets to Claude for tagging. One team owns it, and no reuse is planned. A platform engineer proposes building an MCP server first. What is the right assessment?

options.text: Fine-tune a tagging model instead
Build the MCP server, since every integration should use MCP
Use a direct API integration now; MCP adds a protocol layer and maintenance without a reuse need, so revisit it if other surfaces need the capability
Use agent-to-agent delegation

architect-professional.explanation: MCP pays off when one capability serves many clients or surfaces, and one app with one owner is the direct-API case (C). B adds maintenance for a benefit that doesn't exist yet. D adds autonomous-system machinery to a single call. A skips a simpler option that works.

architect-professional.q: Which TWO observations are signs of capability bloat in a production agent? (Select TWO)

options.text: Two tools have overlapping descriptions, and both plausibly handle 'find a customer'
Each subagent's tools are scoped to its responsibility
The reporting agent uses read-only credentials
It exposes 45 tools, and invocation logs show only 9 ever used
Tool descriptions state when not to use each tool

architect-professional.explanation: Unused tools that ship with every request (D) and overlapping tools that blur selection (A) are classic signs of bloat. Scoped toolsets (B), read-only credentials for a read-only job (C) and boundary statements in descriptions (E) are the cure.

architect-professional.q: An agent connects to six MCP servers exposing 300 tools, and every request front-loads all of their definitions. Tool selection is poor and costs are high. What is the best fix?

options.text: Add more examples to the system prompt
Shorten every tool description to one line
Move to a model with a larger context window
Progressive discovery: load tool definitions on demand (for example with tool search and deferred loading), and give each agent only the servers its responsibility needs

architect-professional.explanation: Loading tools as the agent narrows in cuts tokens and improves selection accuracy, and scoping servers per responsibility removes tools that never belonged (D). A bigger window (C) holds the same noise. One-line descriptions (B) make selection worse. Examples (A) add tokens without reducing the tool count.

architect-professional.q: A company assistant answers questions over the document store using a service account that can read every folder, including HR and legal. A contractor asked about salaries and got an answer. What is the root fix?

options.text: Remove HR documents from the index
Run retrieval and tools with the calling user's identity and permissions, and attribute every access to that user in the logs
Add a system-prompt rule: 'Never discuss salaries'
Filter out responses that contain the word 'salary'

architect-professional.explanation: The shared over-privileged account erased per-user authorization and made every access unattributable, so the fix is acting as the caller (B). C is a probabilistic patch, A breaks legitimate HR use, and D is easy to get around and blocks legitimate answers.

architect-professional.q: Engineers search an internal knowledge base with exact error codes such as 'E-4031.' Semantic search returns conceptually similar documents about other errors. What is the best fix?

options.text: A larger embedding model
Hybrid search: keyword matching for exact identifiers combined with semantic search, then re-ranking
Retrieve more chunks per query
Fine-tune the generation model on error codes

architect-professional.explanation: Exact identifiers such as error codes and SKUs need keyword matching, which hybrid search adds alongside semantic retrieval (B). Better embeddings (A) still treat codes as fuzzy meaning. More chunks (C) add noise. The generation model (D) can't fix documents that were never retrieved.

architect-professional.q: A contract-extraction service has three complaints: wrong values, slow responses at peak hours, and a rising monthly bill. Which THREE metrics should the monitoring plan track? (Select THREE)

options.text: Field-level accuracy against a labeled dataset
Average response length
p95 and p99 latency
Number of prompt revisions per month
Cost per document and tokens per task

architect-professional.explanation: Each complaint maps to a metric: wrong values to accuracy (A), slowness to tail latency (C), and the bill to cost per unit of work (E). Prompt revision counts (D) and response length (B) measure activity, and neither shows whether the complaints are fixed.

architect-professional.q: A team tuned its prompt against the same 200 examples it uses to report accuracy. Testing shows 98%, and production shows 84%. What went wrong, and what is the fix?

options.text: The eval set leaked into prompt development and inflated the score; tune on a separate development set and report on a held-out set that mirrors production
The model is too small; upgrade the tier
Production traffic is low quality; filter it
200 examples is too few; add 20 more of the same kind

architect-professional.explanation: Tuning against the test set overfits to it, so the score stops predicting production (A). C blames the data the system has to handle. B changes the model without fixing the measurement. D keeps the same leak with a slightly bigger set.

architect-professional.q: A team wants to ship a new prompt, new retrieval settings and a tier change together, because 'it felt better in 15 spot checks.' What is the correct approach?

options.text: Run 15 more spot checks
Ask the stakeholders which version they prefer
Test one variable at a time with a success metric and sample size set in advance, then ship each change only on a significant result
Ship all three, since the spot checks were positive

architect-professional.explanation: A clean experiment changes one variable and decides on a metric chosen in advance (C). With three changes at once (D), a win or a loss can't be attributed to anything. Preference (B) and more spot checks (A) are still the feels-better method.

architect-professional.q: Traces show the correct policy passages are retrieved, yet answers still state the wrong refund window. Where is the failure, and what is the first fix?

options.text: Raise the number of retrieved passages
The index is stale: rebuild it
Retrieval failure: re-chunk and re-embed the corpus
Generation is poorly grounded: tighten the instructions to answer only from the retrieved passages and cite them, and evaluate faithfulness

architect-professional.explanation: When the right documents arrive and the answer is still wrong, the failure sits in generation and grounding (D). C and B fix retrieval, which the traces show is working. A adds noise to a context that already contains the answer.

architect-professional.q: Answers about leave policies leave out exceptions. Traces show the retrieved chunks contain the rule sentence, while the exception sits in the next paragraph, which isn't retrieved. What is the best fix?

options.text: Retrieve 30 chunks instead of 5
Move to a more capable model
Tell the model to remember that policies have exceptions
Re-chunk along the document's structure (whole sections) with some overlap, so rules and their exceptions stay together

architect-professional.explanation: Chunks smaller than the unit of meaning split rules from their qualifiers, so structure-aware chunking fixes the retrieval unit (D). More chunks (A) might catch the exception along with plenty of noise. No model (B) can use a paragraph it never receives, and an instruction (C) can't supply the missing text.

architect-professional.q: An agent reads inbound customer emails and can issue refunds. Which TWO controls are deterministic, as opposed to prompt-based? (Select TWO)

options.text: An output filter that blocks any reply containing a full account number
Few-shot examples of the agent declining suspicious requests
A system-prompt rule: 'Never issue large refunds'
A persona instruction: 'You are a careful agent'
Tool permissions that cap a refund at $100 per call and send larger amounts for human approval

architect-professional.explanation: Permission limits (E) and output filtering (A) are enforced in code, whatever the model decides. C, D and B shape behavior probabilistically, and a cleverly written email can talk the model past them.

architect-professional.q: A moderation pipeline handles 500,000 low-risk comments a day and occasionally receives legal threats. Which human-in-the-loop design fits?

options.text: Have a human review every comment
Automate routine decisions with sampled QA, and route legal threats and cases below system-set thresholds to human reviewers
Remove humans entirely
Let the model escalate whenever its self-reported confidence is low

architect-professional.explanation: Humans go where the risk is high, and sampling covers the routine volume (B). Reviewing everything (A) destroys the efficiency case. C leaves legal threats unhandled. Self-reported confidence (D) is poorly calibrated, so the thresholds have to be set by the system.

architect-professional.q: A US telehealth company with patients in the US and Germany plans to use Claude to summarize clinical notes. Which TWO frameworks apply? (Select TWO)

options.text: FedRAMP
HIPAA, for US patients' health information
GDPR, for the personal data of patients in the EU
None, since Claude is a third-party service
Only HIPAA, since the company is based in the US

architect-professional.explanation: The framework follows the data type and the jurisdiction: US health data brings HIPAA (B), and processing EU residents' personal data brings GDPR wherever the company is based (C). FedRAMP (A) covers cloud services for US federal agencies. E ignores the German patients, and D confuses using a vendor with being exempt.

architect-professional.q: Your observability stack stores full prompts and responses, including customer personal data, in a log platform that 300 engineers can read. What is the risk, and what is the fix?

options.text: Data leakage through logs: redact personal data before logging, restrict access to the people who need it, and set a retention limit
Ask the model to leave personal data out of its responses
Encrypt the stored logs and leave access as it is
No risk, because the logs are internal

architect-professional.explanation: Logs and traces are a leakage channel, so the fix minimizes what's stored and who can see it (A). Internal access (D) still exposes customer data to hundreds of people. Encryption with unchanged access (C) protects the storage while every reader still sees the data. B leaves the personal data in the prompts, and the model can't be relied on to keep it out of responses.

architect-professional.q: A vice president asks you to 'make customer support better with AI.' What should you produce first?

options.text: A comparison of model benchmark scores
A working prototype to show next week
Discovery outputs: a measurable success criterion, a constraint inventory, a data and access map, a stakeholder map with decision owners, and a baseline of the current process
A signed vendor contract

architect-professional.explanation: Professional engagements start with discovery, because every later design choice depends on what success means and which constraints apply (C). A prototype (B) built without discovery answers a question nobody has defined. Benchmarks (A) and contracts (D) come after the requirements are known.

architect-professional.q: Stakeholders ask for a guarantee that the assistant 'never gives a wrong answer.' What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Commit only to 99.9% uptime
Promise 100% accuracy to secure approval
Refuse to set any accuracy target

Commit to measured targets, such as at least 96% accuracy per slice on a held-out set with an error budget, escalation paths and a remediation plan, and explain that LLM outputs have a measurable error rate

architect-professional.explanation: Probabilistic systems get SLAs built on measured rates, error budgets and remediation (D). B sets up a broken promise. C leaves stakeholders nothing to hold the system to. Uptime (A) says nothing about answer quality.

architect-professional.q: Which statement best communicates a model-tier recommendation to business stakeholders?

options.text: 'We chose the newest model available.'
'The top tier scores higher on industry benchmarks.'

'The balanced tier resolves 91% of tickets at $0.02 each, and the top tier resolves 93% at $0.08. At a million tickets a month, the extra two points cost about $60,000 a month, so we recommend the balanced tier with escalation for complex tickets.'
'The balanced tier is fine.'

architect-professional.explanation: Architect-level communication puts the trade-off in business terms: outcome, cost, and the recommendation that follows from them (C). B is engineering language with no business meaning. D gives no basis for the decision, and A offers novelty as a reason.

architect-professional.q: Which TWO artifacts belong in the handoff to the team that will operate the system? (Select TWO)

options.text: The architect's personal working notes
The kickoff slide deck
A raw export of the project chat channel
Runbooks covering escalation paths and known failure modes
Eval baselines and an inventory of prompts and their versions

architect-professional.explanation: Operators need to know how to respond to problems (D) and what normal looks like, along with what is deployed (E). Personal notes (A), kickoff slides (B) and raw chat (C) aren't operational documentation.

architect-professional.q: Claude Code runs in your CI pipeline, and the team agrees it must never run git push or curl anywhere the repository is used. Where should this restriction live?

options.text: Each developer's `~/.claude/settings.json`
Deny rules in the committed project settings, such as `Bash(git push *)` and `Bash(curl *)`, which the client enforces
A wiki page
A `CLAUDE.md` instruction

architect-professional.explanation: Permission rules in version-controlled project settings apply everywhere the repository runs, CI included, and the client enforces them (B). User settings (A) don't reach CI or other developers. `CLAUDE.md` (D) is guidance the model weighs. A wiki (C) is invisible to the tooling.

architect-professional.q: A platform team built a code-review subagent and a release-notes skill that every repository in the company should use, in the same version. What is the best way to distribute them?

options.text: Package them as a plugin (or deploy them through managed settings), so every developer gets the same versioned definitions
Post the prompt text in a chat channel for developers to copy
Ask each developer to copy the files into `~/.claude/`
Paste both into every repository's `CLAUDE.md`

architect-professional.explanation: Plugins bundle skills and subagents for distribution, and managed settings can push them to the whole organization, which keeps one maintained version (A). Copy-and-paste distribution (B, C) drifts as soon as the originals change. `CLAUDE.md` (D) holds always-on instructions and can't define a subagent or an on-demand skill.
